en: Preface to the Verses on the Life and Deeds of Śākyamuni Tathāgata Composed by Yi Sŏkki,
Grand Master for the Promotion of Merit, Vice Director of the Secretariat, Acting Minister of the Office of Works,
and Director of the Institute for Advanced Learning, with authority over the compilation of imperial edicts.

Now, as for those who practice the Way of the Confucians: although they may not yet have exhausted the source of the Five Constant Virtues, if they practice them—knowing that the sages and King Wenxuan established their teachings for the world as the foundational vehicle and inner sanctum—and explain them roughly when questioned, they may be called Confucians.
It is the same for those who follow the Śākya: having abandoned their secular surnames to join the Śākya clan, they take the Tathāgata, their original teacher, as their guide.

The great cause for appearing in the world to perform transformative teachings must first be detailed in full; only then can one be called a son of the Śākya. Alas, there has never been a second such person.
Even if there were, how could one have ever heard or seen even a fraction of their deeds? Now, for the first time, there is Master Mo from Xing Shan, whose style name is Wuji.
He is a man of simplicity without artifice, whose appearance accords with his inner heart. In his youth, he traveled to Mount Tiantai, where he specialized in...

I have meticulously refined the provisional and the middle within the emptiness [of the Three Truths], personally recording the traces of the Tathāgata’s deeds. I have compiled them in five-character verse, adding annotations to each line.

These two scrolls are intended to be embroidered and carved into woodblocks for wide dissemination. As for one who possesses broad learning and comprehensive mastery, they would recognize the phoenix by its feathers upon seeing this.
Furthermore, regarding the lineage of Śākyamuni, I have not yet studied it in the detail that was spoken from the Golden Mouth.
How could I dare set hand or foot within it? There is nothing more that can be done. I shall merely praise his powerful memory and his refined exposition.
Written on the fourth day of the fourth month of the Gengwu year of the Dazhuan era of the Great Yuan, by the Elder Heiyuan at Keting.
Verses on the Life and Deeds of Śākyamuni Tathāgata (with Preface), composed by the late scholar of the Tiantai school, Fuan Wuji. In examining this in detail:

the Dharma-nature is perfectly interfused and without dual characteristics; how could it harbor distinctions between the primary and secondary realms, or the faculties and their objects? True Suchness is pure...

There is but a single source; how could it be divided into self and other, or sentient beings and Buddhas? Yet sentient beings are oblivious to this wondrous principle, and for many kalpas have concealed their own spiritual radiance.
Though they constantly dwell within the treasury of the three virtues, they remain perpetually ignorant of it; though they lie upon the bed of suchness, they likewise do not realize it.
Therefore, I, the Muni, take pity on those who are thus deluded and inverted, wishing to entrust them with the treasure within their own homes.
Furthermore, he revealed the pearl within his robe; thus, though not coming, he came, spreading clouds of his body throughout the Sahā world.
Though not speaking, he spoke, nourishing the rain of Dharma upon the parched earth of the Vojakya. For forty-nine years, he established more than three hundred assemblies;

though not delivering beings, he delivered all conscious beings who were at their limit. Though not entering extinction, he entered extinction, passing into *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*. His skillful means are inconceivable.
Reflect upon this: how can the extent of his benefit be described by mere analogy? From the twin śāla trees until today, nearly two thousand three hundred years have passed;
from the Five Indias to this land, a distance of sixty-eight thousand *li* has been traversed.

Yet his lingering influence still vibrates afar, dispelling the thick clouds of affliction; his residual grace moistens the distant reaches, bringing glory to even withered things. Vast indeed is his compassion!
...the ocean. How majestic is the mountain of benevolent virtue! Alas, we sentient beings, due to the conditions of our fundamental karma, have wandered through various realms;
we failed early on to hear the teachings of the Brahma-voice, nor did we encounter the time of the True Dharma.
Suddenly, we were born into the hardships of the final age, and moreover, our natures are exceedingly stubborn and unruly. Yet, fortunately, we have received [your] compassion.
I, Hua, have presumptuously joined the ranks of the Śākya disciples. My appearance may resemble that of a follower of the Way, yet my conduct is entirely contrary to the precepts.
Although I recite the sutras and treatises, I do not understand their fundamental tenets; when I search through commentaries and sub-commentaries, I seek only material gain.
Therefore, lacking the wisdom born of reflection and cultivation, how could I hope for the merit of realization? To reflect upon this, one cannot help but feel shame. I have humbly...
Hearing the Dharma as one who wishes to discern the heterodox and enter the noble, correct Path, one should first study the teachings to understand the Buddha’s methods of transformation.
Only then will one have partially grasped the very heart and liver of the sages and saints, and may become an eye for both humans and devas.
Only in this way can one be called a Son of the Buddha; otherwise, how could one avoid being a follower of Māra? It is just as in worldly custom: if one does not know his own father...

Regarding their names, dates of birth and death, the extent of their merits and demerits, the various karmic deeds they have performed, and whether they were noble or base, skillful or clumsy—these are called "beasts with human heads.

There is no filial impiety greater than this. As for those who claim to be disciples of the Buddha (śākyaputrīya), if they do not understand the Master’s clan name and personal name, the years and months of his birth and passing, the length of his lifespan, or the provisional and ultimate, the manifest and hidden meanings of the various teachings he proclaimed; [how can they be considered true followers?]
To keep this secret is surely a vulgar practice that mocks the appearance of a monk. What transgression could be more contrary to principle than this?
One must know that the fault of such unfiliality and insubordination will not escape the suffering of the Avīci Hell without interruption.

Now, the traces of our Buddha’s appearance in the world and his activities of transformation, the universal reach of his bequeathed Dharma and the conditions through which he benefited sentient beings, the matters concerning the formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness of the world-systems, and the causes for the varying scales and durations of the kalpas—all these are set forth in the sūtras and śāstras, wherein they may be clearly reflected.
Nevertheless, among us newly ordained śrāmaṇeras, many are unable to seek them out extensively; thus, the ignorant are numerous. Therefore, now...
I, this unworthy one, have relied upon the text of the *Tiantai sijiao yi*, further excerpted the words recorded in various sūtras and śāstras,
and carefully examined the explanations manifested in the various biographical records, compiling them into verses totaling seven hundred and seventy-six lines.
Furthermore, where the meaning within a passage was not yet fully manifest, I have annotated it beneath the relevant text so that readers may understand it easily.

This is like seeing the distant by looking at what is near, or knowing the broad by relying on the concise. Nevertheless, as the citations were somewhat numerous and the phrasing not entirely elegant, I am aware that public criticism will fall upon me;
yet, I hope this will serve as a resource for the initial practice of beginners, and that those who are proficient will find it useful.
May the scholar not take this as a cause for derision. Written on the day of the full moon in the twelfth lunar month of the first year of the Tianli era, the year Wuchen (1338).
*Eulogy on the Life and Deeds of Śākyamuni Tathāgata*, Volume One.
"Śākya" is translated here as "Capable Benevolence" (*Néng rén*); this is his clan name. "Muni" is translated as "Silent Sage" (*Jīmò*); this is his title. It signifies benevolence...
"Compassionate toward all beings" means that his three karmas (body, speech, and mind) are free from worldly clamor and distraction. "Tathāgata" is the foremost of the ten titles;
it signifies one who has come by means of the path of reality to achieve perfect enlightenment. Furthermore, the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"He comes from nowhere, nor does he go anywhere; therefore, he is called Tathāgata. Now, the realm of the Buddhas is neither land nor body; it accords with the capacities of sentient beings.
To firmly establish the basis and its manifestations (*śāśraya-vijñapti*), the holy teachings of a single lifetime generally elucidate the four lands and three bodies (*tri-kāya*). These are:

first, the Land of Common Residence of the Defiled and Pure, where ordinary beings and sages dwell together; second, the Land of Skillful Means with Remainder, inhabited by those of the Three Vehicles who have severed the afflictions of views and cultivation, and who are the objects of transformation for the *nirmāṇakāya*.
Regarding the *nirmāṇakāya*, there are two types: the inferior *nirmāṇakāya* which transforms [beings] in the Land of Common Residence, and the superior *nirmāṇakāya*...

1. The Land of Expedient Transformation (*nirmāṇa-upāya-kṣetra*). 2. The Land of True Reward and Non-obstruction (*vipāka-avighna-kṣetra*), where Bodhisattvas of the Dharma-body who have severed the fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*) reside;

this is the realm transformed by the Reward-body (*saṃbhoga-kāya*). 3. The Land of Constant Quiescent Light (*nitya-prasāda-āloka-kṣetra*), which is the dwelling place of the wondrously enlightened Dharma-body alone.
The present Sahā world is the realm transformed by the Inferior Response-body (*hīna-nirmāṇa-kāya*). Nevertheless, the three bodies are one essence, and the four lands are [not distinct].
They are distinct. Why? The Dharma-body is the essence (*tǐ*); the two [other] bodies are its function (*yòng*). Quiescent Radiance is the essence; the three lands are its function.
Thus, the function arises from the essence, and the three and four are clearly distinguished. Yet, the essence within the function, the three and four, are one.

It is like extending a fist to form fingers, or closing the fingers to form a fist: the fist is the essence, while the fingers are the function. Though essence and function appear different, they are in fact one.
[The Buddha] said: "I, the Lord of the Śākyas, do not move from the tranquil light of the *sukhāvatī* (Pure Land) while traveling and transforming beings in the Sahā world.
Without abandoning the *dharmakāya*, I manifest the *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya*. Thus one knows that the Sahā world is the tranquil light, and the tranquil light is the Sahā world;

the *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya* are the *dharmakāya*, and the *dharmakāya* is the *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya*. Furthermore, there is another master who clarifies the four lands (*catur-bhūmi*), stating: first, the *dharmatā-bhūmi* (Dharma-nature land)... [text fragment ends].
1. The land where the [Dharmakāya] itself resides. 2. The Land of Self-Enjoyment (*svasaṃbhogakāya*), where the self-enjoyment reward body resides;

these two lands are identical to the aforementioned Land of Constant Quiescent Light (*nityapraśāntaprakāśa*). 3. The Land of Other-Enjoyment (*parasaṃbhogakāya*), where the other-enjoyment reward body resides;

it manifests a portion of subtle marks for Bodhisattvas from the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) upward, and is identical to the aforementioned Land of True Reward (*sambhogakāya-bhūmi*). 4. The Land of Transformation (*nirmāṇakāya*).

The Land of Transformation (*nirmāṇakāya-bhūmi*) is where the coarse aspects of a single portion are manifested for bodhisattvas prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) and for ordinary beings of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
This refers to the land of preliminary skillful means (*pūrvopāya-bhūmi*) and the land of cohabitation of the defiled and the pure (*saṃkliṣṭa-vyavadāta-sahabhū-bhūmi*).
How many errors have there been from those who, failing to distinguish the meaning of the three bodies (*trikāya*) and four lands (*catasro bhūmayaḥ*), engage in mutual debate!
Within the Sahā world, there are three thousand great thousandfold realms;
in each and every realm, there is one Mount Sumeru.
"Sahā" is also called *So-ha*; this is translated as "Endurance" (*Kāṃkṣan*). This means that the sentient beings of this land are able to endure and tolerate [suffering].

This is because all things are characterized by suffering. For instance, although the heavenly realms are places of pleasure, when the signs of decline appear, their suffering exceeds that of the hells.
As for the five lower realms, they consist purely of suffering without any pleasure; yet, beings therein mistake suffering for pleasure.

The term "trichiliocosm" (three thousand great thousand worlds) will be explained below. Mount Sumeru is also called Sumeru; this is translated as "Wondrous High. It is composed of four precious substances.
It is composed of: white silver in the east, blue lapis lazuli in the south, gold in the west, and black crystal in the north; for this reason, it is wondrous.
It is high because it rises above all other mountains, reaching eighty-four thousand *yojanas* in height. Its depth below the water is likewise the same.

The *Abhidharmakośakārikā* states: "Sumeru has four terraces, each separated by ten thousand [yojanas]. They extend outward sixteen thousand, eight thousand, four thousand, and two thousand [yojanas] respectively.
The Vajra-Head (Kīṭa), the Wreath-Bearer (Mālādharin), the Ever-Joyful (Sadāmada), and the Great King’s Retinue (Mahārājika) dwell in succession upon these four levels.
They also reside on the other seven mountains. A yojana is also called a yojana (*yojana*). Twenty-four finger-widths constitute one cubit (*hasta*)."
An elbow (*hasta*) is one chi and five cun. Six chi make one bow (*dhanus*).
Five hundred bows make one *krośa*, which is approximately six li, or three thousand chi. Eight *krośas* make one *yojana*, which is twenty-four thousand chi.
Surrounding it on all sides are seven mountains, all composed of the seven precious gems. Within each lies a sea of fragrant water, filled with various flowers.
As for these seven mountains: the first is Yugandhara (Holding the Pair), forty-two thousand yojanas in height and the same in breadth. The mountain...
The inner waters are eighty thousand yojanas wide. The second mountain, Yugandhara, is twenty-one thousand yojanas high and its width is likewise.
The inner waters within this mountain are forty thousand yojanas wide. The third mountain, Īṣādhara, is eleven thousand five hundred yojanas high and its width is likewise.
The inner waters within this mountain are twenty thousand yojanas wide. The fourth [mountain], Sudarśana...
Mount Cakravāḍa is five thousand two hundred and fifty yojanas high, and its breadth is likewise. The water within this mountain is ten thousand yojanas wide.
The fifth is Mount Aśvakarṇa, which is two thousand six hundred and twenty-five yojanas high, and its breadth is likewise;
the water within this mountain is five thousand yojanas wide. The sixth is Mount Vinitākara, which is one thousand three... [high].
It is one hundred and twelve yojanas and a half in height, and its breadth is likewise. The water within this mountain is two thousand five hundred yojanas wide.
The seventh mountain is Matsya-mukha (Fish-Mouth), six hundred and fifty-six yojanas in height, and its breadth is likewise.
The water within this mountain is one thousand two hundred and fifty yojanas wide. Thus, between these seven mountains, there are seas of fragrant water.
In each there are *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* flowers, covering the surface of the water everywhere.
Next is the salt-water ocean, where the dragon Sāgara is the lord; within it are the four great continents.
The salt ocean ruled by the four wheel-turning kings is three hundred and thirty-six thousand yojanas in breadth and eighty-four thousand yojanas in depth.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states that there are two thousand five hundred great rivers in Jambudvīpa in the south, and [in Aparagoyānī in the west...]
There are five thousand great rivers. In Pūrvavideha in the east, there are seven thousand five hundred great rivers. In Uttarakuru in the north, there are ten thousand great rivers.
Combined across the four continents, twenty-five thousand great rivers flow continuously and without interruption into the great ocean.
Furthermore, ten Radiant Dragon Kings rain down into the great ocean, so that the water exceeds the previous amount twofold. Moreover—
There were eighty billion great dragon kings, such as the Dragon King Śata-prabha, each raining down into the great ocean;

all of these increased successively, doubling in volume compared to the preceding ones. Furthermore, from within the palaces of these eighty billion dragon kings, water issued forth individually and flowed into the great ocean;
all of these likewise increased successively, doubling in volume compared to the preceding ones. [The Dragon King] Sāgara...
From within the palace of King Jambūdhvaja’s prince, water issues forth, twice as much as before.
Furthermore, from within the palace of the Naga King Sāgara, water issues forth, again twice as much as before. This water that issues forth is the color of dark-blue lapis lazuli;
it surges forth at specific times, and for this reason, the tides of the great ocean do not miss their appointed time. It is also said that the great ocean possesses four blazing lights.

The Great Jewel is clear and radiant; it is spread across the bottom [of the ocean]. Its nature is extremely fierce and hot, and it is constantly able to drink up and contract immeasurable great waters.
If this jewel did not exist, everything from the four continents up to the Peak of Existence would all be submerged and swept away.
Sāgara means "Salt Sea" (in Chinese); it is named after its location. And...
In this ocean, this dragon is the sovereign; all others are its subjects. Furthermore, the *Loutan jing* (Loka-prajñapti-sūtra) states:
"Violent winds arise in great force, blowing and excavating the great earth to a depth of three million three hundred thousand *li*.
All the waters of the world flow and converge there, perfectly filling it to form the great ocean. There are three reasons why its water is salty: the first is that within the ocean..."
There is a great fish, its body twenty-eight thousand *li* in length; it makes the water within it impure, and for this reason the taste is salty. Other details are not recorded here in full.
As for the four continents (*caturdvīpa*), they are also called the four worlds under heaven. They are situated in the great oceans on the four sides of Mount Sumeru.
The eastern one is called Videha, also known as Pūrvavideha; this is translated as "Superior Body. It is seven thousand [yojanas] in circumference.
The *yojana* is [a unit of measure]. Its shape is like a half-moon. The people are sixteen cubits tall and have a lifespan of five hundred years.
Even in the midst of darkness, they can perceive various forms. The range of the ear-consciousness extends as far as the flight of an arrow.
To the south is Jambudvīpa, also called Ābhāsavatī; this is translated as "Excellent Gold. It is six thousand five hundred *yojanas* in circumference and its shape is like the box of a chariot.

The people there are three and a half cubits tall; their lifespan is one hundred years, though it is not fixed. To the west is Aparagodānīya, also called Godānīya, which means the Continent of Cattle-Wealth.
It is seven thousand yojanas in circumference and is shaped like a full moon. The people are eight cubits tall and have a lifespan of two hundred and fifty years.
Regarding the objects perceived by visual consciousness, mountains and walls do not obstruct them; their eyes can also hear sounds.
The north is called Uttarakuru, also known as Kuru-dvīpa; this means "Superior Continent.
It is eight thousand yojanas in circumference and is shaped like a square seat. The people are thirty-two cubits tall and have a lifespan of one thousand years, with none dying prematurely.
Beyond the mountain barriers, they see clearly without obstruction. As for what is heard by the ear, whether near or far, it can all be heard.
Furthermore, regarding the birth and growth of humans, the three continents are similar; the northern continent is slightly different.
This is to say that when a person there gives rise to a desire for a woman, they gaze at her intently and then depart; she follows after them to where he has gone.

In that grove, if those men and women were relatives—such as parents, uncles, or cousins—and thus ought not to engage in sexual desire, the trees would not bend to provide shade, and they would each disperse.
If, however, they were not relatives and ought to engage in sexual desire, the trees would bend to shade their bodies, and they would enjoy themselves as they pleased.
When those women became pregnant, they gave birth within seven or eight days; whether it was a boy or a girl, they would abandon [the child] immediately after birth.
They place it at a crossroads. Any travelers who pass by point their fingers toward it and rinse their mouths; from their fingers, fat and milk emerge.
After seven days have passed, the child grows up and becomes equal to those people—the boys join the ranks of men and the girls join the ranks of women.
When that person dies, they place the corpse at a four-way intersection, where *uṣṭrikāṅga* birds take up the dead body and carry it away to another region.

These four continents are governed by the four types of wheel-turning kings (*cakravartin*). The gold-wheel-turning king appears when the human lifespan is eighty thousand years and transforms the four continents.
The silver-wheel-turning king appears when the human lifespan is sixty thousand years and transforms three continents.
The copper-wheel-turning king appears when the human lifespan is forty thousand years and transforms two continents.
The iron-wheel-turning king appears when the human lifespan is ten thousand years and transforms only one Jambudvīpa. These four wheel-turning kings possess sovereign majesty and power.

He is fully endowed with the seven treasures and enjoys them according to his wish. Day and night, he is able to travel throughout the worlds under his jurisdiction, teaching and transforming beings through the ten virtuous paths.
As for the Golden Wheel-turning King, he does not merely traverse the four continents; he may even ascend to the heavens.
Outside, there are iron mountains surrounding [the world], below which lie the various hells. The sun, moon, and constellations revolve around the midpoint of Mount Meru.

The Iron Encircling Mountains (Cakravāḍa) are three hundred and twenty-eight yojanas high; their breadth is likewise. According to the sūtra, they are twelve billion eight [hundred million... (Note: The final line appears to be a fragment of a numerical calculation regarding the dimensions of the world-system.)
It is one hundred and seventy-five *yojanas* in height; its circumference on both sides is each three times that. This is the Lesser Iron Ring Mountain (*Cakravāḍa*).

As stated in the *Yinben jing* (Sūtra on the Origin): "Beyond Mount Sumeru and the other great kings of mountains, as well as beyond the great oceans, there is the Iron Ring Mountain, six million eight hundred thousand *yojanas* in height and likewise in breadth.
Beyond this, there is furthermore an Iron Mountain, [six million eight hundred thousand *yojanas* in height]..."
Its breadth is likewise equal. Between these two mountains, in a place of pitch darkness, there is a hell named Avīci.
It consists of seven layers of iron walls, measuring exactly three hundred and sixty thousand li in both length and breadth. Seven tiers of iron nets cover it from above.
All manner of suffering is gathered therein; those who have committed the most heinous evil deeds receive this physical form as their retribution.
Within a single day and night, there are eighty-four thousand births and deaths during one period of increase and decrease [of a *madhyama-kalpa*].
One day in this place is equivalent to sixty minor *kalpas* in Jambudvīpa. In this manner, after passing through one *madhyama-kalpa*, they proceed sequentially until eighty-four thousand *kalpas*.
Furthermore, there are the eight cold and eight hot great hells, each with its own retinue. Their...
The types [of hells] are immeasurable. Among them, those who undergo suffering do so according to their own karma, with varying degrees of severity, lasting for kalpas and the like.
As for "hell" (dīyù), the Sanskrit term is *naraka*, which here means "instrument of suffering. It is so named because it lies beneath the earth.
An ancient master, citing a verse from a sutra, said: "Jambudvīpa is seven thousand yojanas wide; everywhere within it there are solitary..."
The solitary prisons are located either amidst mountain forests and vast wildernesses, or on the shores of great oceans and rivers, or within city walls and local shrines;
they number eighty-four thousand. Thus one should know that these various minor hells exist everywhere.
The city of the sun measures fifty-one *yojanas* in circumference; because it is composed of fire-crystal (*tejo-maṇi*), it is hot. From summer...
As for the days: at the winter solstice, because the moon gradually moves away from its orbit, the days become shorter; because the light is increasingly obstructed, it becomes colder.
From the winter solstice until the summer solstice, because the moon gradually approaches its orbit, the days become longer and warmer.
The city of the moon measures fifty yojanas; half is composed of white crystal and half is composed of black crystal.
Cold. From the new moon (*śuklapakṣa*) to the full moon (*pūrṇimā*), the bright surface gradually appears and the dark surface gradually recedes; thus people see a circular form.

From the full moon to the dark moon (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*), the bright surface gradually diminishes and the dark surface gradually increases; thus people see a deficient shape. Yet, in its essential nature, there is actually no increase or decrease.

This is from the *Śìshì huìyào* (Essentials of the Buddhist Community). Furthermore, the *Yīnběn jīng* (Sūtra on the Fundamental Causes) states: "The movement of the sun [causes] the lengthening and shortening [of days]."
During the six months when the moon travels northward, it gradually shifts six *krośas* toward the north within a single day; therefore, the moon’s diameter gradually increases.
During the six months when it travels southward, the same occurs; therefore, the diameter gradually decreases. The *Lokasthāna-śāstra* states:
"As for the waxing and waning of the moon, if the moon follows behind the sun, the sunlight obscures the moon, gradually covering it until the fifteenth [day]."

The sun covers the moon until it is completely obscured. If the sun moves ahead of the moon, the moon becomes clear day by day, and it is likewise so until the fifteenth day, when it is fully complete (and so forth). Occasionally there are eclipses, as the sutras state:
"It is because the Asura King Rāhu obstructs [the light]. However, this differs from what is discussed by the secular masters of Yin-Yang.

This is so; yet there is also scriptural authority for it. Furthermore, when the sun and moon shine equally upon the three continents at one time, it is sunset in the eastern continent (Pūrvavideha), dawn in the western continent (Aparagodānīya), and midnight in the northern continent (Uttarakuru).

The lengths of day and night across spring, autumn, winter, and summer are likewise equal for all. Therefore, a verse in the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "The sun and moon [are situated] halfway up Mount Meru... (5...)
Eleven [yojanas] and fifty [yojanas]. At midnight, sunset, midday, and sunrise, the four continents are equal [in illumination], and so forth.
The secular treatises state: because the sun moves slowly, it completes one circuit of the heavens in one year; because the moon moves swiftly, it completes one circuit of the heavens in one month.
The dimensions of the stars are unequal: the largest are eighteen *krośas*, the middling are eleven *krośas*, and the smallest...
They span four *krośas* and are immeasurable in number; their names are likewise manifold. Each presides over matters such as the calamities and blessings of the human world.
Therefore, if they do not lose their regular measure, the world will be peaceful and prosperous, and sages and worthies will appear.
Should they lose their measure and manifest strange portents, the state will surely suffer disaster—either the sovereign will face peril or pass away, or the ministers...
The people will rise in rebellion; the years will be calamitous and grain will be expensive; wars will break out and diseases will spread.
Thus, the three luminaries abide according to the wind at a height of forty-two thousand yojanas. The *Lotus Sūtra Commentary* states: "The sun is a transformation of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva;
the moon is a transformation of Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva; and the stars are transformations of Gaganagañja Bodhisattva."
When ordinary beings behold the Great Sage in person, how could they fail to revere and honor him, just as one does the sun, moon, and stars?
The Four Kings dwell within the mountain’s belly; Trāyastriṃśa resides upon its summit.
Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, and Paranirmitavaśavartin—these four heavens dwell in the sky. Their lifespans and merits increase twofold compared to those before.
These six devas are all collectively termed the Four Kings of the Desire Realm:
in the east is the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra (Holder of the Nation); in the south is the Heavenly King Virūḍhaka (Increase);
in the west is the Heavenly King Virūpākṣa (Broad Eye); and in the north is the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa (Much Hearing).
These Four Heavenly Kings reside on the four sides of the fourth terrace of Mount Sumeru. They possess great authority and protect the world.

Their bodies are half a *li* in height, and their lifespan is five hundred years. Fifty human years constitute one day and night for these devas; by this reckoning, their lifespan is nine million human years.
They are situated forty-two thousand *yojanas* above the earth. "Trāyastriṃśa" (the Heaven of the Thirty-three) is what this term means.
On the summit of Mount Sumeru, there are eight heavens in each of the four directions (making thirty-two), with Śakra residing in the center.
The bodies of those devas are one *li* in height, and their lifespan is one thousand years. One hundred years in the human realm constitutes one day and night for these devas;
by human reckoning, this corresponds to thirty-six billion years. These two heavens are situated eighty-four thousand *yojanas* above the earth.
The union of these two in pairs constitutes the formation of yin and yang. Those who practice the ten wholesome deeds of the highest grade are born in these two heavens.
Yāma is also called Suyāma; this means "Time. Their bodies are one and a half *li* tall, and their lifespan is two thousand years.
Two hundred years in the human realm constitute one day and night in this heaven. Tuṣita is also called Dōshitsu; this...
Regarding the Heaven of Contentment (Tuṣita): its inhabitants are two *li* tall and have a lifespan of four thousand years. Four hundred human years constitute one day and night for this heaven.

In this second heaven, beings form the union of male and female by holding hands. In the Heaven of Delighting in Transformations (Nirmāṇarati), the inhabitants are two and a half *li* tall and have a lifespan of eight thousand years.
Eight hundred human years constitute one day and night for this heaven. [In the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Transformations...]
The bodies of the gods in this heaven are three *li* in height, and their lifespan is sixteen thousand years. One thousand six hundred human years constitute one day and night for these gods.
These two heavens [the Yāma and Tuṣita] form the principles of yin and yang through mutual gazing and smiling. The four heavens above this dwell in the void, supported by clouds;
their distances from the earth successively double those of the preceding ones, until the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, which is ten thousand *li* from the earth.

It is thirty-four thousand four hundred *yojanas* in extent. Those who practice the ten superior wholesome deeds (*daśa-kuśala-karma-patha*) while also engaging in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) are born in these four heavens.
Māra Pāpīyān dwells within these heavens. From the five lower destinies (*gati*) up to these heavens, they are collectively termed the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*).
The *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* asks: "The inhabitants of the four continents distinguish day and night by means of the solar and lunar disks. [How do those in the heavens] desire..."
How are the days and nights of the gods known? Answer: When the *padma* lotuses close and the *utpala* lotuses open, and beings are inclined toward much sleep, that time is night.
When the *utpala* lotuses close and the *padma* lotuses open, and beings have little desire for sleep, that time is day.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The various gods of the desire realm [use] lamps and candles..."
Because they have practiced the giving of bright jewels and other such things, their bodies are constantly radiant; they do not require the light of the sun and moon.

The eighteen heavens of the Four Dhyānas have already abandoned the coarse distractions of desire, yet because they have not yet escaped the cage of form, they are called the Realm of Form (Rūpadhātu).
Regarding the eighteen heavens of the four dhyānas: there are three heavens of the first dhyāna. First, the Brahmakāyika Heaven;

their bodies are half a yojana in height, and their lifespan is twenty intermediate kalpas. Second, the Brahmapurohita Heaven; their bodies are one yojana in height, and their lifespan is forty intermediate kalpas. Third, the Mahābrahmā Heaven;
their bodies are one and a half yojanas in height, and their lifespan is sixty intermediate kalpas. [The bodies and lifespans of these heavens...]
They do not exceed those preceding them because they are difficult to transcend due to the absence of vitarka and vicāra. These three heavens cover the four continents.

As for the three heavens of the second dhyāna: first, the Parīttābha (Limited Light) Heaven; their bodies are two yojanas in height, and their lifespan is two great kalpas. Second, the Apramāṇābha (Immeasurable Light) Heaven;
their bodies are four yojanas in height, and their lifespan is four great kalpas. Third, the Ābhāsvara (Radiant Sound) Heaven; their bodies are eight [yojanas in height].
The *yojana*. Their lifespan is eight great kalpas. These three heavens cover a small chiliocosm.

[The bodies of the gods in the Heaven of Limited Radiance do not double in size compared to the preceding one because they are free from applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*) and are subject to the hardships of kings and ministers; their lifespan doubles compared to others because suffering and its origin are easily eliminated.
In the third dhyāna, there are three heavens. First is the Heaven of Minor Purity (*Parīttaśubha*); the body length is sixteen *yojanas*.
The life span is sixteen great kalpas. Second, the Heaven of Immeasurable Purity (Apramāṇaśubha): the body height is thirty-two yojanas, and the life span is thirty-two great kalpas.
Third, the Heaven of Universal Purity (Śubhakṛtsna): the body height is sixty-four yojanas, and the life span is sixty-four great kalpas.
These three heavens cover the intermediate chiliocosm. There are nine heavens in the fourth dhyāna: first, the Cloudless Heaven (Anabhraka).

Their height is one hundred twenty-five yojanas, and their lifespan is one hundred twenty-five great kalpas [this heavenly body and lifespan are three yojanas and three kalpas less than those of the preceding heaven because they are free from clouds and the three calamities].
As for the two types of Puṇyaprasava (Merit-Born) devas, their height is two hundred fifty yojanas, and their lifespan is two hundred fifty...
The third is the Vast Fruit Heaven (*Bṛhatphala*). The bodies of its inhabitants are five hundred *yojanas* in height, and their lifespan is five hundred great kalpas.

These three heavens above are dwelling places for ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*). Those who practice the ten superior wholesome deeds (*daśakuśalakarmapatha*) while also engaging in seated meditation are reborn therein.

Furthermore, there are non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) who separately cultivate the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*), which is subsumed within the Vast Fruit Heaven; their bodies and lifespans are likewise the same. Four.
In the Avṛha Heaven, the height of the beings is one thousand yojanas and their lifespan is one thousand great kalpas.

In the Atapa Heaven, the height is two thousand yojanas and the lifespan is two thousand great kalpas. In the Sudarśana Heaven, the height is four thousand yojanas and the lifespan is four thousand great kalpas.
In the Sudṛśa Heaven, the height is eight thousand yojanas and the lifespan is eight thousand [great kalpas].
The Great Kalpas. In the eighth heaven, Akaniṣṭha, the body height is sixteen thousand yojanas and the lifespan is sixteen thousand great kalpas.
Regarding these five heavens above, those who dwell in the third fruit [of the path]—if they delight in wisdom, they are born in these heavens;
if they delight in meditative concentration, they enter the four formless attainments—the nine Mahāvaśavartin deities have the following body height and lifespan:
Their measure is incalculable. They are the dwelling place of Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage. These nine heavens cover the great trichiliocosm;
as for the length and breadth of their demarcated boundaries, they ultimately cannot be measured by the number of *li*. Furthermore, as stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*:
"If a large stone were dropped from the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, it would take eighteen thousand three hundred and eight..."

"In the thirteenth year, he finally reached the ground... (and so forth). Although these heavens of the four dhyānas are free from the coarse matter and distracted minds of the desire realm, they remain bound by the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), like a bird confined in a cage and lacking mastery.

[In some places it is said that within the four dhyānas, the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñin*) is considered one such lack of great mastery, because these celestial beings are the ultimate lords of the realm of form.]

Above are the four spheres of emptiness (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), whose meditative bliss surpasses the four dhyānas. Being free from form (*rūpa*) and consisting only of the four aggregates (*skandha*), they are called the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

As for the four spheres of emptiness: first is the Sphere of Infinite Space, with a lifespan of twenty thousand great kalpas; the lifespan of this deva does not double [as it does in the lower realms].
Regarding the former: because they have first become free from the bonds of form, the lifespan in the second [dhyāna], the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, is forty thousand great kalpas;
in the third, the Sphere of Nothingness, it is sixty thousand great kalpas; and in the fourth, the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception, it is eighty thousand great kalpas.
As for why the lifespans in these four formless spheres do not double the preceding ones but increase by only twenty thousand, it is solely due to the inferiority of their wisdom.
Therefore it is so. Furthermore, these four heavens have no distinct locations; they are not separate from the realms of desire or form.

Nevertheless, because the karma cultivated by each is distinct, they do not know one another’s respective practices. Since these heavens are superior to the four dhyānas, they are arranged above them according to their meaning.

These four heavens have already transcended the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) and possess only the four aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness (vedanā, saṃjñā, saṃskāra, and vijñāna). Moreover...
Among the eight consciousnesses, the first five do not exist; there are only the latter three.

From the First Dhyāna up to the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception, if one speaks from the perspective of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana), they perform only karma that leads to rebirth in those same stages or in the stages immediately above them.
When their karma is exhausted, they transmigrate according to that karma, forever lacking the capacity to enter the Path.
Collectively termed the "Three Realms," Specifically, there are twenty-five [existences]. This constitutes the measure of a single land, the realm transformed by one Śākyamuni.
The Three Realms are the Desire Realm, the Form Realm, and the Formless Realm. The twenty-five existences (*bhava*) are: the four continents, the four... [heavens], and so forth.
The evil realms; the six heavens of desire along with the Brahma heavens; the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments; the realm of non-conception;
and the anāgāmin—these are also called the six destinies. They consist of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, asuras, humans, and devas.
This constitutes one land, which is the transformation of an inferior response-body Buddha of sixteen feet.
When these [worlds] reach one thousand, it is called a small chiliocosm; when a small chiliocosm reaches one thousand, it is called a medium chiliocosm;
and when a medium chiliocosm reaches one thousand, it is called a great trichiliocosm.
Thus, each of these three thousand realms is surrounded by its own Cakravāḍa mountains.
The *Shishi huizao* (Essentials of the Śākya Clan) states: Within the Iron Ring Mountains (*Cakravāḍa*) and within the oceans, there are four continents and Mount Sumeru;

above these are the twenty-eight heavens together with one sun and one moon, constituting the measure of a single world-system (*cūḍikā-lokadhatu*). When such systems are counted up to one thousand, they are completely encircled by the Great Iron Ring Mountains.

This is called a small chiliocosm (*sāhasra-cūḍika-lokadhātu*). When one thousand of these small chiliocosms reach their full number, surrounded by an Iron Encircling Mountain (*Cakravāḍa*), it is called a medium chiliocosm (*dvisāhasra-madhyama-lokadhātu*).
When one thousand of these medium chiliocosms reach their full number, surrounded by an Iron Encircling Mountain, it is called a great trichiliocosm (*trisāhasra-mahāsāhasra-lokadhātu*).
Thus, there are ten billion such realms, all of which are governed by the Buddha and are equally reached by his voice and teaching. — *Brahmajāla-sūtra* (Fanwang jing)

Commentary: Question: The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that one great trichiliocosm contains one hundred *koṭi* worlds, while the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā* and other texts state that the measure of a *koṭi* corresponds to ten billion (*bǎiyì*).
Why, then, is it stated here only as "ten billion"? Answer: There are many types of "billion" (*yì*).
One hundred thousand is taken as one *koṭi* (億); alternatively, one million, ten million, or even ten million times ten million may be taken as one *koṭi*.

In the *Yogācārabhūmi*, it is based solely on one hundred thousand being a *koṭi*, whereas this sutra takes ten million as a *koṭi*. Thus, while the sacred teachings differ in various places, they do not contradict one another.
These various lands and realms are spread out like a chessboard upon the wheel of earth. Beneath it, the three wheels of gold, water, and wind support the wheel of earth in succession;
the thickness of the earth wheel is eighty-four thousand yojanas, three times the extent of its circumference. The thickness of the golden wheel is three hundred and twenty million [yojanas].

It is ten thousand *yojanas*. According to the *Sūtra*, it is twelve hundred and thirty-four million five hundred thousand *yojanas*. The thickness of the water wheel (*āpa-maṇḍala*) is eight hundred million *yojanas*.
It is described as being like the golden wheel (*kāñcana-cakra*). The thickness of the wind wheel (*vāyu-maṇḍala*) is sixteen hundred million *yojanas*, and its breadth is immeasurable.
These measurements of the four wheels are calculated solely based on the dimensions of a single Jambudvīpa surrounding a single Mount Sumeru.
If one speaks according to the Great Trichiliocosm, it cannot be measured by the number of *li*.

When the world is about to be formed, Brahmā first establishes [the foundation]; the realms of the Four Dhyānas and the Desire Realm, along with their sentient and insentient environments, are formed in succession.
First, the wind-circle arises in the lower realm, its extent equal to the Great Trichiliocosm.
Spread upward and spread sideways, like the shape of a tray or a roof;
The gods of Ābhāsvara spread clouds that completely cover the wind-circle (vāyumaṇḍala), Pouring down rain as thick as a great axle;
The water is so deep its bottom is difficult to reach, and when struck by the wind above, it becomes gold, While the remainder below forms the water-circle; Furthermore, rain falls from the sky.

When the waters fill the golden wheel, the wind blows them into the great earth; Mount Sumeru and the various mountains, the four continents, and the rivers and seas are all established anew as before.
Those whose merit in the second dhyāna is exhausted descend to be born on this superior Golden Continent;
their bodies are vast and their lifespans immeasurable, and they travel through the air with light shining afar.
The savory earth-essence (*pṛthivī-rasa*) cakes, the forest creepers, and the non-glutinous rice—when they greedily consumed these various superior flavors, they immediately perished.
Next, fragrant rice grew; people again vied to eat it, and their radiance vanished and was lost.
Then the male and female sexual organs appeared, due to the force of their past habitual tendencies.

Engaging in impure conduct, from this their descendants multiplied; as the people grew wealthy and prosperous, they gradually practiced perverse and unwholesome deeds, and upon death filled the three evil realms. Fearing evil, they cultivated various virtues and were reborn in the three continents and the six heavens.
Thus, the sentient beings and the physical world of the five destinies were fully brought into being.
Abiding for twenty periods of increase and decrease, the events of the kalpa of destruction subsequently arise.
Beginning from the Avīci Hell up to the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, sentient beings gradually abandon their abodes.
Once the physical world is entirely empty, seven suns appear; the oceans dry up, the mountain rocks melt, and the great earth blazes with fiery radiance.
The great trichiliocosm is entirely reduced to ashes, As flames soar up to the First Dhyāna Heaven.
The three heavens ascend in succession, all proceeding to the Second Dhyāna; The space below becomes like a black cavern.
Such is the general outline of the kalpas of formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness. Within these four kalpas, there are eighty cycles of increase and decrease.
This constitutes one fire kalpa; seven fire kalpas constitute one water kalpa. After seven water kalpas, there are again seven fire kalpas, followed by one wind disaster.
The fire disaster arises from the earth and destroys up to the First Dhyāna;
the water disaster arises from the Second Dhyāna and dissolves the receptacle world like salt melting away; the wind disaster arises from the Third Dhyāna.

When the joints of the dry branches are destroyed, the four dhyānas are free from external calamities. The kalpas of formation and destruction by fire arise and perish together with the celestial palaces;
water follows next, and wind is the most extensive. Once destroyed, they are formed again in a cycle that knows no end.
When the wind calamity has rotated a hundred times, it is called one asaṃkhyeya kalpa.
Thus, throughout immeasurable kalpas, the appearance of a Buddha is exceedingly rare.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "Rain falls from the sky, filling the trichiliocosm.

A wind-wheel arises and blows it into the palaces of the gods of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*). Next, another wind arises and forms the palaces of the gods of the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*). Thus it is said.
In succession, various winds arise, forming the great kings of mountains such as Sumeru, followed by the formation of the great earth, extending even to the palaces of the *nāgas* and the *asuras*.
Furthermore, treatises such as the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* state: "When the world is about to emerge, the Great Brahmā King first establishes it alone.
After one cycle of increase and decrease has passed, [the realms of] the Brahma-purohitas, the Brahma-kāyikas, and those of the desire realm [are formed]."

Once the four heavens dwelling in space and their sentient and material environments have been successively formed, next there arises in the lower realm a great wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*) equal in measure to a trichiliocosm.
It has two aspects: namely, spreading upward and spreading laterally. That which spreads upward serves as the foundation;
that which spreads laterally serves as the walls. Its shape is like a shallow basin or a roof-ridge, and it is as solid as diamond (*vajra*). Upon it is the Heaven of Light-Sound (*Ābhāsvara*).
O Deva, a great cloud of the treasury of gold spreads forth, completely covering the wind-circle (vāyu-maṇḍala).
It rains down a great torrential rain with drops as large as chariot axles, filling the world-system until the water reaches a depth of one billion one hundred and twenty million yojanas.

Subsequently, winds arise and strike the water, forming a layer of gold three hundred and twenty million yojanas thick; the remaining eight hundred million yojanas below constitute the water-circle. Thus it is.

Because it is supported by the wind-circle (vāyu-maṇḍala), it does not leak or disperse. Within the space, clouds of the various elemental matrices (dhātu-garbha) arise again, raining down all kinds of rain that fills the gold-circle (kāñcana-maṇḍala).
Next, wind arises again to strike the water and solidify it, forming the earth-circle (pṛthivī-maṇḍala).
That which is of the first, most refined nature forms Mount Sumeru; the next nature forms the seven golden mountains; and the lowest nature [forms the remaining features].

The various mountains and lands were formed; the plains became continents, and the deep embankments became oceans. From the highest reaches down to the lowest, everything was established according to its ancient order.
The devas of the Ābhāsvara Heaven, their merit exhausted, descended to be born here below, all transforming into human form. Their bodies were one thousand *zhī* tall, or perhaps two thousand *zhī*.
They took joy as their food, their bodily radiance shone afar, they traveled through the air with ease, and there were neither men nor women.

There was naturally a soil-fertility (also called "earth-essence") that was white in color and sweet in taste; they vied with one another to take and eat it, and thus the soil-fertility eventually disappeared.
Next, a ground-skin (also called "earth-cake") arose, yellow in color and sweet in taste. Subsequently, forest-clusters (also called "forest-branches") arose, shaped like forests.
All produced fruits; when cut, they exuded sap like pure honey. Next, non-glutinous rice grew, reaching a height of seventy [units] (some say four inches).
Next, fragrant rice grew, which possessed husks and bran; because of eating this, excrement and urine remained in the body.
Desiring to eliminate [these afflictions], two paths arose; they possessed male and female organs, and there were husbands and wives, as well as fields and houses.
Due to the influence of greed and defilement, their radiance faded and their supernormal powers vanished. The sun and moon first appeared, thereby distinguishing day from night.

As the people gradually became depraved and committed unwholesome deeds, because of their creation of evil, they were reborn in the realm of hungry ghosts, the intermediate states, and the hells. Beholding...

Practicing evil and good, they are gradually reborn in the other continents of the east, west, and north, as well as among the Four Great Kings and the Trāyastriṃśa gods; this is called the kalpa of formation (*vivartakalpa*).

The kalpa of abiding (*sthitikāla*) may be understood accordingly. As for the kalpa of destruction (*saṃvartakalpa*), at the end of the kalpa of abiding, sentient beings pass away without being reborn.
At that time, the kalpa of destruction begins. From the three miserable realms, the four continents, and the six heavens of the desire realm, beings are successively cast out first.
Once the lower realms have become empty, the heat of the sun increases fourfold; the ditches and ponds dry up completely, and the vegetation withers away.
When the second and third suns appear, the great rivers run dry. When the fourth and fifth arise, the springs of the oceans parch. When the sixth and seventh appear together—
The mountain rocks all melt; the great earth blazes with radiant heat; flames surge upward. The devas of the First Dhyāna Heaven flee toward the Second Dhyāna Heaven.

The three-thousandfold world system is entirely reduced to ashes and embers. This is the Kalpa of Destruction (Saṃvarta-kalpa). When the Kalpa of Emptiness (Śūnya-kalpa) occurs, the world has been destroyed;
there is only vast emptiness and darkness, like a black cavern. Thus, each of the four kalpas—formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness—passes through its respective duration.

Because there are twenty periods of increase and decrease, they constitute eighty periods. During the period preceding the formation eon (*vivartakalpa*), one period of increase and decrease forms the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*);

during the subsequent nineteen periods of increase and decrease, sentient beings (*sattva*) are formed. During the period preceding the destruction eon (*saṃvartakalpa*), nineteen periods of increase and decrease destroy sentient beings.

The final increase and decrease destroy the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*). Furthermore, within the twenty cycles of increase and decrease during the *sthiti-kalpa* (abiding kalpa), the first consists solely of decrease and the last consists solely of increase. Regarding what are called the kalpas of increase and decrease:

when the world was first formed, this Jambudvīpa consisted of eighty thousand kingdoms, towns, and villages, and its inhabitants were wealthy, joyful, and free from the afflictions of cold, heat, or disease; the king governed with righteous rule.
They practiced the ten wholesome deeds and revered one another like fathers and sons; their lifespan was immeasurable.

Upon reaching the beginning of the *sthita-kalpa* (the abiding eon), the kings failed to practice the correct way, and the people gradually became depraved; consequently, their lifespan decreased until it reached one hundred thousand years.
Thus it continued to diminish by one year every hundred years until it reached ten years; this is called the *apacaya-kalpa* (the eon of decrease). From this point on—
At ten years of age, the lifespan of a son is double that of his father; this increases until it reaches eighty thousand years, which is called an *utkalpa* (aeon of increase).
Regarding the phrase "the son’s age is double that of the father," the *Āgama* Sūtra states: when humans were ten years old, they killed one another.

The ṛṣis exhorted them to abstain from taking life, and those people were reborn with a lifespan of twenty years. Furthermore, by abstaining from taking what is not given, their lifespan doubled to forty years.
Furthermore, by abstaining from sexual misconduct, one's lifespan is doubled to eighty years. By abstaining from false speech, it is doubled to one hundred and sixty years.
By abstaining from divisive speech, it is doubled to three hundred and twenty years. By abstaining from harsh speech, it is doubled to six hundred and forty years.
Furthermore, by abstaining from frivolous speech, [the lifespan] doubles to two thousand five hundred years—[this practice being difficult, it is doubled by an additional five hundred].
Furthermore, by abstaining from covetousness and envy, it doubles to five thousand years. Furthermore, by abstaining from malice, it doubles to ten thousand years.

Furthermore, by abstaining from wrong views, it doubles to twenty thousand years. Furthermore, by abstaining from unlawful greed, evil desires, and perverse conduct, it doubles to forty thousand years. Furthermore...

Through such acts as filial piety toward one’s parents, reverence for śramaṇas and brahmins, and the cultivation of meritorious deeds, one increases [the lifespan] by eighty thousand years—[in certain sūtras it is stated as eighty-four thousand, which is an incremental increase within this doubling]—for one kalpa of increase and decrease.
This amounts to 1,680,000 years. This kalpa is called the "Wheel" (Araba). Based on twenty...
A *alava* kalpa consists of thirty-three million six hundred thousand years. Eighty such cycles of increase and decrease constitute one *kalpa* of fire destruction.
After seven further cycles of fire destruction have passed, there is then one cycle of water destruction.
Forty-nine cycles of formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness (*saṃvarta-vivarta*) must first pass before seven cycles of water disasters occur.
Together, these constitute fifty-six cycles of formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness. After this, seven cycles of fire disasters are completed, followed by one wind disaster.
Each wind disaster endures through sixty-four cycles of formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness. One complete cycle of formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness totals—
The total duration is one million three hundred and forty-four million years. The fire calamity utterly destroys the First Dhyāna because it possesses *vitarka* and *vicāra*.

The water calamity utterly destroys the Second Dhyāna because it possesses the sensation of joy (*prīti*). The wind calamity utterly destroys the Third Dhyāna because it possesses inhalation and exhalation (*āśvāsa-praśvāsa*).
The matter regarding the fire calamity is as explained above. As for the water calamity, it extends from below the First Dhyāna.

After the world has been destroyed by fire seven times, at the end of the eighth cycle of destruction, water arises simultaneously throughout the second dhyāna realm, destroying the receptacle world like salt dissolving in water; this water and the receptacle world vanish together at once.
The reason why there is only one such water disaster at the end of the eighth cycle of fire disasters is that... [the text continues].

Because the lifespan of the Śubhakṛtsna devas of the Second Dhyāna is eight great kalpas. After it has been thus destroyed, the Second Dhyāna is formed once more, continuing as before until the wind-disaster;
this occurs after seven cycles of fire-disasters and one cycle of water-disasters, following which [the destruction] takes place within the Third Dhyāna.
The co-nascent winds arise and destroy the receptacle world, like the wind that withers the limbs and joints. These winds and the receptacle world perish simultaneously.

As for why there are wind disasters during the sixty-four cycles of the kalpa of destruction, it is because the lifespan of the Śubhakṛtsna devas of the third dhyāna is sixty-four great kalpas. The reason the three disasters do not reach the fourth dhyāna is...

Because of the purity of equanimity and mindfulness. The Abhidharma-śāstra states: "Regarding the palaces and so forth outside the four dhyānas, although they lack external calamities, they are said to undergo formation and destruction because they arise and perish simultaneously with the palaces themselves. Furthermore, *kalpa* (劫) is here translated as "period of time" (*kāla-bhāga*).
There are the kalpas of famine, the kalpas of pestilence, the kalpas of warfare, the kalpas of increase, and the kalpas of decrease; these are all minor kalpas (*antarakalpa*).
The combination of one cycle of increase and decrease—or twenty cycles of increase and decrease—constitutes a middle kalpa (*madhyakalpa*).

When eighty such cycles of increase and decrease are unified, it is termed a great kalpa (*mahākalpa*). Furthermore, a sutra states: "It is like a great city, forty *li* square" (from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*).

[It is said to be] one hundred *yojanas* in extent. It is filled with mustard seeds. There is a long-lived deva who, after three years [some sutras say after one hundred years], takes away a single mustard seed.
Although the city has become empty, the kalpa is not yet exhausted. This is the lifespan of one kalpa for a Brahmā-deva. Furthermore, the *Yingluo jing* says:
"A stone measuring one *li*, ten *li*, or forty *li* in length and breadth, and a celestial garment weighing three *zhu* [in the human world]..."
The sun, moon, and years serve as the measure of time. Every three years, one wipes [the surface]; when this stone is exhausted, it is called a *kṣudra-kalpa* (minor kalpa).
When it reaches eighty *li*, in the Brahma-heavens there are pearls of hundred-jeweled radiance that serve as the sun, moon, and years. Every three years, one wipes [them];
when these stones are exhausted, it is called a *madhyama-kalpa* (intermediate kalpa). When it reaches eight hundred *li*, in the Śuddhāvāsa heavens there are mirrors of thousand-jeweled radiance.

Taking the number of days, months, and years as the measure, when one sweeps away this rock once every three years until it is completely exhausted, this is called a *mahākalpa*, which constitutes one *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*.

Furthermore, the verse on kalpas states: "Taking the wind-disaster (*vāyu-vipatti*) as a single unit, counting until the point of unknowability—this extremely long duration of time is called one *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*. [In the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the enumeration of *asaṃkhyeya* numbers is listed in the...].
One hundred and five positions. Master Ci'en Ji said: "When the number of kalpas of wind-disasters reaches over one hundred cycles, it is called one asaṃkhyeya.

Though the reflections are infinite, The original moon has never been two.
The *Shishi huizao* (Essentials of the Śākya Clan) states: "The capital of the Dharma King encompasses the entire trichiliocosm.
However, if one refers specifically to Chengdu, this Jambudvīpa is his constant dwelling place. Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says:

He replied: "The kingdom of Kapilavastu is the center of the three thousandfold great thousandfold world system, which contains ten billion suns."
It is the center of the moon. All Buddhas of the three periods arise from there; for the majestic spiritual power of a Buddha does not arise in a peripheral region, as such a place is tilted.

Furthermore, according to this sutra, Jambudvīpa possesses five things that surpass the three other continents up to the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations: first, agility; second, right mindfulness; third, the appearance of a Buddha.
The world is the place of abiding; the fourth is the ground for cultivating practice; the fifth is the place for practicing the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
A sutra states that the Buddhas do not appear in the three continents because the people of those lands are difficult to transform. The sentient beings of this land possess sharp and swift faculties;
they are extremely fierce and courageous, and thus it is not difficult for them to attain the Way. For this reason, all Buddhas of antiquity were born in this land.

Furthermore, if one calculates the total across the three thousand great thousand-fold worlds, there are ten trillion [worlds]. Since there is one Buddha in each nation, this results in hundreds of billions [of Buddhas].
These are all Buddhas of manifested traces; their original source is Śākyamuni (Loṣanā). Thus, the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* says:
"I, Loṣanā, am now seated upon the lotus pedestal. Upon the thousand petals surrounding me, I further manifest a thousand Śākyas. On each petal..."

There are ten billion lands, and in each land there is one Śākyamuni; thus there are a thousand, ten thousand, and a hundred million [Śākyamunis]. This is the original body of Vairocana. Furthermore, it is said:

"The Buddhas upon the thousand petals are my transformation bodies (nirmāṇakāya); the thousand, ten thousand, and hundred million Śākyamunis are the transformation bodies of those thousand Śākyamunis," and so forth.
Thus, it is like the moon rising in the sky and its reflection appearing in all waters: though the reflections are infinite, the moon—

In this Jambudvīpa, there is a land named Kapilavastu; the king’s name is Śuddhodana, and the queen’s name is Māyā.

According to the *Yinben jing* (Sutra on the Original Causes), at the beginning of the kalpa, the flavors of earth-essence (*pṛthivī-rasa*), earth-skin (*pṛthivī-tvak*), and earth-bark (*pṛthivī-valkala*) arose in succession.

After they had passed away, non-glutinous rice grew; it would sprout again by evening after being harvested in the morning. People became greedy and began to hoard it, so that once harvested, it no longer grew.
Subsequently, they began to encroach upon and steal from one another, yet there was no one capable of resolving these disputes.

They deliberated and established a wise man named Trāṇamitra as a sovereign king of impartiality to reward the virtuous and punish the wicked, with the multitude collectively providing for him. From this, the concept of a "people's ruler" first arose. This was the beginning of equality.

The princes and their descendants succeeded one another until the thirty-third generation, King Sutasoma, who attained the rank of a Universal Monarch (Cakravartin) and ruled over the four continents.
This lineage continued down to King Siṃhahanu, totaling one hundred and ten thousand fifty-six kings.
King Siṃhahanu fathered four sons: the first was named Śuddhodana, the second Śuklodana, and the third...
King Droṇodana had two sons: the first was named Siddhārtha, and the second was named Nanda. King Śuklodana had two sons: the first was named Devadatta, and the second was named Ānanda.

King Droṇodana had two sons. [The son of King Amṛtodana] was named Amṛtodana. King Śuddhodana had two sons: the first was named Siddhārtha, and the second was named Nanda. King Śuklodana had two sons: the first was named Devadatta, and the second was named Ānanda. King Droṇodana had two sons.
One was named Mahānāman; the next was named Aniruddha. The two sons of King Amṛtodana were named Vatsa and Bhadra;
their daughter was Amṛtā. All of them left the household life and realized the Way.
Māyā—here translated as "Great Illusion"—was said to have been the most beautiful of all when she was first born; the people of the country all remarked, "This is no mere human."
That which was produced was created by the gods of the Heaven of Skillful Transformations (Nirmāṇarati), and for this reason it was called "illusion" (māyā).

A physiognomist divined and said, "This girl shall give birth to a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin Rāja). The *Śākya-hui-yao* states: "In the city of Devadaha, there was an elder named Suprabuddha."
She gave birth to eight daughters. King Śuddhodana welcomed them all into the palace;
he took the first, Māyā, and the eighth, Prajāpatī, as his own queens, while he bestowed the remaining six upon his three younger brothers, each of whom took one as his queen.

In the seventh month, on the fifteenth night of the year Gēichǒu of the reign of King Zhāo of the Zhou dynasty, the Lady experienced a miraculous dream in which a person riding an elephant entered her womb;

shortly thereafter, she became pregnant. From then on, she received celestial offerings and all manner of exquisite flavors from the human realm, such that she no longer touched her lips or tongue with ordinary food.
"Zhou Zhao" (King Zhao of Zhou) is the title of a King of the Jizhou dynasty in this land of Zhendan. The details of his life are as follows; there is no need to record them here.
The *Sutra on Cause and Effect* (*Hetuphala-sūtra*), the *Lalitavistara-sūtra*, and other texts state that Śākyamuni Tathāgata was a great bodhisattva named Shanhui (Kalyāṇabuddhi).
He was born in the Tuṣita Heaven and served as the lord of the devas. There were sixty billion devas who deliberated, saying: "The Bodhisattva..."

The Bodhisattva will descend; in which land shall he be born? The Bodhisattva replied: "In the Jambudvīpa of the trichiliocosm, in the kingdom of Kapilavastu, which lies at the very center of the earth.
Furthermore, there are sixty kinds of clans in that country, yet the Śākya clan is most flourishing.
Among them, King Śuddhodana’s lineage is the foremost; they are descendants of the Ikṣvāku line, the successors of the noble kings, and are of virtuous nature."
He practiced benevolence and virtue. His wife was chaste and kind, like a celestial jade maiden. For five hundred previous lifetimes, she had constantly been the mother of a Bodhisattva;

it was now time for him to descend his spirit into her womb. Furthermore, the *Sūtra of Auspicious Responses* (*Ruiying jing*) states: "The Bodhisattva, riding a white elephant and wearing a crown of solar essence, departed from the Tuṣita Heaven.
Attended by all the devas who filled the void, they played music and scattered flowers, while a great light shone everywhere."
When he descended into his mother’s womb, the assembly of Tuṣita Heaven thought to themselves, "We too shall descend to be born in the human realm;
when the Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, we wish to hear him preach the Dharma.

They then took rebirth within the families of various kings, ministers, brahmins, elders, and householders, totaling nine hundred and ninety million. At that time, the lady saw [the following] in a dream while she was sleeping:
A man riding an elephant entered his embrace; upon awakening from the dream, he realized his own body was heavy. Heaven presented him with food and drink that arrived spontaneously;

he no longer took pleasure in the flavors of the human world. This was the fifteenth day of the seventh month in the twenty-third year of King Zhao’s reign during the Zhou dynasty, the year of Gui-chou.
In the year of Jiayin, the following year, on the eighth day of the fourth lunar month, a noble and upright man was born from the right side [of his mother].
The miraculous and auspicious events at the time of his birth cannot be fully described:
the heavens rained down flowers that scattered upon the earth, dragons sprayed water to bathe his body, and as soon as he was born, lotuses supported his feet.

When he reaches the age of nineteen, he will surely become a Wheel-Turning King; yet if he should renounce the household life, he shall realize all-encompassing wisdom.

He emitted a great radiance that illuminated the entire trichiliocosm. Such auspicious responses numbered thirty-four (the texts are too numerous to record here).

When the ministers, both internal and external, beheld these auspicious omens, they marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence and thus named [the boy].
Sarvārthasiddha (in the language of China, "Sudden Auspiciousness") was so named because at the time of his birth, all manner of auspicious signs suddenly appeared.
The king summoned the brahmins skilled in physiognomy within the kingdom to examine him; they all declared, "When he reaches the age of nineteen, he shall become a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*);

It was thus born. The *Āgama* and *Śrī-samparigraha* (or *Sūtra of Auspicious Responses*) and other scriptures also speak in this same way.
How, then, can one doubt the many consistent accounts based on discrepancies in one or two places? Therefore, the *Shishi Huiyao* states:

"Regarding the meeting of the two regions and what was transmitted by the Tripiṭaka masters, it is reasonable that the Buddha was born during the reign of King Zhou Zhao; this is the more logical view. If one follows the Zhou calendar: [The text continues with the calculation of dates.]

Mahāprajāpatī.

At seven years of age, his wisdom surpassed that of men; there was no art he did not master. At ten years of age, his strength was peerless;
he could hurl elephants and shoot forth the *yao* (shooting stars).

The scripts of the *nāgas*, *yakṣas*, and *asuras*, among others, were distinguished by their origins and details;

By the side of the road, the Prince threw [an arrow] into the air and caught it again with his hand so that it was not harmed.
Once they had reached the garden, he marked targets at various distances to shoot them. Devadatta set up a drum forty *li* away but could not surpass it;

He took the bow from the ancestral king’s armory, which no one from ancient times to the present had been able to string. Once the Crown Prince drew it, its sound shook the city.

After his arrow struck the drum, it pierced through into the earth, causing a spring of water to gush forth—[the *Xiyu ji* states that this spring exists to this day, and all who drink from it are immediately healed]. He then proceeded toward the Iron Ring Mountains (*Cakravāḍa*).
The mountains shook in six ways throughout the great trichiliocosm, and the great assembly was struck with awe, marveling at such an unprecedented event.
