He replied, "It means the formless realm. The Prince then asked, "What is the meaning of 'triloka'? He replied, "It means the three worlds. The Prince then asked, "What is the meaning of 'dvādaśāyatanāni'? He replied, "It means the twelve sense bases. The Prince then asked, "What is the meaning of 'aṣṭādaśadhātavaḥ'? He replied, "It means the eighteen elements. The Prince
He became stained by the six sense objects and then manifested supernatural powers, soaring into the air and departing.
The four preceding signs as well as this bhikṣu were all conjured by the devas of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven in order to awaken the Prince.
Having seen this, he returned to the palace with a troubled mind and no joy; the Great Father King, greatly wondering at this,
sought to dispel his sorrowful heart by providing various sources of pleasure, yet in the end it did not change his original resolve,
as he only thought of leaving the household life and wishing to escape its four afflictions.
The Crown Prince went out through the four gates and beheld various inauspicious sights; returning to the palace, he was filled with sorrow and distress.
His father, the King, was struck with wonder and alarm, and rebuked his attendants: "How is it that you did not clear the roads? Why have you allowed these inauspicious things to be seen by him?"
The ministers submitted their reports, fulfilling the King’s strict commands; there was nothing they did not inspect. Yet [the object] appeared suddenly before them, its place of origin unknown.
"This is not the fault of your subjects," [the King thought]. Knowing this to be a celestial portent, the King did not punish his ministers.
Thereupon, wishing to dispel the Prince’s sorrow, he provided hundreds of thousands of kinds of music and further added beautiful maidens to entertain him. Thus it continued until the end.
Without turning his mind [back], he earnestly addressed his father: "I pray that you grant me permission to leave the home life. Upon hearing this, the King wept and said:
"You should lay aside this intention; such afflictions have been difficult to avoid since ancient times. Why do you alone worry about them?"

"If you can indeed have an heir, I shall grant your wish. The Prince followed his father’s words and, pointing to his consort’s womb, said: "In the sixth year after this kalpa, a son will surely be born.
The Prince desired to go forth into homelessness, but the King wept and would not permit it. As he persisted earnestly without ceasing, the King said: "If you..."
"Son, you may then be permitted to leave the household life. The Prince then pointed to Yaśodharā’s womb and said, "Six years from now, you shall give birth to a son.
Subsequently, after the Prince had left the household life, six years later Yaśodharā indeed gave birth to a son.
All the Śākyas were enraged and wished to punish or kill her. The Queen stood before a fire pit and took an oath, saying, "If I have committed any wrong, may mother and child both [perish]..."

[The fire] was extinguished. If his physical remains [were to be found], Heaven shall serve as witness. Thereupon, he embraced his son and threw himself into a pit, which transformed into a lotus pond.
As the lotuses bore up his body, the King and the people of the nation finally ceased their doubts.

A sutra states that in a previous life, Rāhula was a king whose elder brother renounced the world to become a practitioner of the Way, joining the assembly to cultivate the path. One night, by mistake...
He used water from another vessel and openly confessed before the assembly, vowing that the monastic community should impose a formal penalty.
However, the assembly deliberated and declared, "This is not a true transgression," and would not grant his request. He then went to the king’s presence and earnestly petitioned for punishment.

Because the offense was minor, he was not imprisoned; instead, he was confined in the rear garden. Due to other affairs, he was forgotten there for six days without being released. By these causes and conditions...
He remained in the womb for six years. Furthermore, in a previous kalpa, Yaśodharā was traveling with her mother;

when they were on a long journey and she grew weary, she falsely claimed she had urgent business and entrusted the items she was carrying to her mother to go on ahead. Consequently, she fell behind by about six *li*.
For this reason, she carried the child in her womb for six years.

The father did not believe these words; though he knew in his heart [the truth], he did not dare to detain him. He constantly ordered the fourfold army to guard the consort, never allowing them to leave her side even for a moment.
Then the physiognomist reported: "If the Prince does not renounce the world now, after seven days have passed, he will become a Wheel-Turning King. The report was submitted to the King himself.
Nevertheless, he came to respond. Upon hearing this, the king was filled with joy and immediately commanded his ministers to maintain rigorous preparations day and night.

The four divisions of the army were stationed as guards, and the sound of the city gates opening and closing could be heard for forty li. He further commanded Yaśodharā to redouble her vigilance and scrutiny.
On the eighth day of the second month in the year of Ren-shen, at the hour of midnight when people were settled in their quarters, the Prince commanded Channa to bring the horse Kanthaka.
The Four Heavenly Kings supported the horse’s hooves, while Śakra and Brahmā held banners and parasols to guard him as he departed through the northern gate.
Suddenly, the various devas vanished from sight, and he traveled for three yojanas.
Resting in the quiet forest, he entrusted his crown and necklace to Chandaka;
Returning to his father the King’s presence, he used his sword to shave off his beard and hair, And immediately made this vow: "May all sentient beings, like me, eliminate their afflictions."

When the Prince reached the age of nineteen, on the eighth night of the second month in the year of Ren-shen, the various devas descended before him, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, and said:
"Through diligent and arduous practice over immeasurable kalpas, you have now reached full maturity."
"It is fitting that you leave the household life. The Prince replied, "The King has commanded his inner and outer officials to maintain strict guard;
I wish to depart, but have no way to do so. The devas said, "We shall employ skillful means to ensure that no one knows of it.
The Prince immediately summoned Chandaka, and Kanthaka came forward. The Four Great Heavenly Kings supported the horse's four hooves and received Chandaka. Thus [the Prince departed].
Brahmā held up his canopy, and the northern gate opened of its own accord without making a sound. Having completed his departure from the city, the devas suddenly vanished.
At dawn, the Prince traveled three *yojanas* with Chandaka and arrived at a secluded grove where they rested for a short while.
Thereupon he proclaimed: "The Buddhas of the past, seeking Bodhi, cast aside their finery and shaved off their hair and beards; I too shall do likewise."
Now it was likewise. He then removed his precious crown, necklaces, and other ornaments, entrusting them to Chandaka, and returned to his father the King.
Immediately, with a sharp sword, he shaved off his own beard and hair; Śakra received the hair and ascended to heaven to erect a stūpa for it.
Chandaka wept aloud, and the horse also neighed mournfully as they returned along the road. The father king, the paternal aunt, Yaśodharā, and the others did not see him.
The Crown Prince cried out in grief and fainted; the entire kingdom mourned him with longing, searching for him everywhere without success.
Eventually, he arrived at the dwelling of a hunter. He traded his precious robes for coarse cloth and went to visit all the various sages, inquiring after the methods for cultivating the Way.
Finding that none of these were the path to liberation, he disciplined himself and departed.
Having finally reached the banks of the Nairañjanā River, the Prince sat alone to quiet his thoughts.
After the Prince had cut off his hair, he went to the hunter’s dwelling and traded his robes of the seven precious gems for a coarse cloth *saṃghāṭī* robe, which he put on.
He then proceeded to the forest of the seer Bhārgava, where he saw that the various seers used grass, tree bark, and leaves as [their clothing].
As for their clothing, some eat flowers, fruits, grasses, and trees; some take only one meal per day, or one meal every three days;
some serve fire, water, the sun, and the moon; some lie upon thorns, or sleep before fire and water.
When the Prince asked the reason for such ascetic practices, they replied, "We wish to be born in heaven. The Prince told them, "Though the heavens are pleasant, [they are attained through] merit..."
"Throughout the cycle of saṃsāra, one ultimately ends up in the realms of suffering. Why then cultivate the causes of suffering to seek out the retribution of suffering?
Having said this, he departed for the abode of the seers Ārāḍa Kālāma and Udraka Rāmaputra to inquire about the method for severing birth, old age, sickness, and death.
The seer replied: "If you wish to sever them, practice meditative concentration (dhyāna), free yourself from sensual desires and unwholesome states, and attain..."
From the first dhyāna up to the state of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, having transcended various marks—this is called ultimate liberation;
it is the further shore for those in training. The Prince reflected that what he had known and seen was not the ultimate state;
it merely exhausted the coarse fetters, yet subtle fetters still remained. It was not the crossing to the further shore. Thus the Prince disciplined himself.
After these two sages had thus sought the supreme Dharma, they proceeded further until they reached the banks of the Nairañjanā River, where they sat in peaceful meditation.
When the King heard this, his distress increased; he selected and dispatched five men to attend them, [instructing them] that each day they should eat but a single sesame seed.
Eating a single grain of barley once every seven days, three men could not endure the hardship; they abandoned him and departed.
Two remained to attend to him at his side. For six years, his mind did not waver.
When the father-king heard of this, his grief redoubled. He immediately selected five men from among the eminent and virtuous of the kingdom who had many descendants.
Each of them sent one son—named Kauṇḍinya, Mahānāman, the Prince of the Koliyas, Daśabala-Kāśyapa, and Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra—to follow and attend upon the Prince.
Whenever he traveled, whether crossing mountains or traversing valleys, he would not choose his path;
the five men could no longer endure these hardships and said, "This madman—how can we follow him?"
"If I were to leave and return home, the King would destroy my family; it would be better to remain here. The Prince sat in quietude and practiced austerities in the forest, observing the precepts.
He ate one sesame seed and one grain of wheat per day, and for seven days he ate one sesame seed and one grain of rice. Even if there were anyone who begged from him,"
He gave these to them as well. After the five men had followed him for a long time, they found his suffering unbearable;

three of them abandoned him and departed. The Prince thought to himself: "I now practice asceticism, My body is emaciated like a withered tree, And the thread of my life is nearly severed. Self-starvation is not the true path; It benefits neither myself nor others."
"I shall accept food and drink, and only then will I attain Buddhahood.
At that time, there was a cowherd girl nearby who offered him milk-rice. When the Bodhisattva accepted it, the two women were startled and departed.
The Prince had practiced austerities for six years; he was as emaciated as a withered tree. Thereupon, he reflected: "If I remain in this state of weakness..."
He took the path with his body. Those non-Buddhists would have said, "Self-starvation is the cause of Nirvana. [The Buddha thought], "I shall receive food and only then attain the Way.

Having formed this thought, a devaputra from the Śuddhāvāsa heavens descended and exhorted Nandabalā, the cowherd girl outside the forest, to offer him wild deer meat. Once he had finished receiving the food, his body became radiant.
Joyful, the two men were startled; they thought he had regressed from his original state and departed again.
On the eighth day of the second month of the year Guiwei, he went alone to the Bodhi tree, subdued Māra, and attained Perfect Enlightenment, endowed with immeasurable merit.
The Prince went alone to the Pippala tree, where the Buddhas of the past had likewise sat upon a seat of grass. Śakra, having manifested as a man, offered him pure and soft grass;
having accepted it, he spread it out for a seat and sat down cross-legged. He gazed at the tree and entered into contemplation, moving the heavens and shaking the earth.
He emitted a great radiance that eclipsed the palaces of Māra; Pāpīyān was struck with terror, and his four daughters were sent forth.
He went to where the Prince was; with ten thousand forms of seductive charms, he sought to delude him, but the Prince remained unmoved.
Pāpīyān again led a host of eight billion beings back to harass and destroy him, saying: "If you do not rise and depart, I shall hurl you into the ocean! The Bodhisattva replied:
"First move my pure water jar, and only then will you be able to hurl me. The entire host of eight billion...
His power could not cause the vase to move even slightly. Māra then commanded King Yama to bring forth all the instruments of suffering in the Avīci hell toward the Bodhisattva’s location.
The Bodhisattva slowly raised his ūrṇā-kośa (white tuft of hair), and the hearts of the hell-beings attained refreshing coolness;
they cried out, "Namo Buddha," and were immediately released from their place of suffering. As Māra drew near, he wished to challenge him with debate.
By the power of his wisdom, the Bodhisattva extended his hand and pressed upon the earth; the earth shook, and Māra along with his host fell down, overturned.
Having thus subdued Māra, the Bodhisattva’s fetters were untied and his outflows (*āsrava*) exhausted; birth and death were severed.

When the morning star appeared, he suddenly attained great awakening and realized equal and perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), becoming endowed with the eighteen unique qualities, the ten kinds of supernormal powers (*ṛddhi-vidhi*), and the four [bases of psychic power].
He was free from all fear. At that time, the great earth shook with eighteen signs; the devas performed music and scattered flowers and burned incense.
The offerings presented by the eight classes of beings, including devas and nāgas, filled the void of space.
This was on the eighth day of the second month in the third year of King Zhou Mu’s reign, the year Guiwei. That year, the Prince had reached the age of thirty.
Furthermore, regarding the eighteen dharmas mentioned above: first, no loss in bodily conduct; second, no loss in verbal conduct; third, no loss in mindfulness;
fourth, absence of divergent characteristics; fifth, absence of non-concentrated mind; sixth, absence of relinquishment without full awareness; seventh, no decrease in aspiration.
Eight, no decrease in diligence; nine, no decrease in mindfulness; ten, no decrease in wisdom; eleven, no decrease in liberation;
twelve, no decrease in the knowledge and vision of liberation; thirteen, all bodily actions proceed in accordance with wisdom;
fourteen, all verbal actions proceed in accordance with wisdom; fifteen, all mental actions proceed in accordance with wisdom.
Sixteenth, unimpeded knowledge of the past; seventeenth, unimpeded knowledge of the future;

eighteenth, unimpeded knowledge of the present. As for the ten powers (*daśabala*): first, the power of what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-bala*); second, the power of karma; third, the power of meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*); fourth, the power of the faculties (*indriya*);

fifth, the power of inclinations (*ruci*); sixth, the power of dispositions (*carita*); seventh, the power of knowing the paths leading to all destinations; eighth, the power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*); ninth, the power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*); tenth, the power of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).

This concludes [the section on the ten powers]. Regarding the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*): first, fearlessness regarding all-knowledge; second, fearlessness regarding the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*); third, fearlessness regarding the teaching on obstacles to the path;

and fourth, fearlessness regarding the teaching on the path to the exhaustion of suffering. Regarding the eighteen marks (*lakṣaṇa*): these refer to the six modes—thundering, roaring, awakening, shaking, rising, and surging—each of which has three varieties.
Specifically, for each there are: trembling, universal trembling, and complete universal trembling; the same applies to the remaining five. Thus, they total eighteen.
Eighthly: Furthermore, Bodhiruci cites a verse from a sutra which says: "Eight years he was an infant; seven years he was a youth.
Four years he studied the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*); ten years he experienced the five desires. At nineteen he left the home life; for six years he practiced asceticism.
At thirty-five he attained the Way; at seventy-nine he entered *parinirvāṇa*. Moreover, the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states: "Seven..."

At thirty years of age he left the household life; at thirty, he attained the Way. Regarding these three different accounts, they arise because the capacities and perspectives of those with the Great and Small Vehicles differ.
At that time, he had this thought: "The wondrous Dharma I have attained I shall extensively expound and reveal."
Having already attained the Way, he brought benefit and happiness to all bodhisattvas; for twenty-one days, he contemplated the skillful means for benefiting sentient beings.
As the Lotus Sūtra says: "From the time I first sat at the site of enlightenment, observing the trees and walking in meditation, for twenty-one days I contemplated."
Reflecting thus upon these matters during the first seven days, [I thought]: "The wisdom I have attained is subtle, profound, and supreme.
Yet the faculties of sentient beings are dull; they are attached to pleasure and blinded by ignorance. How can such as these be delivered?
At that time, the Brahma Kings, the various Śakras, Lords of the Devas, and the Four World-Protecting Heavenly Kings requested me to turn the wheel of Dharma. (The second seven days)
I reflected thus for seven days: "If I were to preach only the Buddha-vehicle, sentient beings would not believe or accept it; they would destroy the Dharma and fall into evil realms.
It would be better for me not to preach the Dharma at all, but to enter nirvana quickly. Then I called to mind the Buddhas of the past.
"By the power of the skillful means I have practiced, the path I have now attained should likewise be taught as the three vehicles...
Having reflected thus, he proceeded to the Nyagrodha Grove. For twenty years he preached the four Āgamas; for eight years he preached the Vaipulya sūtras;
for twenty-two years he preached the various Prajñāpāramitā sections; and for eight years he preached the Lotus Sūtra and the Nirvāṇa Sūtra.
The two sutras state that after he had saved all those with whom he shared a karmic connection and his great task was completed, he reached the age of seventy-nine and entered *parinirvāṇa*.
Such is the general outline. Now, citing the Patriarch’s own words, I shall briefly indicate their essentials. As stated in the *Tiantai Sijiaoyi*:
"Master Zhizhe, using the five periods and eight teachings, analyzed and interpreted the holy teachings of one lifetime that flowed eastward."

The teachings are exhaustively complete without exception. Regarding the "five periods": first, the period of the *Avataṃsaka*; second, the period of the Deer Park; third, the period of the Vaipulya; fourth, the period of the *Prajñāpāramitā*;

and fifth, the period of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and *Mahāparinirvāṇa*. These are called the five periods. Regarding the "eight teachings": the sudden, the gradual, the secret, and the indeterminate.
These four are termed the "modes of transformation," which are like worldly medical prescriptions. [The remaining four are] the Tripitaka, the Shared, the Distinct, and...
"Round. These four are called the teachings of transformation (*nirmāṇa-dharma*). They are like preparing medicinal decoctions. These constitute the eight teachings.
[First, regarding the time of the *Avataṃsaka*: when the Tathāgata first attained perfect enlightenment, he was at the Site of Enlightenment (*śamatha-mārga-maṇḍala*).

He was surrounded at once by the forty-one stages of the Great Beings of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya-mahāsattva*), as well as the devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings whose roots had matured in previous lives, like the moon enveloped by clouds.]
At that time, the Tathāgata manifested the body of Vairocana and preached the *Pūrṇa-sūtra*; therefore, it is called the Sudden Teaching.

[Second, regarding the period at the Deer Park: Because the Buddha’s sudden teaching was of no benefit to those with the capacities of the three vehicles, he did not move from the site of enlightenment (Ajapāla-nyagrodha) but traveled to the Deer Park.
There, he cast off the precious and noble robes of Vairocana and donned the tattered and soiled garments of the six-foot-tall [Śākyamuni].
Kāśyapa, [the Buddha] likewise descended from Tuṣita Heaven, entered the womb and was born, took a consort and begot a son, left home to practice austerities for six years,
and thereafter sat upon a seat of grass beneath the Bodhi tree to become a Lesser Response-body Buddha (hīna-nirmāṇakāya) of one *zhang* and six *chi*.
For those with the faculties of the Three Vehicles, he taught the arising and ceasing of the Four Noble Truths, the twelve links of dependent origination, the six perfections, and so forth.
The Dharma. Having heard it, people practiced according to the teachings and realized the truth of the partial [vehicle]. [Regarding the third period of the Equal Dharma:
those followers of the Two Vehicles were attached to the Lesser Vehicle, claiming it to be ultimate and unable to enter the Great Vehicle;
therefore, the *Vimalakīrti*, *Saṃdhinirmocana*, *Laṅkāvatāra*, *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*, *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, *Śrīmālā-devī-siṃhanāda*, and other Mahāyāna sūtras were taught.]

[Sūtra]: Fearing that [the previous teachings] were partial, he rejected the Small Vehicle; extolling the Great, he praised the Perfect. When those of the Two Vehicles heard this Dharma, they felt inward shame and remorse;
their minds gradually became pure and refined as they felt ashamed of the Small and aspired to the Great. [The Fourth Period, the Time of Prajñā]:

As the faculties of sentient beings gradually matured, he next taught the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā*, the *Prasphullitaprajñāpāramitā*, and the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā*.

In the various Prajñāpāramitā sections such as the *Prajñā*, he summoned Subhūti and Śāriputra to instruct the bodhisattvas, enabling them to understand the interpenetration and purification of all dharmas.
These three periods, being contrasted with the sudden teaching of the *Avataṃsaka*, are collectively termed "gradual.

Fifth, during the period of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and *Nirvāṇa*, the capacities and conditions of the disciples had matured; thus, he was able to lead them toward the opening, revealing, awakening, and entering of the Buddha’s [Dharma].
...of knowledge and vision. Next, he preached the Lotus Sūtra to open up the previous sudden and gradual teachings and bring them together into that which is neither sudden nor gradual;
thus it is said that "the provisional is opened and the real is revealed," "the three are brought together and unified into one," and "the provisional is set aside and the real is established.

Those śrāvakas, having received the command to turn the wheel of teaching during the time of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, all knew the Dharma-treasury; therefore, when they reached the assembly of the Lotus Sūtra, [the Buddha] revealed, showed, awakened, and caused them to enter the state of Buddhahood.
Regarding their knowledge and vision, they are merely granted the prediction of attaining Buddhahood. Next, as for the teaching on *nirvāṇa*, there are two meanings.
First, for those who are not yet mature, the four teachings are further expounded to fully discuss the Buddha-nature, enabling them to realize true permanence and enter Great *Nirvāṇa*.

Therefore, it is called the "Teaching of Gathering the Scattered. Second, for those of dull faculties in the final age who give rise to views of annihilationism within the Buddha-dharma—thereby shortening their life of wisdom and losing their Dharma-body—the Buddha establishes three kinds of provisional means to support the one perfect reality; therefore, it is called the "Teaching of Upholding the Vinaya and Discoursing on the Eternal.

If one discusses its timing and flavor, it is identical to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*; if one discusses its internal divisions, it contains both pure and mixed [teachings], as well as the Small [Vehicle].

[They are] different. Why? Because the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* exclusively teaches the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), whereas the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* teaches the four teachings in a mixed manner.

Question: The meanings of the five periods and the sudden and gradual [teachings] are thus established. What are the meanings of the secret, indeterminate, *xiang*, *tong*, *bie*, and *yuan* [teachings]?
Answer: Regarding the secret teaching, within the first four periods, the Tathāgata’s three wheels of inconceivable power [act simultaneously].
Therefore, for some individuals he teaches the sudden approach, while for others he teaches the gradual approach; these do not know of one another, yet each is able to gain benefit.

Thus it is called the "Secret Teaching. Regarding the "Indefinite Teaching": among the four periods [of the Buddha's life], the Buddha expounds the Dharma with a single voice, yet sentient beings each attain understanding according to their own kind. This is the inconceivable power of the Tathāgata.
Power: It can cause sentient beings to obtain sudden benefit from gradual teachings, and to obtain gradual benefit from sudden teachings.
Because the benefits obtained in this way differ, it is called the "Indeterminate Teaching.

Regarding the methods for practitioners to cultivate, sever delusions, and realize the Way within the four teachings such as the *Piṭaka*, they cannot be recorded in full; I shall now briefly indicate them. As for what is called the "Teaching of the *Piṭaka*":
This refers to the Tripiṭaka of the Hīnayāna: first, the Sūtra Piṭaka, which consists of the four Āgamas;

second, the Abhidharma Piṭaka, which includes treatises such as the *Abhidharmakośa* and the *Mahāvibhāṣā*; and third, the Vinaya Piṭaka, which comprises the five divisions of the Vinaya and so forth.

Śrāvakas practice based on the four noble truths of arising and ceasing, severing all afflictions of view and thought within the three realms to realize the truth of partial liberation. Pratyekabuddhas...

Contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination, one awakens to the principle of the true reality. Such a person has exhausted both the views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) and further erodes the residual habit-energies (*vāsanā*);

therefore, they rank above the *śrāvakas*. The Bodhisattva, relying on the realm of the Four Noble Truths, gives rise to the Four Great Vows and cultivates the practices of the Six Perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*).
Having completed three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, he enters the stage of the "Worldly First" (*laukika-agra-dharma*), giving rise to true outflow-free wisdom (*anāsrava*).

He suddenly severs the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of both views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-saṃjñā*) beneath the Bodhi tree, attaining the body of an Inferior Responsive Transformation Buddha (*hīna-nirmāṇa-buddha*) of one *zhang* and six *chi* in height.

For the sake of those of dull faculties belonging to the Three Vehicles, he preaches the Four Noble Truths of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-vyaya-catur-āryasatya*), manifesting the appearance of an aged bhikṣu and entering *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*. [The term "entry" applies universally.]
Regarding the "Shared Teaching" (Tongjiao): it encompasses the preceding Tripitaka teachings and extends to the subsequent Distinct and Complete teachings.

Furthermore, because the three types of practitioners within this teaching equally employ the path of wordless silence to realize that the substance of form enters into emptiness, it is called the Shared Teaching. Śrāvakas merely sever the afflictions of views and thought within the triple world;
they cannot eliminate habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), which is like burning wood into charcoal. Pratyekabuddhas further penetrate these habitual tendencies, as if... [burning them away].
Just as charcoal turns to ash, so too may a Bodhisattva, even if they have severed [afflictions] to the point of exhaustion, become identical to those of the Two Vehicles.
Yet, by sustaining residual habits (*vāsanā*) to moisten their rebirths, they sport with supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) and purify Buddha-fields.

When the conditions of sentient beings ripen, they suddenly sever the remaining habits beneath the Bodhi tree of the seven jewels, taking a celestial robe as a seat, and manifesting in a body that is both inferior and superior to attain Buddhahood. For the sake of those of the Three Vehicles, they preach the Dharma of non-...

Regarding the Four Noble Truths, although the three types of practitioners realized by both the Tripiṭaka and Shared Teachings are the same, they differ eternally in terms of "great" versus "small" and "skillful" versus "clumsy.
Why is this? The Tripiṭaka Teaching is "small" because it does not penetrate the Great [Vehicle], and it is "clumsy" because it analyzes form to enter emptiness.

Although within its own teaching there are distinctions of superior, middling, and inferior among these three types of practitioners, when compared to the three types of practitioners of the Shared Teaching, they are all uniformly dull-witted.

The faculties (*indriya*). In terms of their universal application, they are "greatly skillful. They are called "great" because they constitute the initial gateway to the Mahāyāna; they are "skillful" because the substance of form (*rūpa*) enters into emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

Although within this teaching there are three types of persons—superior, middling, and inferior—if one looks at them from the perspective of the *Āgama* teachings, they are all uniformly considered "sharp" (*tīkṣṇa*).
Within the *Prajñā* and *Vaipulya* sections, the *Sādhāraṇa-prajñāpāramitā* and others belong to this very teaching. As for the term "shared *prajñā*," it is shared...
[This refers to the teaching of the Two Vehicles. [Regarding the term "Distinct Teaching" (biejiao): it is distinct from the two preceding teachings and distinct from the subsequent Perfect Teaching.

At the very moment one first gives rise to the mind of enlightenment, one immediately attains perfect awakening.
Furthermore, he caused the great beings to each discourse on the dharmas of the five stages.

Such a perfect teaching is borne by those of great capacity, like a massive mountain; though the small may sit within its presence, they cannot carry it.
Like those who are deaf or mute, or like the son of a deceased family; one day arriving at his house and seeing his father’s majestic and dignified presence, he flees in fear.
The *Avataṃsaka* takes the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) as its essence: it is perfectly interfused and unobstructed, where the one and the many are non-dual, encompassing all from beginning to end.
Without arising or ceasing, it is inconceivable. "Kṣaṇa" here refers to a single thought-moment (*ekacitta-kṣaṇa*). The "three periods" are the past, present, and future.
This means that within a single thought-moment, one completely encompasses the limits of the three periods. As for the "three dharmas":

Furthermore, the great bodhisattvas such as Vajradhvaja and Dharmamati, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, each spoke on the Dharma of the five stages.
The "Gates" refer to the stages of dwelling, practice, direction, the grounds (*bhūmi*), and so forth, up to the wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).

Furthermore, when the youth Sudhana first encountered Mañjuśrī on the eastern side of the city of Awakening, he suddenly realized the *dharmadhātu*. Regarding those of great capacity, the Sūtra says: "For example, when the sun rises, it first shines upon..."

Therefore, although those of the two vehicles may occupy the same seat, they are as if deaf or mute. Thus, the *Sijiao yi* states:

Reflecting upon the skillful means employed by the Buddhas of the past, I now realize that the path I have attained should likewise be taught through the three vehicles.
At that time, the Buddhas of the ten directions all appeared and praised me, saying, "Excellent!
Just as the Buddhas of old have practiced, you too should temporarily employ skillful means; cast off this precious garment of *śamatha*."
Wearing robes sixteen feet long and soiled with dust, he did not stir from the field of tranquil extinction, yet traveled to the Deer Park to first teach the five former companions.
There he turned the Wheel of the Four Noble Truths; upon hearing it, they immediately attained fruition.
From this point, the names of the Three Jewels appeared in the world. For twelve years thereafter, he preached the four Āgama sūtras.
All those who possess the three vehicles, by relying on cultivation, all realize the Way;

this is called the teaching of "half-letters," like using yellow leaves to stop a child's crying. It is as when a father employs skillful means to lead his son to remove filth, yet once he has received the wage for a single day, he considers himself sufficient.

For the sake of sentient beings, he distinguishes and teaches the three vehicles. Having heard the voice of the Buddhas, I immediately proceeded to Vārāṇasī.
The mark of the quiescence of all dharmas cannot be expressed in words; yet, by the power of skillful means, he spoke for the sake of the five bhikṣus (and so forth).
Furthermore, the analogy of fine garments and soiled clothes is as explained in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. I shall now present a brief summary thereof.
There was a householder whose son had been lost for a long time. That son, while wandering about, eventually arrived at his father’s residence.
Seeing his father’s majestic and dignified presence, he was struck with fear and fled. The father saw him from afar and recognized him as his own son; he sent a messenger to seize him.
The impoverished son cried out in alarm and fell to the ground in a swoon. The elder, employing skillful means, removed his precious garments and immediately clothed him in soiled raiment. Then...

The explanation is divided into two sections. Specifically, from the "Introductory Chapter" to the "Chapter on Peaceful Practices," comprising fourteen chapters, is called the Trace Gate (*jimon*).

all three bodies accomplished from the time of the Great Penetration (*Mahāvyūha*) until the present day are termed "traces. The *Miaole ji* states:
Others do not perceive the present *迹* (traces) and *本* (source) of this sūtra; they merely know to seek the *dharmakāya* exclusively through the superior [aspect].

In this way, the fundamental dharma (*法本*) becomes inferior when compared to the superior versions shared by other sūtras. If one obtains the long version of the original text, one remains close to the *迹* and does not lose it.

If one speaks only of the *dharmakāya*, one has already lost the intermediate stage, let alone the distant original source. The *Xuanyi* states: "The *迹* [of this sūtra] and those of the various sūtras..."
There are points of agreement and points of difference. Fundamentally, it differs entirely and eternally from the various sutras. The commentary states:

regarding the traces, they agree with the various sutras in that they are "perfect" (en) within their respective sections; they differ in that these various sections concurrently incorporate the three teachings.
Regarding the fundamental [reality], it differs entirely and eternally because the various sections do not clarify the primordial foundation of long antiquity.
Having completed the explanation of the traces of his career, he now wishes to reveal the lifespan of his original ground.

He summons his original retinue to proclaim what has never been spoken before: from the time the Buddha attained enlightenment until now—throughout immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, as numerous as the atoms of buddha-fields—the kalpas that have passed exceed even this; such is the venerable One who is in his final birth before Buddhahood.
Since even he cannot fathom its limit, how much less so for other sentient beings? How could they know even a small fraction of it?
Though it is said that he has entered nirvāṇa, this is not true extinction; it is like a physician who goes to another land for the sake of treating his mad son.
The "Chapter on the Lifespan of the Tathāgata" states: "Since I attained Buddhahood, immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas have passed.

Suppose one were to grind five hundred thousand million billion *nayuta* *asaṃkhyeya* trichiliocosms into fine dust, and then pass beyond five hundred thousand million billion *nayuta* *asaṃkhyeya* lands [with each grain of dust]."
"Take one mote of dust from this. Continuing in this manner until all these motes of dust have been exhausted, would it be possible to know the number of these lands?
Maitreya Bodhisattva and the others addressed the Buddha together, saying, "These worlds are immeasurable and boundless."

"In this matter, we too have not attained full understanding. The Buddha said, "If all these worlds—both those where atoms are placed and those where they are not—were entirely reduced to dust, and one were to count one kalpa for each atom, the time since I attained Buddhahood would exceed that number.
Since then, I have constantly remained in this Sahā world, preaching the Dharma and teaching and transforming beings."
He also guides and benefits sentient beings in immeasurable other lands. It continues until it says:
"For example, there was a skilled physician who expertly treated all manner of illnesses. This man had many sons, and due to certain circumstances, he traveled far away to another country.
Later, his sons drank the poison of others. At that time, their father returned home and saw his sons."
Some have lost their original minds, while others have not. Relying on the prescribed methods, he refines the medicine and gives it to them to drink.
Those whose minds have not been lost recover from their illness upon drinking the medicine; however, the others whose minds have been lost are unwilling to take it.
The father thinks to himself: "I must now employ skillful means to make them take this medicine. He then reflects: "I am now old and infirm; the time of my death has come."
"This is an excellent medicine; I have now left it here for you to take and consume. Having given this instruction, he departed for another country and sent a messenger back with the message:
"Your father has already died. At that time, when the sons heard that their father had passed away, their hearts were filled with great sorrow and distress, and they thought to themselves:
"If our father were still alive, he would have compassionately protected us; now he has abandoned us."

When one’s parents pass away in a distant land, one reflects upon being orphaned and exposed, with no further reliance or support; the mind then becomes awakened, and one takes the medicine, whereby the illness is entirely cured.

The Buddha is also like this. If he were to remain long in the world, beings of meager merit would see the Buddha constantly present and would thus harbor feelings of complacency and indolence, failing to conceive the thought that such a meeting is difficult to encounter or to give rise to a heart of reverence. For this reason, the Tathāgata...
Although their coming was not real, they speak of "extinction" (nirvāṇa), and so forth. Regarding those who were originally his retinue:

after the Buddha had finished teaching the traces [of his career], he wished to manifest his original ground and his disciples from that time. They emerged from the earth in numbers beyond description;

all had long planted the roots of virtue, were endowed with various samādhis, and possessed great supernatural powers (*abhijñā*). They were not those converted by him when he attained enlightenment at Gayā. As...

The father is young and the son is old; this causes the multitude to lack faith. For this reason, the Tathāgata speaks of a long life span in order to resolve the doubts of the multitude and cause them to obtain great benefit. This is the tenth stage of faith.
When the Buddha spoke of the span of his life, those who gained benefit were beyond counting; the multitudes of atoms within the eight realms all resolved their minds upon Bodhi.

Furthermore, there were various Bodhisattvas who increased their path and diminished their births—many attained the stage of the Three Worthies, some ascended to the Ten Holy Grounds, and others entered the Diamond Mind.
Those who dwell near the stage of Great Enlightenment and attain this supreme victory—
according to the "Chapter on the Differentiation of Meritorious Qualities," when the Buddha spoke of his long lifespan, six hundred and eighty trillion *nayuta* of sentient beings,
as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, attained the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); furthermore, there were a thousand times more bodhisattvas.

They shall attain the *dhāraṇī* of hearing and retaining [the teachings]. Furthermore, even Bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms within one four-continent world-system shall, in a single lifetime, attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

It is further said: "If there are sentient beings who, upon hearing that the Buddha’s lifespan is thus long and far-reaching, are able to give rise to even a single thought of faith and understanding, the merit they obtain shall be immeasurable and limitless. If there should be...
If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*,
practice the five *pāramitās* for eighty quadrillion (*nayuta*) *koṭis* of kalpas, then compared to this merit, the former merit does not equal even a hundredth part,
a thousandth part, a hundred-thousand-million-billionth part— indeed, it cannot be reached by any calculation or analogy.
It cannot be reached by analogy. If there were anyone possessing such merit who were to regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, it would be impossible.
Furthermore, the *Miaoxuan* states: "Upon hearing of the merits of the original ground, they become even more profound and vast."

It is immeasurable and cannot be compared to the benefits previously attained within the traces [of the path]. Why is this? Because the Buddha-realm becomes increasingly profound and its merits are likewise vast;
therefore, it causes these bodhisattvas to increase their Path and diminish their births (the "Path" refers to the three virtues, and "births" refers to ignorance).
Regarding this ultimate stage, the *White Lotus Society Text* states: "During the Buddha's lifetime, even those who were ready to receive the teaching had not yet heard of his long-lasting lifespan.
We, living now in the final five hundred years, have heard the Buddha reveal and clarify the lifespan of his original ground;
how can we not feel joy and fulfillment in forming such a supreme connection?"
Such a perfectly wondrous Dharma, I remained silent for many years without speaking. Today I finally expound it, like a king untying the jewel from his topknot.

This is called the "perfect within the perfect," the "king among kings," the supreme flavor of the clarified butter, and the excellent medicine for all ailments. For those who rejoice in it for even a single thought-moment—
The merit thereof is beyond measure. When the Buddha spoke this sutra, eight human years had passed.

The sutra says: "For example, it is like a powerful Wheel-Turning King who, having achieved victory in battle, bestows various rewards upon his soldiers—elephants, horses, chariots, fields, and houses;
or grants them clothing, various precious jewels, male and female slaves, and wealth."
He joyfully bestows gifts. Just as a king, seeing one who is brave and capable of performing difficult deeds, unties the bright jewel from his topknot and gives it to him, so too is the Tathāgata.
As the Dharma King, he transforms the world through great compassion and according to the Dharma.
Seeing all people undergoing various sufferings and desiring liberation, yet battling against the various Māras, he speaks for the sake of these sentient beings.

Through various dharmas and great skillful means, I have preached these various sutras. Now that I know sentient beings have gained strength from them, I finally preach this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* Sūtra at the very end, like a king removing the bright jewel from his topknot to bestow it upon another.
This sutra is the most honored, the supreme among all sutras; I shall protect it and not reveal it recklessly. Now is precisely the right time for you.

Thus it is said. Regarding the phrase "the perfect within the perfect," this refers to the meaning of perfection within the aforementioned three periods [of the Buddha’s teaching]. It is non-dual and indistinguishable from the perfection of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

As for the other [teachings], such as the *Avataṃsaka*, which combine the distinct with the perfect, they are coarse; [in that case, the *Avataṃsaka* combines the distinct teachings while preaching the perfect].

At the Deer Park, only the Tripitaka was taught. In the Vaipulya [sūtras], the "half" was contrasted with the "full. In the Prajñāpāramitā, both the Shared and Distinct [vehicles] were included, while the Perfect Teaching was correctly expounded [only] after waiting for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* to open, harmonize, and sublate [the other teachings]. Only then could it be called "wondrous.

One should know that the transformation of the coarse into the wondrous is due to the merit of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*; therefore, it is said to be the "most perfect within the perfect" and the "most wondrous within the wondrous. As for the phrase "the king among kings":

Regarding the term "King" (王者), the *Myōryaku-ki* states: "In the past, before they had united, it was as if two or three minor kings within a single country each governed their own subjects without having submitted to a great state.
After they had united, however, they were collectively brought under a single transformation, so that the people had no second ruler."

In a country there are not two kings. Now, having abolished the various minor kings and established only one king, the Master of Expedient Teachings [the Buddha] taught that the name "king" is not without meaning.
Regarding the term *amṛta* (ghee), the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) states: "The cow is a metaphor for the Buddha; the milk is a metaphor for the *Avataṃsaka*."
Curd is a metaphor for the Tripiṭaka; fresh butter is a metaphor for the Vaipulya; matured butter is a metaphor for the Prajñāpāramitā;
and clarified butter (ghṛta) is a metaphor for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and *Nirvāṇa*. Regarding the statement that it is "an excellent medicine for illness," the Sūtra says:

"This sūtra is the excellent medicine for the illnesses of the people of Jambudvīpa. If a person has an illness and hears this sūtra, the illness will be extinguished; they shall neither grow old nor..."
"Death. The commentary on the text explains: "Not aging is bliss; not dying is permanence.

This means that those who hear this sutra attain the understanding of permanence and bliss, which remains vividly in their hearts, free from all fear or apprehension. Regarding the term "rejoicing," the sutra says:
"If there is anyone who hears this sutra and, having rejoiced, departs from the Dharma assembly and goes to another place—whether it be a city or a town..."
In streets, villages, hamlets, and fields, they expound the teachings according to what they have heard and to the best of their ability.
Others, having heard it, likewise rejoice and teach it in turn. Thus it is passed on in succession until it reaches the fiftieth person.
The merit of that fiftieth person who rejoices is immeasurable and boundless, beyond the reach of calculation or analogy—even if one were to count for four hundred million billion years.
In incalculable worlds, there are sentient beings within the six realms of existence. Suppose there is a person who seeks merit and provides them with all the articles of entertainment they desire.
To each and every sentient being, he gives as much of the seven treasures as would fill Jambudvīpa, along with palaces, towers, and pavilions made of those jewels.
Having practiced such giving for a full eighty years, he further proclaims:
Through this Dharma transformation, they all simultaneously attained the stage of *srotāpanna*, up to and including the stage of *arhat*.

The merit of these people, compared to the merit of the fiftieth person who rejoices upon hearing even a single verse of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, does not equal even one part in a hundred thousand million billion.
The holy master Zhiyi of Tiantai extensively expounded and calculated this comparison, saying: "Even if [the former] were to fill the Jambudvīpa..."
The merit of all the people of Jambudvīpa does not equal the merit of a single person in Aparagoyānī.

The merit of all the people filling Aparagoyānī does not equal the merit of a single person in Pūrvavideha. The merit of all the people filling the three continents does not equal the merit of a single person in Uttarakuru.
The merit of all the people filling the four continents does not equal the merit of a single Cāturmahārājika deva. Four...
The merit of the gods does not equal that of a single Śakra; even the merit of the gods of the six heavens does not equal the merit of a single Brahmā.

The merit of Brahmā does not equal the merit of a Lesser Sage (hīna-ārya); the Lesser Sage does not equal the merit of one who has realized the Truth (tattva-ārya). One who has realized the Truth does not equal the merit of a Lesser Bodhisattva (kṣudra-sattva);
the merit of a Lesser Bodhisattva does not equal the merit of a Great Bodhisattva (mahāsattva). A Great Bodhisattva does not equal this fifth [level].
Regarding the merit of ten people rejoicing upon hearing the Lotus Sūtra: why is this? It is because that [merit] is not the Buddha-dharma;
it is not real; it is not perfect. Although they abide in the final fruit, it does not equal my initial resolve. Such is its meaning.

Furthermore, as for this fiftieth person: at first, they possess but a single moment of understanding; they rejoice in themselves and rejoice in others, yet they have not yet engaged in practice, so their benefit does not extend to others.
Such is the merit they have obtained. Therefore it is said: "When a fine *śāla* tree (a species of wood) stands upon the ground, its sprouts are already a hundred spans in girth;
when a *koka* bird (a species of bird) is still within its shell, its voice surpasses that of all other birds—how much more so, then, at the very beginning?"

Among those in the assembly, there were some who, upon hearing this, rejoiced with sympathetic joy. Furthermore, a sutra states: "It is only after billions of billions of kalpas, reaching even beyond the inconceivable, that one may hear this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
Even if the world were consumed by the fires at the end of a kalpa, it would not be difficult to enter those flames carrying dry grass without being burned;
yet, for me to have this sutra read for even a moment in the evil age after my parinirvāṇa—this is [far more difficult]."
"It is difficult. This sutra is difficult to uphold. If one upholds it even for a moment, such a person is praised by all Buddhas;
this is called one who upholds the precepts and practices dhūta austerities... (and so forth).
The work of transforming conditions being now complete, the time for *nirvāṇa* has arrived.
On the fifteenth day of the second month in the final year of Ren-shen, he proceeded directly to the city of Kuśinagara, between the twin *śāla* trees.
There, he earnestly instructed the assembly, saying: "I am now perpetually entering extinction; those who have any doubts,"
"You should come and ask. Receiving this command, they vied with one another to inquire;

He answered each question as it arose for the entire assembly of devas and humans. They all scrambled to present their final offerings, Yet he remained silent and refused them all, Accepting only the offering of Cunda.

The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: On the morning of the fifteenth day of the second month, the World-Honored One emitted light that illuminated the great trichiliocosm, reaching even the sentient beings of the six realms throughout the ten directions;
those who encountered this light had their transgressions extinguished. Furthermore, there were fifty-four assemblies [of followers].
At that time, they gathered like clouds and cried out with one voice, "Alas! Alas! How is it that the Sun of Wisdom has suddenly set?
Then all the celestial kings and human kings vied with one another to present offerings, but the Buddha would not accept them; he accepted only the offering of the elder Cunda.
According to the *Jinglü yìxiàng* (Heterogeneous Phenomena of the Sūtras and Vinaya), when the Buddha was about to enter parinirvāṇa, there was an elder named...
Cunda said, weeping, to the World-Honored One: "From this day forward, we shall be without a master and without a savior;
poor, destitute, and solitary. We wish to seek from the Tathāgata our sustenance for the future. We only pray that you will compassionately accept our humble offering and then enter parinirvāṇa.
The Buddha said: "I shall now eliminate your poverty for you, raining down the rain of the unsurpassed Dharma upon your bodies."
It is like a field that causes the sprouts of the Dharma to grow and enables you to fulfill the *dāna-pāramitā*.
At that time, humans and devas all came to offer their gifts, yet the Buddha accepted none of them. The great assembly cried out: "How marvelous! Cunda has accomplished such great merit;
our offerings have been rendered in vain. Desiring to satisfy the hopes of the multitude, the World-Honored One manifested [emanations] from every single pore.
The Buddhas were immeasurable; each and every Buddha had an immeasurable assembly of bhikṣus, all of whom received offerings.
Śākyamuni Tathāgata himself accepted the offerings presented by Cunda.
The Buddha, fearing that beings of the final age would give rise to the view of annihilation regarding the Dharma—
thereby shortening their life of wisdom and losing the Dharmakāya— further established three kinds of provisional means to support the one perfect reality:
that all possess Buddha-nature, that all dharmas are eternal, and [the case of] the butcher Pāṇḍuka.
Establishing the ground, one attains Buddhahood instantly; even Ajātaśatru, the king who committed the five heinous crimes, had his offenses extinguished and realized the wondrous realization.
Know that the dharma of nirvāṇa is such that sin and merit are fundamentally equal. If you wish to swiftly attain Buddhahood, you must study this dharma.
The meaning of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* has already been shown previously; there is no need to record it here at length.
As for the butcher Wide-Forehead (*Pṛthu-lalāṭa*), upon hearing the words that "all things possess Buddha-nature," he cast down his butcher’s knife and became a Buddha on the spot.

Furthermore, when King Ajātaśatru heard the words of Devadatta regarding the killing of his father, Bimbisāra, his mind immediately became distressed and feverish, and a rash broke out over his entire body.

There was a boil for which none of the physicians in the world were able to provide a cure. There was a great physician named Jīvaka who addressed the king, saying, "To treat this illness, nothing is as effective as taking refuge in the Buddha.
The king followed his advice, and they went together to the place where the Buddha was.

Upon hearing that the nature of sin is empty, he gave rise to the bodhicitta, and the sores on his body were immediately healed, and so forth. [This illustrates] the five periods of the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world.
The sequence of the teaching is as follows.
Now, although the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, preach various dharmas in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings, they do not exceed four gates:
first, the gate of existence; second, the gate of emptiness; third, the gate of both existence and emptiness; and fourth, the gate of neither existence... [neither non-existence].
It is not the gate of emptiness (*śūnyatā-mukha*). The gate of emptiness is taught for the sake of transforming those who cling to existence;

even the gate of neither existence nor emptiness is taught for the sake of transforming those who cling to both existence and emptiness. Therefore, the Buddha has no fixed teaching, nor is the Dharma fixed;
he merely teaches and reveals in accordance with the capacities and needs of sentient beings. Alas! Now that we are far removed from the Sage, we live in an age of strife and contention.
Truly, the minds of sentient beings are hardened by attachment; they compete over self and others, failing to take as their foundation the Great Meaning of the Tathāgata’s skillful means.
Within the Dharma of the single source, they divide it into branches and contend with one another, even to the point of mutual destruction. How painful, how painful!
Now, this unworthy one relies on the teachings of the Patriarchs to offer a single analogy that encompasses all doctrines, in order to still these disputes. It is like the great ocean.
Its hidden currents flow through the four continents and the world, reaching everywhere. Thus, whether on level ground, high plateaus, or even on mountain peaks, one finds water by digging;
or when encountering a fissure in rock, it gushes forth as a spring. Many springs combine to form a stream; many streams combine to form a river;
and many rivers flow into the great ocean, becoming of one single taste. This is...
This means returning to the source and reverting to the origin. Those various waters each have their own names—some are called certain springs, some certain streams, and some certain rivers;
yet their source is but a single sea. In this way, all these waters ultimately flow back into the sea.
How could there be such designations as "great" or "small," "profound" or "shallow"? It is the same with the Dharma-gates.

When the Tathāgata first attained perfect enlightenment, he initially preached the *Avataṃsaka*. However, for those of small capacity, it was like speaking to the deaf—of no benefit. Thereupon, moved by compassion, he established skillful means to lead such beings;
thus, he provisionally taught the *Āgamas*, followed by the *Vaipulya*, then the *Prajñāpāramitā*, and then...
He preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*. Although the names of such teachings differ, their meaning is one and the same. Why is this?
At the end, on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, he opened up the provisional and revealed the real, causing all dharmas to merge into a single flavor, equal and without distinction.

Thus the sutra says: "The true reality of all dharmas is that the characteristics of the world are eternal. It is known that although there are a thousand differences and ten thousand distinctions, [they are ultimately one].
It is not that these are not the sublime Dharma. According to the *Avataṃsaka*, there is nothing that is not the *Avataṃsaka*;
according to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, there is nothing that is not the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. According to the *Prajñāpāramitā* and the Vaipulya sūtras, it is likewise in every respect.
Alas! Some people have not yet understood this principle; those who rely on the *Avataṃsaka* claim that it alone is the root while all else are but branches. [They thus] indulge in...
Those who claim that the *Lotus Sūtra* alone is the king while all other sūtras are merely subjects say:
"Only this is correct; others are not. They delude themselves and delude others; their delusion is extreme.

If one follows the fundamental tenets of the Mahāyāna, one ought to transcend narrow attachments and achieve unhindered, harmonious integration. If one maintains such attachments, how can that be the practice of the Mahāyāna?
O person! Furthermore, as for the various great masters of antiquity, they were certainly not unaware of such meanings.

That they, while at the margins of the propagation of the Dharma, forcefully constructed arguments of right and wrong or suppressed and exalted this or that—this was precisely the skillful means of a Bodhisattva of Great Power to transform others.
How much more so for the Great Sage Tathāgata; throughout the entire Tripitaka, it is stated everywhere that this sutra...

First, it is merely for the sake of circulation. Furthermore, there are those who revere Chan and say, "Chan is a separate transmission outside the teachings," regarding it as a superior dharma while disparaging the scriptural teachings.
These people do not realize that within the teachings, the essential point of the mind is exclusively revealed.
Thus, this delusion arises; it is simply the fault of not having read the sutras early on. What is there to wonder at?
Furthermore, the reason our Buddha, the Tathāgata, extensively expounded the various teachings was none other than to manifest the True Principle.
As a sutra says: "The wondrous essence of Vairocana pervades all places; there is not a single dharma that is not the Buddha-dharma. This is so.

This is because there is no ultimate truth that exists apart from words and letters. If one seeks the truth apart from the text, it is like searching for gold within a collection of miscellaneous vessels.
If one claims that the truth transcends words and letters, such a person is merely a scholar of the Tripiṭaka.
Only when one contemplates the non-duality of principle and text can one be called a practitioner of the Mahāyāna. Therefore, my Master Zhizhe of Tiantai, in the *Fahua Xuanyi*, stated:

In explaining a single word of the sutra, all six sense-objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) are taken as the sutra. For instance, a single color of black ink can express immeasurable teachings, immeasurable practices, and immeasurable principles.
If one knows that the word is not a word, is neither a word nor a non-word, and is free from the two extremes of inversion, this is called purity.
Being pure, there is no karma, which is called the self (*ātman*). Being the self, there is no suffering, which is called bliss. When there is no suffering, [one attains liberation].
That which is without birth and death is called "constant. Why is this? Characters are conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); that which is beyond characters is ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
That which is neither character nor non-character is the single true reality (*eka-tattva-satya*). This single truth is the three truths; the three truths are the single truth.

To understand characters in this way is to constantly read this sūtra without holding a scroll in one's hand, and to universally recite all the scriptures without uttering a word with the mouth. Thus spoke the Buddha.
It does not appear in the world; it constantly emits the Brahma-voice. Without mental deliberation, it universally illumines the Dharma-realm.
One should know that the black characters are the root of all dharmas; the same applies to blue, yellow, red, and white. This is taking form as the sūtra;
sound, fragrance, taste, touch, and mental objects are likewise so. Furthermore, regarding the method for reciting the sūtra while contemplating the mind, it asks: "What is the sūtra?"

This is the scripture; this is the binding axis. The reciter should attend to it with the mind and recite it with the mouth, producing it through the harmony of the gums and palate. Is there a self-body? Is there no self-body? Who is the one who recites?
Upon thorough investigation, one finds that ultimately there is no "I" capable of reciting. Although there is no scripture being recited, there is the scripture as a physical volume.

Regarding paper, ink, and written characters: although there is no one capable of reciting them, my own body exists; although they are neither internal nor external, they are not separate from the internal and external;
although they are not the sutra scrolls themselves, they are not separate from the sutra scrolls; although they are neither mind nor mouth, they do not issue forth apart from mind and mouth.
From beginning to end, there shall be no error or deviation; this is called the inconceivable and subtle threefold contemplation (*trividha-vipaśyanā*).

Among the Buddhas of the three periods of time, there are none who have not been born from this contemplation. If one can thoroughly comprehend that every phrase and every sentence is the secret treasury of the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*), and if one recites them so as to permeate the mind, then they will permeate the perfectly interfused three truths (*tri-satya*) inherent within the nature of the mind.
...and thus it was manifested. How could one possibly realize the principle apart from the text? (The above is the Patriarch’s teaching.
Viewed in this light, the mind and the teaching should not be two different things. What "mind" is there that is transmitted separately outside the teachings?
If you take the World-Honored One’s holding up of the flower as being the separate transmission, even this does not fall outside the teachings. As for Bodhidharma’s addressing Huike...

The Master said, "Bring forth your mind, and I shall settle it for you," and he further instructed him using treatises such as the *Xuemai guanxin lun* (Treatise on Observing the Mind through the Bloodline).
Is this not the Teaching? Moreover, the Sixth Patriarch, Master Huineng, attained enlightenment upon hearing the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and greatly propagated the style of our school.
How can one say that there is a "separate transmission outside the Teaching"? Furthermore, those who realize the principle by relying on the Teaching are fully recorded in the biographies.
Record: These books were piled as high as mountains. Among them, there were those who attained their original nature upon seeing a single verse;
those who achieved wondrous enlightenment through recitation; those who developed wisdom through copying; those who attained thorough penetration by examining just a few characters;
and those who reached the truth merely by wearing the text upon their heads. Those who obtained such benefits were beyond counting. If...
It is not that the mind is purely teaching, nor that teaching is purely mind; how could evil ever be thus?
Indeed, when Jīvaka holds poison, it all becomes a wondrous medicine; whatever Maṇibhadra grasps is nothing but a precious treasure.

Even if a person with eyes acts crudely or speaks wildly, it never deviates from principle. Therefore, although the former sages may have spoken words that appear contrary to the teachings, they were merely...

"In order to resolve these manifold doubts," the Venerable One replied, "So be it. The King immediately issued a proclamation to assemble the sages and worthies from afar. He addressed the Saṃgha, saying:

Furthermore, six hundred and twenty-eight Daoist practitioners from the various mountains of the Five Peaks, such as Lü Huītong, left the household life. Two hundred and thirty palace ladies and attendants also left the household life.

More than fifty people followed his example by chewing their tongues until they died. Thereupon, the Emperor was greatly pleased and established ten monasteries:
seven were located outside the city to house monks, and three were inside the city to house nuns.
From the Han dynasty down to the Tang, many Buddhist scriptures (peidie) emerged. Translated into complete collections, they comprise more than six thousand fascicles (*zhù*).
During the Western Jin period, two hundred and sixty works were translated, one hundred and eighty monasteries were built, and [the number of] monks and nuns...

There were three thousand seven hundred people. During the Eastern Jin period, two hundred and sixty translations of scriptures were produced, one thousand seven hundred and sixty-eight temples were built, and there were twenty-four thousand monks and nuns.
During the Song period, one hundred and ten translations of scriptures were produced; one thousand nine hundred and thirteen monasteries were constructed;
and there were thirty-six thousand monks and nuns.
During the Qi period, seventy-two sections of translated scriptures were produced; two thousand ten monasteries were built;
and thirty-two thousand five hundred monks and nuns resided there.
During the Liang period, two hundred and thirty sections of translated scriptures were produced; two thousand eight hundred and forty-six monasteries were built.

There were more than eighty-two thousand seven hundred monks and nuns. During the Later Liang period, one hundred and eighty monasteries were established, housing three thousand two hundred monks and nuns.
During the Chen period, eleven translations of scriptures were produced; one thousand two hundred and thirty-two temples were constructed;
and there were thirty-two thousand monks and nuns.
During the Yuan-Wei period, forty-nine translations of scriptures were produced; thirty thousand and eighty-five temples were constructed; and [there were] monks...
There were two million nuns.
During the Gao Qi period, fourteen sections of translated scriptures were produced and forty-three monasteries were constructed.
When the number of monks and nuns was missing from the records, sixteen sections of translated scriptures were produced and nine hundred and thirty-one monasteries were constructed.
During the Sui dynasty, eighty-two translations of Buddhist scriptures were produced; three thousand nine hundred and eighty-five monasteries were constructed;
and there were two hundred and thirty-six thousand two hundred monks and nuns.
From the Yongping era of the Han dynasty to the Yongjia era of the Jin dynasty, there were only forty-two temples.

When the Later Wei established their capital at Luoyang, they constructed over one thousand monasteries; when the Later Zhao established their capital at Ye, they built over eight hundred monastic sites.

Among these sixteen kingdoms, there were certainly no small number of monks and nuns who translated scriptures and founded monasteries; however, because these states were usurpers and illegitimate, they are not recorded here. Furthermore...

From the Tang dynasty through the Five Dynasties, up to the *Da Song Jin Que Lu* (Great Song Record of the Golden Gate), it is evident that the flourishing propagation of Buddhism was unsurpassed during the three dynasties of Tang, Song, and Jin.
Although their records are missing, the general pattern may be known from the foregoing. The *Preface to the Phonology and Meaning of the Tripitaka* states:

"Regarding the scriptural treasury of the Buddha’s single lifetime, beginning with the preaching of the *Dharmacakra-pravartana Sūtra* and culminating in the discourse on the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, [the origin]..."
From its inception to its conclusion, there were a total of ten billion sections (*bhāṣya*). Within these sections, the number of fascicles was so doubled and multiplied that it defies calculation.
Since the golden coffin vanished from sight, after the first millennium, there arose Arhats, Bodhisattvas, Tripitaka masters, and Śrāmaṇeras who stood preeminent in their respective eras.
The disciples of these two [traditions] vied with one another, giving rise to mutual slander and curses, even killing their own teachers. From that time onward, the Māras and heterodox schools...

[The teachings] became truly numerous [in India], yet they were encroached upon and damaged by heterodox doctrines. Thereupon, the great nāga Śaṅkha, following the Buddha’s final injunctions, took all the sūtras and vinaya and entered the palace of Anavatapta;
this is known as the "Oceanic Treasury" (Sāgara-piṭaka). Subsequently, the virtuous masters such as Dharmaratna and Dharmagupta...
Each [of these collections] took the remnants of the Dragon Canon from Western India to be translated in the Eastern Land of Thunder (China).

Throughout successive dynasties, they have been widely propagated, totaling over four thousand four hundred scrolls; including miscellaneous records and biographies, they comprise six hundred and thirty-nine cases in all. Alas!
These are but the lingering rays of the Buddha-Sun and a single drop from the ocean of Awakening. It would be like mistaking a speck of dust for the great earth, or pointing to a single...
"Grass was made into Mount Sumeru. Furthermore, the *Shishi huoyao* (Essentials of the Buddhist Community) states:

From the year of the *dingmao* cycle during the reign of Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty until the year of the *gengwu* cycle in the Kaiyuan era of the Tang dynasty, the Mahāyāna Tripiṭaka currently circulating in the world consists of a total of six hundred and eighty-six works, comprising two thousand seven hundred and sixty-two fascicles. As for the Hīnayāna Tripiṭaka...

In total, there are three hundred and thirty sections, comprising one thousand seven hundred and sixty-two fascicles; together with the above, they amount to four thousand five hundred and seven fascicles.
Through successive generations of emperors and their various ministers and officials, these have been propagated and expounded with a single-minded dedication.

The state prospers and the person is at peace. As for those who slander [the Dharma], they shall incur calamity in this very life, and their suffering in future lives shall likewise be great; once it has come to pass, what can regret avail?
Alas! As listed above, the kings, dukes, and ministers of successive dynasties translated scriptures, constructed temples, and glorified [the teachings].
The holy transformation that universally benefits all living beings is such as this.

Were it not for the Great Beings who receive the Buddha’s mandate to propagate the Dharma, how could such a thing be possible? Alas, those who disparage this and thereby bring calamity upon themselves!
They do not cease their minor delusions, yet they entangle themselves in great suffering for long kalpas. Many such cases are recorded in the biographies; there is no time to list them all here.
A full record has been compiled. Now, I shall briefly cite one or two instances to demonstrate this.

At the beginning of the Wei dynasty, Emperor Wu first held the Buddhist teachings in high esteem; he frequently invited eminent monks to engage in discussion with him and established numerous Buddha images on a grand scale.
Various offerings were made. There was the official Cui Hao, who did not believe in Buddhism; he frequently spoke with the Emperor, repeatedly slandering it.
Because the Emperor regarded him as eloquent and learned, he placed considerable trust in him and grew somewhat indifferent toward the Buddha. Later, the Emperor set out on a western campaign.
Upon arriving in Chang’an, he entered a monastery to observe it. There, śramaṇas were gathered together drinking wine.
He entered an empty hall and saw that there was property, bows, furs, and goods entrusted for storage by local governors and wealthy men.

The Emperor then grew resentful and issued an edict to execute the śramaṇas of Chang’an, burn and destroy the Buddha images, and command all four quarters of the realm to act exactly as had been done in Chang’an.
"If there are those who harbor or conceal śramaṇas, they shall all be executed at their gates. Furthermore, he issued an edict stating:
"In the past, the Later Han was deluded by perverse and false beliefs and became confused regarding the eternal laws of Heaven.

Consequently, government and instruction failed to prevail, rites and righteousness were utterly ruined, and the Way of Ghosts flourished, treating the laws of the King with utter contempt. From that time until now, successive dynasties have suffered calamity and disorder. Heaven..."
The punishments were extreme and the executions severe; the population was nearly exterminated. Within a radius of five *fu*, everything has been reduced to mounds and ruins.

For a thousand *li* there is desolation, and no human traces are to be seen—all of this stems from these [rebellions]. I, the Emperor, have inherited the celestial mandate and find myself presiding over the final decadence of this era.

Desiring to eliminate the false and establish the true, I wish to restore the governance of the ages of Fuxi and Nonghuang. I shall sweep away the barbarian deities and obliterate their vestiges. From now on...
Thereafter, those who served the Hu deities or fashioned their images—whether in clay or bronze—were executed by the gate.
This was entirely due to the followers of Liu Yuanzhen and Lü Boqiang of the Han dynasty, who adopted the fabricated words of the Qihu (the Kushans).
They employ the hollow and false doctrines of Zhuangzi and Laozi, attaching them to [the Buddhist teachings] and augmenting them; all of these are not true.

This has led to the point where the royal law is neglected and no longer enforced. Only an extraordinary man in this world could perform extraordinary deeds—none other than I who can eliminate these deceptive artifacts of successive dynasties.
All those possessing Buddha images and foreign scriptures shall destroy them by smashing and burning.
He was incinerated; all śramaṇas, regardless of seniority or juniority, were buried in mass graves. This occurred in the third month of the seventh year of the Zhenjun era.
In the second month of the thirteenth year, he broke out with leprosy and passed away.
When Emperor Wu wished to destroy Buddhism, there was a śramaṇa named Jing’ai, whose years and virtue were flourishing and whom both monastics and laypeople looked to for refuge.
Upon hearing this, he said: "Since I am a disciple of the Buddha, how could I witness its extinction while remaining seated with this physical frame, maintaining a complacent stillness?
He immediately submitted a memorial to oppose the plan. Although the Emperor accepted his words, his resolve had already been made.
