Because he was in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), he did not hear [the summons]. Da’ai then entered the Southern Mountains and inscribed a verse upon a rock, saying:
"May I, having cast off this body, Swiftly attain mastery over my own form. Wherever there is benefit to be found, I shall protect the Dharma and save sentient beings.

[He continued: "...Having thus spoken, he cut the flesh from his own body and spread it upon the rock; he drew out his entrails and hung them from a tree, and holding his heart in his hands, he passed away. Furthermore, at Yizhou..."

As for those who had accumulated [faults] at the gates and along the paths, he next went out to admonish them. When they would not heed his words, he and seven like-minded companions fasted before an image of Maitreya.
After seven days of ritual prostrations and repentance, they all passed away simultaneously on the spring equinox of the second year of the Chengguang era of the Qi dynasty.

The Emperor assembled the śramaṇas and issued an edict, saying: "I have received the Mandate of Heaven to bring peace and unity to the realm. Throughout the world, [the Dharma] has been propagated..."

The three teachings have now all been abolished. However, as for Confucianism, its expansive literary tradition, its administrative arts, its rites and righteousness, and its loyalty and filial piety are appropriate for the world;

therefore, it must be preserved. Furthermore, the True Buddha is formless, and one expresses devotion through remote veneration. Yet the Buddhist scriptures extensively praise the construction and honoring of images, pagodas, and temples;
such magnificent and elaborate constructions bring about immense merit. Since these [images and structures] are truly insentient, how [can they produce merit]?
They were able to bestow favors upon the foolish, who placed their faith in them and exhausted their precious wealth, all to no avail but for increased expenditure;
therefore, they must be eliminated. All scriptures and images shall be destroyed. The kindness of parents is profound, yet these śramaṇas show them no respect;
their rebellion is extreme, and they shall all be returned to their homes to honor filial governance. This is my intention—what do the various virtuous ones think? At that time...
More than five hundred people, including the eminent monk Shamen Shangtong and others, looked at one another without speaking, merely bowing their heads and shedding tears.
Thereupon, Dharma Master Huiyuan stepped forward and replied: "That the true Buddha is formless is indeed as Your Majesty’s decree states.

However, living beings who possess ears and eyes rely upon the scriptures to hear of the Buddha and depend upon images to represent the Truth. If these are now abolished, there will be no means by which the Way may flourish."
Jing said: "The Emperor says that the True Buddha of empty space is known by all of us naturally; there was no need for scriptures or images. Yuan Huiyuan replied:
"Before the reign of Emperor Ming of the Han, scriptures and images had not yet arrived. Why, then, did the sentient beings of this land not know the True Buddha of empty space?

If one could know the existence of the Dharma naturally without relying on scriptural teachings, then before the Three Sovereigns, when written characters did not yet exist, people should [have known it as well]."

"One knows for oneself that the Five Constants and other such dharmas exist. Why, then, did the people of that time recognize only their mothers and fail to know their fathers, behaving no differently than birds and beasts? The Emperor had no answer. Tanyuan spoke again:

"If you claim that images are insentient and thus neither bring guilt nor merit, then how can it be that the images in the seven ancestral temples of the state are sentient and yet are falsely honored and served?"
The Emperor did not answer this challenge, but instead said: "The Buddhist scriptures are the laws of foreign lands; they are unnecessary in this land, and therefore I have abolished them.
As for the seven ancestral temples established by my predecessors, I do not consider them correct either, and shall likewise abolish them."
Yuan said: "If one were to reject foreign laws because they are not used in this land, then what was spoken by Zhongni originated in the state of Lu;

it would follow that it should also not be practiced in the territories of Qin and Jin. Furthermore, if you consider the seven ancestral temples to be improper and intend to abolish them, this would be a failure to honor your ancestors.
If the ancestors are not honored, then the order of the *zhao* and *mu* lineages will be lost. Thus,"
"The Five Classics are useless; yet you previously upheld Confucianism—where is that statement now? If the Three Teachings are all abolished in this manner, with what shall the state be governed?
The Emperor replied, "Lu, Qin, and Jin had distinct borders, yet were they not all unified under the transformation of the King?"
Therefore, this does not resemble the difficulty found in Buddhist scriptures. Yuan Hui said:

"If Qin and Jin both follow a single transformation and the scriptural teachings are universally practiced, then although the territories of China (Zhendan) and India (Tianzhu) differ, they are both situated within the four seas of Jambudvīpa under the single transformation of a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin).
Why then do they not equally follow the Buddhist scriptures? Yet now they alone are abandoned. The Emperor [responded].
Furthermore, there was no answer. Huiyuan said, "As for those who leave the Sangha to return home and honor filial support, even the Confucian classics state:
'Establish oneself and practice the Way to bring glory to one's parents. This is precisely what constitutes filial conduct; why must one necessarily return home?

The Emperor said, "The kindness of parents is profound; they provide for one through both physical care and nourishment. To abandon one's kin for the sake of strangers does not constitute ultimate filial piety. Huiyuan replied, "If it is as Your Majesty suggests..."
"Your Majesty, those on your left and right both have parents. Why do you not release them? Instead, you subject them to long-term labor for five years, during which they do not see their parents.
The Emperor said, "I too follow the rotation of service; when my turn comes to rest, I am able to return to serve and support them.

Yuan Hui replied, "The Buddha also permits monks to cultivate the Way according to circumstances during the winter and summer, and to return home to serve and support their parents during the spring and autumn. This is why Maudgalyāyana went out to beg for food."
[The Buddha] provided sustenance for his mother; the Tathāgata carried the coffin to the burial site. These principles are universally applicable and cannot be discarded unilaterally.
The Emperor remained silent. Huiyuan then spoke out with a firm voice, saying: "Your Majesty now relies on your power and authority to act as you please, destroying the Triple Gem.
You are a person of false views. In the Avīci Hell, there is no distinction between the noble and the lowly. How can Your Majesty not be afraid? The Emperor was indignant.
However, Zuo Se stared directly at Yuan Yuan and said, "If only the common people can obtain happiness, I, the Emperor, shall not shrink from the various sufferings of hell.
Yuan Yuan replied, "Your Majesty employs heterodox teachings to transform the people; you are currently planting the karma for suffering.

You shall surely share in the descent into Avīci with Your Majesty—what joy could there be in that? The Emperor offered no reply, but merely said, "Let the monks return for now. At this, [the monks departed].
He destroyed all the monasteries and bestowed them upon the princes and dukes to serve as their residences.

Three million monks were demoted and returned to the status of soldiers and commoners, re-entering the household registers. He scraped away the images of the Buddhas and burned the scriptures and teachings.

The wealth and merit of the Triple Gem were inventoried and brought into the palace. Less than a month after the Emperor had done this, a pestilential vapor began to fester within him; he withdrew to the Yunyang Palace, whereupon—
[Fragment] The *Táng míngbào jì* (Records of Miraculous Retribution of the Táng Dynasty) states:

When Emperor Tiānyuán ascended the throne, he issued an edict to assemble all secular monks and nuns from throughout the empire and commanded that they shave their hair while leaving their beards intact.

All temples previously granted to princes and dukes were confiscated and restored as monasteries, which were then bestowed upon various śramaṇas to maintain. Furthermore, [he] entered and exited the palace, and [issued] orders regarding the property of the Triple Gem.

He commissioned statues, each of which was installed according to its respective invocation; all were exactly as they had been before. Consequently, the Great Teaching once again circulated in the world.
The *Táng Míngbào Jì* (Records of Miraculous Retribution from the Táng) states: In the eighth year of the Kāiyuáng era of the Sui dynasty, Dú Qí of Jǐngzhào died.
After three days, he returned and said, "I saw King Yama. The King asked, 'What office did your father hold? I replied, 'My father served in the Zhōu dynasty.'"
In the morning, he was a high-ranking officer of the Office of Life-Span (Siming). The King said, "If that is so, I have been wrongly pursuing you;
you may be released and returned home quickly. He asked again, "Do you know the Emperor of Zhou? He replied, "I know him very well. The King said, "You may go and see him.
An official led him to a certain place where the doors, windows, rafters, and tiles were all made of iron. Through an iron window, he saw someone inside.
The man was extremely emaciated; his body was the color of iron, and he wore an iron yoke and shackles. Having been granted an audience, he wept and said, "Great Sir, why do you suffer so?
He replied, "I believed the words of Wei Yuanchong and slandered the Buddha-dharma; therefore, I am undergoing this suffering."
Liyi said, "Why have you not cited Wei Yuanchong's commentary? He replied, "I have indeed sought it out;
however, when the authorities searched throughout the three realms, they claimed it could not be found. Had it been here this morning, I would have been released by evening.
Furthermore, he said: 'The Son of Heaven of the Great Sui once ate with me; the granaries, treasuries, jade, and silk were also my store.'"
"Your Excellency, if you return now, I pray that you report this matter to the Son of Heaven and perform great meritorious deeds on my behalf to save me.
You should also cultivate blessings for Yuanchong; come quickly to rescue us. If you do not arrive, there will be no hope of liberation.
I pray that upon your return, you will explain this in detail. When Emperor Wen heard this, he issued an edict throughout the empire, requiring each person to contribute one coin.
This was done to pursue merit.
Emperor Wuzong of the Tang, whose personal name was Yan, in the fifth year of the Huichang era, following the words of Zhao Guizhen, Liu Yuanzheng, and others, extensively destroyed Buddhism.
He issued an edict throughout the empire to abolish monasteries, retaining only one monastery in each prefecture, and [one] in the capital.
In each street of the capital, two temples shall be retained, with thirty monks assigned to each.

As for the images from the monasteries throughout the realm that have been abolished, they are to be entrusted to the Iron Commissioner to be cast into coinage; those made of bronze or iron are to be recast into agricultural implements.

Images made of gold, silver, and other precious metals are to be delivered to the Ministry of Revenue (Duzhi). An imperial decree has been issued regarding all images of gold, silver, and so forth belonging to the gentry and commoners.
A one-month deadline was set. Should they violate this, they were to be dealt with according to the laws on confinement.

Of the great monasteries throughout the realm, more than four thousand six hundred were destroyed; forty thousand *āraṇyakas* [forest hermitages] were abolished; and twenty-six thousand five hundred and more monks and nuns were returned to lay life.
In the third month of the sixth year, the Emperor fell ill; his moods fluctuated between joy and anger, and his illness worsened.

His illness became extremely grave; within ten days, he was unable to speak. Although the ministers requested an audience, it was not granted, and neither those within nor those outside the court knew whether he was at peace.
On the twenty-third day of that month, he passed away at the age of thirty-three.

When Emperor Xuanzong ascended the throne, he changed the era name from Wuda to Dazhong and issued an edict stating that as for the monasteries that had been destroyed, if there were monks of long-standing virtue and renown who were able to restore them, they should be permitted to do so.
He was appointed as the founding abbot. He subsequently executed twelve Daoist practitioners, including Liu Xuanzheng.
Thereupon, the perverse winds suddenly ceased, and the sun of the Buddha shone once more. The blind masses found relief, and the Emperor’s virtue became all the more exalted.

In the first year of Xiande (the year of Yimao), Emperor Shizong of the Later Zhou, named Rong, issued an edict stating that all monasteries throughout the empire not holding an imperial plaque were to be demolished.
In total, thirty thousand three hundred and thirty-six such establishments were destroyed;
their images were melted down to cast coins, and forty-two thousand four hundred and forty monks and eight thousand seven hundred and fifty-six nuns were defrocked. The Emperor—

Before long, they met with untimely deaths and passed away. Furthermore, after the Great Teaching had been suppressed by Wei Wu, Tang Wu, and Zhou Shizong, they all soon suffered from extraordinary illnesses and perished before reaching their natural lifespans; these traces are clearly recorded in historical accounts.
Yet, there are no texts stating that they suffered retribution in future lives, though this can be inferred from the precedent of Zhou Wu. Moreover, as a sutra states: "If a person commits..."

Regarding the five heinous crimes: one who dies while committing these falls into the Avīci Hell like a spear falling from the hand, undergoing immeasurable suffering for thousands of millions of billions of kalpas with no prospect of escape.
What are the five? First, shedding the blood of a Buddha; second, slandering the True Dharma;
third, destroying stupas and monasteries; fourth, killing an ācārya; and fifth, causing a schism in the harmonious Saṃgha. Within this—
Among these five [offenses], one falls [into hell] even by committing just one. Believe these words!

Those dark rulers, with burning evil intent, destroy stupas and monasteries, melt down and scrape images of the Buddha, burn the scriptures, pitfall-trap the śramaṇas, and demote the Saṃgha to the status of commoners.
Having thus fully committed all five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*), after their lives end, they do not fail to fall into Avīci and undergo great suffering.
It is impossible that there should be such suffering and distress. Alas, how lamentable!

Furthermore, there have been not a few instances where ministers and officials brought about calamities for themselves through their slanders and defamations. As cited in the *Supplementary Notes to the Treatise on Tiantai Stopping and Contemplation*:
"Zhou Xiangwei Yuanchong wished to extinguish the Buddhist teachings. In the second year of the Tianhe era, he submitted a memorial to the throne, saying: 'The Tang..."
In the era of the Yu dynasty, the state was secure despite the absence of Buddhist temples; in the Qi and Liang dynasties, the mandate ended even though monasteries existed.
If something benefits the people and strengthens the state, that accords with the Buddha’s mind. Now, the Buddha takes great compassion as his fundamental principle;

he would never subject the common people to arduous labor for the sake of devoutly honoring clay and wood, nor would he request the construction of grand temples to welcome [the Buddha], nor allow the myriad subjects of the four seas to be burdened by such works.
I urge you to establish a righteous course. I observe that monasteries are currently biased toward the Two Vehicles and the Five Classics.
As for the "Universal Welcome Monastery," it makes no distinction between clergy and laity, nor does it choose between enemies and kin.

It takes city walls as stupas and temples, regards the Zhou Emperor as the Tathāgata, uses the suburbs as monastic quarters, treats private couples as the holy assembly, and promotes those of superior virtue as the Three Pillars of Authority, following the elders.
He was appointed as the Elder (Sthavira). He selected benevolent and wise men to serve as administrators and sought those of courage and strategy to serve as Dharma Masters.

Consequently, throughout the six directions there was no sound of the tyrant Zhou, and in the eight quarters there arose the songs of Zhou. Flying creatures and aquatic life dwelt peacefully in their nests and lairs;
those of water and land were each allowed to live out their lives. After submitting these fifteen matters in a memorial to the Emperor, he developed malignant sores on his body. Thus it came to pass.

[This entry is] missing. The *Mingbao ji* (Records of Miraculous Retribution) states: From the beginning of the Wude era until the fourteenth year of the Zhenguan era, Fu Yi constantly slandered and disparaged the Buddha and the monastics.
In the autumn of that year, he died suddenly and was assigned to the hell of Yuezhou. Cui Hao, the Minister of Education, assisted the Wei Emperor Wu in destroying the Great Teaching;
in the end, he was executed by the five punishments and fell into the Hell of the Plucked Tongue. [The entry for] Zhu... is missing.

The *Lín zhuàn* (Biography of Lín) states that in the nineteenth year of the Dàyuán era of the Eastern Jin dynasty, Dharma Master Dao’an cast a statue of the Eighteen-Foot Amitābha Buddha at the Western Capital of Xiāngyáng. It was possessed of considerable spiritual efficacy.

During the time of Emperor Wǔ of the Northern Zhou when the Dharma was suppressed, Sūn Zhézhì, the military governor of Xiāngzhou, being a non-believer in the Dharma, first intended to destroy this golden image. Within the district...
Men and women wailed in grief, filling the roads. The wise, both monastics and laypeople, sighed with sorrow. His rage intensified further;
he rebuked his attendants, ordering them to speedily crush it. First, he ordered one hundred men to bind its head with ropes, but they could not pull it even slightly.
Thinking they were not exerting themselves, he had the overseers flogged. He added another hundred men, yet it still would not move. He added three more...
A hundred men could not move it as before; when five hundred more were added, they finally pulled it over, its sound shaking the earth and making everyone tremble with fear.
Yet Zhe alone leaped for joy. He immediately ordered it to be melted down, shouting aloud in delight at the success. Having finished the task, he returned home;
barely a hundred paces away, he suddenly fell from his horse, lost his voice, stared straight ahead, and could not lift his limbs. This continued until nightfall.

The Emperor then passed away, and the multitude were all filled with joy. Han Yu, the Vice Minister of the Board of Personnel, submitted a memorial titled "A Memorial Remonstrating Against the Buddha’s Bone," which stated:
"If the Buddha possesses a spirit capable of bringing about calamity or fortune, then whatever misfortunes or transgressions there may be should be visited upon my person.

Having presented this to the throne, the Emperor became exceedingly enraged and intended to sentence him to death. Cui Zhi, the Palace Secretary, along with the various remonstrance officials, all submitted memorials to argue against the punishment.
Jiù himself also repented and reproached himself, begging for forgiveness for his crime. Thereupon, he was granted clemency and spared from death, but was banished far away to Cháo Prefecture.
Instances such as these are beyond counting.
The Dharma shall abide in the world for twelve thousand years: one thousand years each for the True Dharma and the Semblance Dharma, and ten thousand years for the Final Dharma.
Within this, five periods of five hundred years each constitute the "Five Firm Periods.
As the faculties of sentient beings gradually undergo change and decline, the Dharma likewise diminishes and vanishes. The first is the Firmness of Liberation.
At this time, human faculties are sharp; meeting the truth, they easily attain the Way. This is no different from the Buddha’s own era.

The second is called "firmness in meditative concentration": when human faculties are somewhat inferior, one must practice *dhyāna* for a long time before attaining the three types of supernormal knowledge (*trividyā*).
The third is called "firmness in extensive learning": as emotional consciousness gradually becomes dull and obtuse, [one relies on learning].
Though they have acquired much learning of the Dharma, their wisdom lacks clarity in discernment.

The four types of stūpas and temples are firmly established, and people vie with one another to build Buddhist shrines; in every place, dharma-grounds (maṇḍalas) are set up, yet those who practice for realization are but one in ten thousand.
Fifth, strife and contention are firm: they merely debate various doctrines, yet fail to comprehend the profound and esoteric meaning.

Regarding the arrogance toward oneself and the disparagement of other schools, Vinaya Master Daoxuan stated: "The first millennium after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa is called the Age of True Dharma (*saddharma*), meaning that those who have realized the truth and attained sainthood are indistinguishable in their awakening.
The second millennium is called the Age of Semblance Dharma (*pratirūpadharma*), meaning that one practices and studies according to the teachings, yet [the realization] is based on the mind..."

Consciousness gradually becomes dull, and one encounters the principles only through successive stages. One maintains pure abiding and subtly accords with the sacred intent; yet, regarding the discernment of wisdom (*prajñā*), it has not been extensively cultivated or clarified.

Because this resembles the Path but is not the true Path, it is called the Semblance Dharma (*saddharma-pratirūpaka*). That which follows the third millennium is termed the Final Dharma (*paścima-dharma*);

from its initial foundation until ten thousand years have passed, the Way of Concentration and Wisdom (*samādhi* and *prajñā*) is separated, and one merely propagates worldly precepts and maintains the protection of dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*).

Although their traces of meditative practice were equal, their mental applications were restless and agitated, completely deviating from right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*). Therefore, both of them became causes for the Dharma of the Final Age (*pāścāttya-dharma*).
The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "The True Dharma (*saddharma*) lasts for a thousand years, and the Semblance Dharma (*pratirūpa-dharma*) likewise.

Because women were permitted to enter the order, the True Dharma was reduced by five hundred years. However, if women can observe the Eight Rules of Respect (*gurudharma*) and practice the Path according to the Dharma..."
Then the True Dharma will remain in the world for another thousand years. It is further said that the Buddha-dharma will remain in the world for ten thousand years:
during the first five thousand years, those who leave home to practice the Way will attain the three types of supernormal knowledge and spiritual wisdom;

during the latter five thousand years, those who leave home to practice the Way will not attain the three types of supernormal knowledge and spiritual wisdom (and so forth). Regarding the statement that nuns observe the eight respects: the first is that a bhikṣu...
1. Those who uphold the great precepts—the bhikṣuṇīs—should receive the true Dharma from them; they must not treat them with contempt or engage in frivolous jesting. 2.
When a bhikṣu has upheld the great precepts for more than half a month, the bhikṣuṇīs should pay him homage and serve him, without harboring thoughts of disorder toward those who are newly trained.
3. Bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs must not reside together in the same dwelling. 4. From oneself...
Examine one another. If there are improper words, accept them without retorting; treat what is heard as not heard, and what is seen as not seen.
Fifth, reflect inwardly on one's own faults and evils; do not speak with a loud voice or display lustful attitudes.
Sixth, when with bhikṣus, inquire only about the matters of the Sūtras and Vinaya; do not engage in idle talk concerning worldly affairs. Seventh.
First, if one violates the laws and precepts, one must go before the assembly every half-month to perform repentance.
Eighth, although a bhikṣuṇī may have observed the great precepts for a hundred years, she must take a seat below a newly ordained bhikṣu and pay her respects with humble reverence.
If bhikṣuṇīs are able to uphold these Eight Rules of Respect for their entire lives, then the True Dharma will remain in the world for another one thousand years.
During the final five hundred years, there will still be those who practice and realize [the truth]; thereafter, it will continue until ten thousand years.

In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, regarding the practice of much cultivation without attaining [the goal] as one, the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata,

during the final five hundred years in this age of turbidity and evil, if there are members of the fourfold assembly who wish to cultivate and practice this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, in the third..."

During these seven days, you should practice with single-minded diligence. When the three weeks have been completed, I shall mount a six-tusked white elephant and, together with immeasurable bodhisattvas, appear before that person and preach the Dharma for them.

Because that person has seen me, they will immediately attain samādhi and a dhāraṇī called the "Revolving Dhāraṇī" (Sūtra-dhāraṇī), [which enables them to retain] hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis [of teachings].
The *Svādhiṣṭhāna-dhāraṇī* (and so forth). From this we know that even during the final five hundred years, there will still be those who cultivate and realize [the path].
These five hundred years constitute the beginning of the *mofa* (Dharma-ending) age. The *Sūtra of the Wondrous Supreme Samādhi* states:
"One hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, one hundred thousand people will leave the household life, and ninety thousand will attain the Way. Two hundred years..."

When one person leaves the household life, ten thousand people attain the Way; even during the five-hundred-year period [of the final dharma], when one hundred thousand people leave the household life, not a single person attains the Way (and so forth).

Furthermore, the *Candragarbha-sūtra* states: "In my age of the Final Dharma, though billions upon billions of sentient beings may initiate practice and cultivate the Way, not a single one shall attain it" (and so forth). Judging from this, within the age of the Final Dharma...
Even if one practices extensively, if there is little direct realization, it serves merely as a seed for future causes.
At this time, those born as humans have meager merit and thick obscurations; they perform many unwholesome deeds and will fall into evil realms at death.
Though they may follow the teachings, their minds are greedy for gain and offerings.
Never having had a single thought of faith, how could the Dharma defile his spirit?
It is like the lion-insect that eats its own flesh; those within the Dharma are likewise: by relying upon it, they destroy themselves.
The *Saptasvapna Sūtra* says: "Though a lion has been dead for many days, the various beasts still feel dread and none dare [approach it]."
After many days have passed, worms will naturally arise within its body and consume all the lion’s flesh.
When the Tathāgata appears in the world, non-Buddhists submit and take refuge; he wanders without fear, just as the various beasts hide away when a lion roams.
After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, the remaining teachings are like the carcass of a dead lion; after many days, the various beasts [devour them].

Terrified, they did not dare approach again. This is a metaphor for the Buddha’s True Dharma: within one thousand seven hundred years, neither external paths nor celestial Māras will be able to destroy it.
After many days have passed, worms arise from within the lion’s body and devour the lion’s flesh until it is gone;
this is a metaphor for after one thousand seven hundred years following the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, when the disciples of the Buddha break the precepts.
This is evil conduct; it destroys the Buddha’s teachings from within.
Furthermore, there is the celestial Māra who assumes the form of a disciple of the Buddha, manifesting strange phenomena to delude the masses.
He disparages the Buddha and praises the ways of Māra; the Buddha’s Dharma is expelled from his heart, and he casts it aside like a discarded sandal.
Magic accords with worldly passions; follow it as one drinks when thirsty.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "These ten kinds of demons, during the time of the final age, will appear within my Dharma, having left the household life to cultivate the Way.

They will claim for themselves that they have already attained the realization of Perfect Enlightenment, yet they will praise lustful desire and violate the Buddha’s monastic discipline. Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*... [text continues]

The *Pán jīng* (Bàn jīng) states: "In the final age, those belonging to the faction of Māra will manifest in the forms of bhikṣus, arhats, and the like, to confound and destroy the True Dharma and revile the precepts.
Seven thousand years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the human lifespan will be reduced to thirty years; from that point on, it will continue until it reaches ten years."
The three calamities arise in succession: during the eon of famine, all grains perish; where can one find refined flavors?
People merely boil their own bones for drink. Emaciated by hunger, many meet their death.
During the eon of disease, non-human spirits flourish, vomiting poison like fierce flames; those who encounter it lose their lives instantly, and corpses fill the entire world.

During the *śastra-kalpa* (the age of swords), people are mostly full of malice; whatever they grasp becomes a blade, and fathers and sons slaughter one another until human lineages are nearly extinguished.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "When the human lifespan is thirty years, there is the calamity of famine. At this time, people frequently engage in [malicious conduct]..."

It is wretched. The devas and nāgas, filled with resentment and reproach, do not send down sweet rain; exquisite food and drink can no longer be obtained, and they must feast together upon boiled, decayed bones.
If they obtain even a single grain of rice, wheat, millet, or barnyard grass, it is as heavy as a maṇi jewel, which they hide away and guard with great care.
Those sentient beings mostly lack physical strength; they stumble and fall, unable to rise, until they are nearly all dead.
Thus, this calamity of famine lasts for seven years, seven months, and seven days and nights before it ceases. When the human lifespan is twenty years, there occurs the calamity of pestilence.
At that time, because the people mostly practice unwholesome deeds and are possessed of all manner of faults, non-human beings emit poison and pestilence spreads.
Those who encounter it perish immediately; it is difficult to treat, and one hears nothing at all of [those who survive].
The names of medicine and physicians will almost entirely disappear. Such calamities of disease will persist for seven months, seven days, and seven nights before finally subsiding.
When the human lifespan is ten years, there will be a calamity of weapons. At that time, sentient beings, by the power of their karma, [will resort to violence].
Fathers, sons, brothers, and sisters do not recognize one another; each gives rise to a fierce and violent intent to kill.
Whatever grass, wood, tiles, or stones they grasp becomes a sharp blade, and they slaughter one another. This calamity of swords lasts for seven days and seven nights before it subsides.
After the calamity has passed, more than ten thousand people remain within this Jambudvīpa (and so forth). *Vibhāṣā*.
The treatise states: "If one can observe the precept against killing for a single day and night, one will not encounter the kalpa of weapons.
If one offers even a single āmalaka fruit to the Saṅgha, one will not encounter the kalpa of pestilence. If one offers even a single morsel of food..."
[He] bestowed [this] upon all sentient beings so that they might not encounter the kalpa of famine (and so forth).

Now, since the appearance of the World-Honored One Śākyamuni during the time when the human lifespan was one hundred years, until the present year of Wuchen in the Tianli era of the Great Yuan, two thousand two hundred and seventy-seven years have passed.
Furthermore, after another four thousand seven hundred and twenty-three years, the human...
The lifespan will cease at thirty years. Why is this so? Because after every hundred years, one year is subtracted; after every thousand years, ten years are extinguished.
Although the scriptures and images remain in the world, there will be none who honor them, and the bhikṣus will practice the conduct of the laity.
Even the sages and worthies shall not arise; at that time, the images will spontaneously crumble.

When the sutras have vanished into the Dragon Palace, only the Dharma of Amitābha shall remain in the world for a hundred years, leading all sentient beings with whom he has a karmic connection to be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Thus we know that the compassionate vows of Buddha Amitābha are most profound and earnest.

During the periods of the True Dharma and the Semblance Dharma, because the hearts of people were pure and simple, there were many sages and worthies who manifested in ordinary forms, harmonizing their light with the dust of the world to extensively benefit sentient beings through the Dharma.

However, by the end of the Final Dharma period, people were mostly flatterers and sycophants; turning their backs on the right path and heading toward the heterodox, they became incapable of receiving transformation.
For this reason, the sages and worthies remained hidden and did not appear. As the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa..."
Ten thousand years later, the images will collapse of their own accord and the sutras will return to the Dragon Palace.
The assembly of bhikṣus will become indistinguishable from worldly people, possessing nothing more than the saṃghāṭī robe and a shaven head.

Furthermore, the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states that at the end of the age, when the Dharma is extinguished and flows into the Dragon Palace, this particular sutra alone shall remain in the world for a hundred years to guide sentient beings toward rebirth in that land.
The above briefly indicates the general outline of the beginning and end of the Buddha’s entire dispensation. Hereafter, I shall roughly describe the intent of this exhortation:
Alas! We sentient beings, With karmic obstructions thick from time immemorial, Are born late in this turbid and evil age;
Though hearing the Dharma does not give rise to faith, It may yet be a source of joy, Provided we reach this moment before it is too late.
A human body is indeed difficult to obtain; To be born as a man is likewise difficult;
To leave the household life is most difficult, And to hear the Dharma is even more difficult. Having now attained these four difficulties, This truly is no small cause.
Regarding the difficulty of obtaining a human body: as a sutra says, it is like a person who boards a ship to enter the great ocean and loses a needle therein.
Searching for it therein, one cannot find it. Later, while traveling by boat again, one suddenly finds that very needle. The difficulty of obtaining a human body is even greater than this.
Regarding the statement that a "great man" (puruṣa) is difficult to obtain, a sutra says: "One cannot obtain a male body through small roots of goodness, merit, or karmic conditions.
Therefore, when our Śākyamuni Buddha was practicing the path of a bodhisattva, he encountered seventy-five thousand...
Ten Buddhas constantly cultivated pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) and thereby escaped the female body.

Furthermore, just like the virtuous nun Shanmiao of this land, who wished to leave behind her female form, she sacrificed her body in alms to sentient beings throughout twenty-seven lifetimes, even making offerings to the Triple Gem.

Yet, upon reaching her final birth, she still had not escaped the female body when she realized the first fruit of the path (*srotāpanna*). Observing this, one sees that—measuring by the span of a hand—...

Now, that which is difficult to obtain—what doubt could there be? When it is said that leaving the household life is difficult to obtain, it is because sentient beings have wandered through the six realms for many kalpas, undergoing all manner of suffering.
This is truly due to being bound by craving from time immemorial. The root of this craving is one’s wife and children;
if one has no wife or children, afflictions will be eliminated, and it will be easy to transcend the world. Formerly, during the Qi dynasty, Emperor Gao...
The Master saw soldiers carrying charcoal, their appearances haggard and emaciated; he took pity on their hardship and exhorted them to leave the household life. Only one man was willing to go.
King Qi sighed and said, "All people possess affection for their kin and loved ones; therefore, they are unable to escape.
Furthermore, even among those who left home early, many still returned to secular life. Leaving the household..."
This is difficult; the principle is evident. Regarding the difficulty of hearing the Dharma, a sutra states:
"Suppose a one-eyed turtle, submerged at the bottom of the ocean, surfaces once every hundred years. Its intention is to encounter a floating log, for it seeks to turn its karmic retribution.
Yet the log drifts west while the turtle may surface in the east, south, or north. If such conditions do not coincide, they will never meet. Thus it is said.
Again it sinks to the bottom of the sea. After another hundred years have passed, it emerges from the sea once more; thus it continues in this cycle for countless kalpas.
To hear the Buddha-dharma is even more difficult than those hardships. Alas! Of the four difficulties cited above, these are the most difficult of all.
That we have now escaped them and entered the gates of the Śākya school is truly a matter of ten thousand felicities. It is fitting that—
Each of you should rouse a courageous mind, protect your life-preserving bag, cross the great ocean, and reach the other shore;
do not harbor the regret of leaving Mount Ratna empty-handed.
I exhort all those who are newly trained: you should give rise to a heart of joy and further contemplate this impermanent body.
Like the flash of a flint, like a well with few fish and scant water, As an elephant crushes and a rat gnaws at a vine, life diminishes moment by moment.
How can one find peace in inhalation and exhalation? Be vigilant at all times regarding the three karmas;
do not associate with evil. Take refuge in the Triple Gem and observe the five precepts and the eight precepts.
The ten grave precepts, the six and eight light ones, and even down to the eighty thousand rules—though one has not yet fully mastered their observance, one should nevertheless recite them daily.
As the *Udānavarga* says: "This day has passed, and life is diminished; like a fish in scant water, what joy can there be?"
[The passage on] "Joy" (and so forth). The well is a metaphor for the human body; the water is a metaphor for the sun; the fish are like human life;

and the drying up and diminishing represent impermanence (*anityatā*). Furthermore, the *Bimbiṣāra-sūtra* (The Sūtra on the Buddha Preaching the Dharma to King Udāyana) states: "In the past, there was a man..."
While traveling through a vast wilderness, he encountered a massive and ferocious elephant; terrified and without refuge, he saw a dilapidated well.
He immediately sought out the roots of a tree and climbed up to hide above the well. There were two rats, one white and one black, gnawing at the tree root from above.
On the four sides of this well were four venomous snakes, intent on biting him, while beneath the well lived three poisonous dragons. He was thus threatened on all sides by these four [perils].
A snake [is below]. Fearing the three dragons beneath, he clings to a tree whose roots are shaking. Upon it is honey, two or three drops of which fall into his mouth.
At that moment, the tree shakes, knocking down a beehive; the swarms of bees fly away and sting the man.
Furthermore, a wild fire breaks out and comes to burn the tree. Great King, you should know that this person suffers great distress.
It is beyond measure. The flavor obtained is extremely slight, while the suffering and afflictions are exceedingly many. The wilderness is a metaphor for birth and death;

the person is a metaphor for the ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*); the elephant is a metaphor for impermanence; the well is a metaphor for the human body; the roots are a metaphor for human life; the two rats, white and black, are metaphors for day and night;

that which gnaws at the tree roots is a metaphor for the diminution occurring in every thought-moment; the four snakes are metaphors for the four great elements (*mahābhūta*); and the honey is a metaphor for the five desires (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*).
The bee is a metaphor for evil thoughts; fire is a metaphor for old age; the three dragons are metaphors for the three evil realms. Regarding the "three karmas," these are body, speech, and mind.

All sins and virtues are created by no means other than these three karmas—namely, killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct of the body; lying, frivolous speech, and the two evils of harsh and divisive speech of the mouth;
and greed, hatred, and delusion of the mind. To let loose the three karmas constitutes the ten non-virtues; to be cautious regarding the three karmas [constitutes the ten virtues].

The ten wholesome actions. Evil leads to the bitter retribution of the three miserable realms; goodness leads to the joyful retribution of humans and devas, and is also the cause for transcending the world to attain Buddhahood.
Regarding the "Three Refuges," it means taking refuge in the eternal Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time.
There are three types of Triple Gem: namely, the identical essence (*samatā-kāya*), the distinct essence (*nirmāṇa-kāya*), and the sustaining essence (*dharmatā-kāya*). Identical...

Regarding "essence" (*tǐ*): this refers to the teaching that within the single true thusness (*tathatā*), there are three [jewels]. First, true thusness as the nature of awakening is called the Buddha Jewel.
Second, true thusness in its sense of providing guidance and support is called the Dharma Jewel. Third, true thusness in its sense of harmonious integration is called the Sangha Jewel.
Regarding "distinct essence" (*bié tǐ*): the Hīnayāna teaches that the sixteen-foot golden body is the Buddha.

The Jewels: The Four Noble Truths, the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, and emptiness are the Jewel of the Dharma. The four fruits [of the śrāvaka] and the pratyekabuddhas are the Jewel of the Saṃgha.

According to the Mahāyāna, the Tathāgatas of the three bodies are the Jewel of the Buddha; the teaching of the two kinds of emptiness is the Jewel of the Dharma; and the three levels of worthies and ten stages of sages are the Jewel of the Saṃgha.
As for those who maintain [the teachings]: statues made of gold, wood, clay, or paint are the Jewel of the Buddha; the words and phrases of the Tripiṭaka are the Jewel of the Dharma.

This is the Dharma Jewel; shaving the head and donning the dyed robes is the Sangha Jewel. Yet, their essence is one. For an ordinary person who resolves to take refuge, there are no distinct entities for the Three Jewels.
Why is this? When taking refuge in the Buddha, one should contemplate that the Dharma, the Reward Body (*saṃbhogakāya*), and the Response Body (*nirmāṇakāya*) are of one essence without distinction.
He is the Great Compassionate Father, capable of uprooting all the sufferings of sentient beings.

To those afflicted by suffering, they bestow immeasurable bliss. When taking refuge in the Dharma, one should keep in mind the Tripiṭaka of Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma; whether Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna, there is no difference between them.
This is a sublime and excellent medicine capable of curing the disease of the three delusions of sentient beings and realizing the bliss of Nirvāṇa. When taking refuge in the Saṃgha...

One should keep in mind that there are three categories of noble ones, sages, and ordinary beings. Whether high or low, they are without interval and constitute a great field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*), capable of removing the poverty and suffering of sentient beings and bestowing upon them all blessings and happiness.

Regarding the terms "noble ones," "sages," and "ordinary beings": according to the Mahāyāna, those from the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) down to the first ground (*bhūmi*) are called "noble ones" (*ārya*);

those in the stages of practice, progress, and abiding are called "sages" (*bhadra*); and those in the ten levels of faith (*śraddhā*) and the five grades of practice (*pañcavidha*) are called "ordinary beings" (*pṛthagjana*). If...
In the Hīnayāna, the Pratyekabuddhas and those who have attained the four fruits are considered noble (*ārya*), while those at the seven stages of preparation are considered virtuous (*bhadra*);
they are also termed ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*). The *Mahā-upāya-sūtra* states: "The Three Jewels are that to which one takes refuge; their meaning lies in providing rescue and protection.
For example, suppose there is a person who has committed an offense against a king and flees to another country seeking rescue and protection. The king of that other country says to him:"
"Come, O Fearless One! Do not leave my realm; do not disregard my instruction. I shall surely protect you.

If you sincerely take refuge in the Triple Gem, have no other inclinations, and do not violate the Buddha’s teachings, then even the evil Māra King can do nothing against you. Furthermore, the *Ājñātakauṇḍinya-sūtra* states:
"In the past, when the life span of a son of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven was nearing its end, the five signs of decay appeared. He observed..."
After his life ended, he fell into the womb of a pig. Distressed and unhappy, a deva told him, "The Buddha can deliver you from this transgression.
He immediately went to the Buddha's presence; having prostrated, he had not yet asked a question when the Buddha addressed the deva:
"All phenomena return to impermanence; this is what you have long known. Why do you grieve? The deva explained the situation in detail to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "If you wish to be free..."
While he was still in the body of a pig, he recited the Three Refuges and immediately followed the Buddha’s teachings. Day and night he took refuge on his own;
when his seven-day lifespan ended, he was reborn in the kingdom of Vaiśālī as the son of an elder. While in his mother’s womb, he recited the Three Refuges three times each day.

Upon being born and falling to the ground, he likewise knelt and recited the Three Refuges. The entire family was deeply astonished and regarded him as a malevolent omen, intending to kill him. Only...
The father, possessing discernment, remarked, "This child is no ordinary person.

While those of the world reach a hundred years of age and still do not understand the need to take refuge in the Triple Gem, how much more so this one who, upon first falling to the ground, was able to recite 'Namo Buddha. Let us watch over him and raise him well.
When the boy reached the age of seven, he said to his parents, "I wish to make offerings to the Buddha and the Sangha. His parents were astonished and granted him permission.
He prepared the ritual offerings. When the Buddha and the assembly of monks came to accept the child’s offering, they preached the Dharma for him.
Both the child and his parents attained the stage of *avaivartika* (non-retrogression), and so forth.
Regarding the five precepts: first, not killing; second, not stealing; third, not engaging in sexual misconduct; fourth, not speaking falsely; fifth, not drinking intoxicants.
Regarding the eight precepts: the first five are as above, with three added: namely, first, not eating after midday;
second, not wearing flower garlands or necklaces, and not sitting on high, wide, or large beds; third, not performing [these acts] oneself.

Regarding "song, dance, and music": one therefore goes to observe and listen to them. As for the "ten grave offenses," they are: first, killing; second, stealing; third, impurity; fourth, false speech;
fifth, selling alcohol; sixth, speaking of others' faults; seventh, self-praise; eighth, greed; ninth, anger; and tenth, slandering the Triple Gem.
As for the "forty-eight light offenses," the first is: upon seeing a *upādhyāya* or *ācārya*, and so forth...

1. When traveling together with others, one should rise to greet them and provide offerings according to the Dharma. 2. One must not intentionally drink alcohol, nor should one encourage others to drink it.

3. One must not eat any kind of meat. 4. One must not eat the five pungent roots (pañca-garaka). 5. Upon seeing those who have violated the precepts, one should instruct them to perform repentance. 6.
Upon seeing a Mahāyāna Dharma Master coming from afar, one should go out to welcome him, invite him, and make offerings to him at the three times of day.
1. To preach the Dharma. 2. Whenever there is a place where the Dharma is being expounded, one should go to all such places to listen and receive it. 3.

Upon seeing those who are ill, one should always provide for them with offerings, no differently than one would for the Buddha. 4. One must not harbor a mind that rejects the Mahāyāna while upholding the Śrāvaka vehicle. 5.
One must not keep weapons such as swords, staves, bows, or arrows—implements for combat and the taking of life. These ten precepts should be studied and practiced.
Furthermore: First, one must not enter military ranks or move about therein for the sake of profit.
Second, one must not engage in the trade or sale of free persons, slaves, livestock, coffins, or vessels used for containing corpses.
Third, one must not slander virtuous people, including kings and ministers, by claiming they have committed grave offenses such as treason. Fourth, one must not set fires to burn or destroy property.

6. In mountains and marshes, one should teach and cause even the disciples of the five Buddhas, as well as all enemies and kin, to receive and uphold the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinaya, causing them to resolve upon bodhicitta.
7. One should first study the Mahāyāna; when seeing newly initiated bodhisattvas come to seek the sūtras and vinaya, one should explain them according to the Dharma.
8. One must not associate with kings or ministers, nor rely on their power and influence to act perversely.
One must not take money or goods. On the sixth watch of the eighth night, one receives the Bodhisattva precepts.

If one cannot understand the causes and conditions of the precepts and the Vinaya, one must not act as a teacher to bestow the precepts upon others. Ninth, when seeing a bhikṣu who upholds the precepts, one must not deceive or slander him.
Tenth, one should constantly practice the release of living beings (*prāṇamokṣa*). Upon seeing those who kill living beings, one should employ skillful means to rescue and protect them.
On the anniversary of the death of one’s parents or siblings, one should invite a Dharma master to lecture on the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* to provide merit for the deceased.
These ten precepts should be studied. Furthermore, first: if someone kills my parents or siblings, I must not seek retribution.
Second, one must not rely on one's own cleverness, wealth, or power to refuse consulting and receiving instruction from learned Dharma masters regarding the sūtras and vinaya.
Third, although one may understand the sūtras and vinaya oneself, when a newly initiated bodhisattva comes to inquire, one must not respond poorly with a disrespectful or malicious mind.
Fourth, one must not set aside the Buddha’s sūtras and vinaya to instead study the heterodox scriptures of external paths or worldly secular texts.

These are the causes and conditions that obstruct the Path. Fifth, one should serve as a master of Dharma preaching, or even as a master of a monastic residence (vihāra), and properly guard the property of the Triple Gem, never using it recklessly.

Sixth, whether one previously resided in a monastic residence or among the great assembly, when a visiting Bodhisattva bhikṣu arrives, one should rise to welcome him, see him off, and provide various kinds of offerings. Furthermore, if a donor...
7. When various members of the Sangha arrive, the master of the monastery should first assign them lodgings for visiting monks.

8. One must not accept special invitations for personal gain or offerings for one's own use. 9. When inviting the Sangha to fulfill a vow or prayer, one should invite them in the prescribed order and must not make special invitations.
10. One must not, for the sake of profit, trade in the sexual services of men or women; nor should one prepare food with one's own hands, grind it oneself, or [perform such tasks].
Grinding grain; practicing divination for good or bad fortune; all incantations, arts, and crafts;
and tenth, one must not act as a go-between for laypeople to facilitate sexual union between men and women. These ten precepts should be studied.
Furthermore, first, if one sees non-Buddhists or any evil persons selling images of Buddhas or Bodhisattvas, or selling the Sūtras and Vinaya, one should instruct and transform them.
One must redeem stolen goods by paying their value. Second, one must not deceive others by using light scales or small measures to take their property;
furthermore, one must not keep cats, raccoons, pigs, or dogs. Third, one must not watch men and women fighting, nor observe battles between armies or conflicts between generals and soldiers;
likewise, one must not listen to the sounds of lutes, harps, *konghou*, or other musical performances. Furthermore, one must not gamble or engage in hunting.
1. One must refrain from games such as chess and *ṣaḍyūta*, even down to divination using fingernails, mirrors, or willow twigs; one must abandon all such evil arts. 2.

One must uphold the prohibitive precepts with fourfold protection, reciting these precepts six times throughout the day and night as if they were a vajra, guarding them like a life-preserving float, and recognizing oneself as a Buddha-to-be who is not yet perfected.
3. One must practice the five forms of filial piety toward parents, teachers, and the Saṃgha.

O Jewel! Furthermore, may I obtain a good teacher and virtuous friends who shall instruct me in the Mahāyāna, causing me to attain understanding and practice according to the Dharma, never departing from my mind for even a single thought-moment.
Sixth, upholding the prohibitions of the Buddhas, I make this vow: "I would rather, with this very body..."
One would rather cast oneself into a great pit of blazing, fierce fire or onto a mountain of knives than ever violate the sūtras and vinaya of the Buddhas by engaging in impure conduct with women.

One would rather have one's body bound all around by a thousand layers of iron chains than, with a body of broken precepts, accept any clothing from a faithful donor. One would rather swallow hot iron for a hundred [lifetimes]...
For a thousand kalpas, one shall never, with a mouth defiled by broken precepts, accept the food and drink of a hundred flavors from a faithful donor.

Furthermore, one should vow that all sentient beings shall attain Buddhahood. Seventh, one should constantly practice *dhūta* (ascetic purification) during the spring and autumn, and engage in seated meditation during the winter and summer.
One should maintain a willow branch, cleansing powder, the three robes, a water flask, an alms bowl, a sitting mat, a mendicant’s staff, an incense burner, and a water-strainer.
A hand-towel, a knife, tongs, tweezers, a rope bed, the Sūtras, the Vinaya, an image of the Buddha, and an image of a Bodhisattva—these eighteen items should always accompany one’s person.
When practicing *dhūta* or sitting in meditation, do not enter dangerous places;

that is to say, lands ruled by wicked kings, deep thickets of grass and trees, or places where lions, tigers, and wolves roam, nor those beset by the perils of water, fire, wind, bandits, or venomous snakes.

Eighth, one should sit in accordance with the Dharma in the proper order; regardless of age, seniority, or social status, those who received the precepts earlier sit in front, and those who received them later sit behind.
Ninth, one should constantly teach and transform all sentient beings, establishing monasteries, Buddha-stūpas, and all places for the practice of the Way.
Furthermore, in times of illness, national calamities, or threats from bandits, or regarding one’s parents and elder brothers...

On the day of a younger brother’s death, during all fasting assemblies, and even in times of calamity by water or fire, or danger from rākṣasas, or when one's body is bound by shackles, fetters, and stocks—whether one has much lust, much anger, or much delusion—all should read, recite, and expound this sutra and vinaya.
These nine precepts should be studied. Furthermore, when conferring the precepts upon another, one must not discriminate.

One may receive the precepts from all kings, ministers, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, laymen, laywomen, lecherous men, lecherous women, those with no sexual organs, those with dual sexual organs, and even all ghosts and animals—provided they understand the words of the Dharma Master.
The only exceptions are those who have committed the seven prohibitions or the seven heinous crimes. Furthermore, those who have left the household life must not prostrate before kings.
1. One must not, for the sake of fame or profit, falsely pretend to understand all the sutras and vinayas and thereby bestow the precepts upon others. 2.
One must not preach these Great Precepts before those who have not yet received the Bodhisattva precepts, nor before those of external paths or heterodox views;
this exception applies only to kings. 3. If one has received the true precepts, one must not intentionally disparage them.
One who commits such an offense shall not receive the offerings of lay donors (*dānapati*), nor may they walk upon the land of a king or drink the water of a king.
Why is this? Because such a person is a great thief within the Dharma, no different from a beast or a block of wood.

Fifth, one should uphold the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinaya; even by flaying one's skin, drawing blood, or breaking one's bones to transcribe them, or by using wood-bark, paper, silk, bamboo, or cloth, this may be done.
One should always make offerings according to the Dharma with the seven precious gems, incense, and flowers.
Sixth, upon seeing any sentient being, one should proclaim: "You all must receive the three refuges and the ten precepts," and so on, even when seeing oxen or horses.
Regarding all livestock, such as pigs and sheep: with mind and speech, one should say, "You are livestock; arouse the bodhicitta.
Seventh, one should constantly practice teaching and transformation. When entering the homes of donors (*dānapati*), one must not stand while preaching the Dharma to laypeople (*avadātavasana*);

rather, one should place oneself upon a high seat and sit while preaching the Dharma, while the people sit on lower seats to listen and receive it. Eighth, one must not intentionally act as a destroyer of the Dharma.
Do not permit my fourfold assembly of disciples to leave the household life to practice the Way. Nor permit the construction of images, Buddha-stūpas, or the Sūtras and Vinaya.
Ninth, do not preach the Buddha’s Dharma and precepts before kings and officials for the sake of fame or renown.
Do not arbitrarily impose restraints upon those who have violated the precepts. Furthermore, if you hear heretics or evil persons slandering the Buddha...
Regarding the precepts: it is as if three hundred spears were piercing one’s heart;
rather than hearing even a single evil word that breaks a Buddha-precept, one would prefer to enter hell for a hundred kalpas. Thus, one should train in these nine precepts (and so forth).
The above ten grave offenses and forty-eight light offenses are from the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*. Furthermore, there are the four hundred bodhisattva precepts and the two [hundred] bhikṣu [precepts].
There are one hundred and fifty precepts for bhikṣus, five hundred precepts for bhikṣuṇīs, three thousand precepts on dignified deportment, and eighty thousand precepts on minute conduct.
All such various precepts are subsumed under the three clusters: first, the precept of restraining from unwholesome conduct, which means there is no evil that is not abandoned;
second, the precept of gathering wholesome dharmas, which means there is no good that is not accumulated; third, the precept of benefiting sentient beings.
Regarding the precepts: this means that there is no one who is not saved. These various precepts are difficult for ordinary beings at the initial stage of the path to maintain in their entirety;
how much more so now, when it has been more than seven hundred and eighty years since the precepts were firmly established?

Because the times are turbid and the faculties of beings are inferior, hindrances are thick and faith is thin; thus, the power to maintain the precepts is difficult. Although they cannot be maintained in their full detail, it is sufficient merely to recite them.
Furthermore, it is most excellent if one upholds the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts for as long as life lasts without violation;
otherwise, even for seven days or down to a single day, it is also effective. Why is this? As the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* states:

"If one observes the śrāmaṇera precepts for one day and one night, at the end of life, one will immediately go to the Land of Ultimate Bliss and be reborn among those of the middle grade. Furthermore...
The Trāyastriṃśa deva cited above recited the three refuges for seven days; thus, by transforming inferior conditions, one attains the superior.
What is called "precept" (śīla) means restraint and discipline; it refers to restraining emotional desires like a monkey wearing a chain, and constraining body and speech.
It is like a horse wearing a bridle. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Among great and grievous illnesses, the precepts are the excellent medicine;
amidst great terrors, the precepts are the protection; within the darkness of death, the precepts are the bright lamp; among the three evil realms, the precepts are the bridge;
in the ocean of the five fears, the precepts are the great ship. Furthermore, the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* says: "Just as a person who wishes to achieve..."
Just as one first prepares the foundation for a house, so it is with a Bodhisattva: wishing to cultivate the myriad practices, one must first purify the *śīla* (precepts).
The *Sapoduo lun* (Śāriputra-abhidharma-śāstra) states: "A person who has first received the precepts is equal to the Buddha. Another sutra says: "The person who receives the precepts..."
Within the six realms of existence, wherever one is born, one will invariably become a king.
It is further said that it is better to receive [the precepts] even if they are broken while standing, than not to receive them at all. Thus, the merit of the precepts cannot be fully described;

it is explained in detail in such scriptures as the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* and the *Śūraṅgama Samādhi Sūtra*, as well as in the various Vinayas. If you wish to know this in full detail, please consult these texts.
Through generosity and patience, diligence, meditation, and wisdom;
by reciting and copying the sūtras and śāstras, and by paying homage to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
whether by repairing Buddhist temples, constructing monasteries, molding or painting sacred images, restoring ancient scriptures and icons, or chanting praises to the Triple Gem.
Some sweep stupas and offer flowers; some burn incense and light lamps; some provide musical offerings;
some support their teachers and parents; some practice worldly benevolence and righteousness; some honor the elderly and show compassion to the young;
some feel pity for all sentient beings; some rejoice in the virtues of others; and some maintain a humble mind and gentle speech.
"Acting according to what is appropriate, even by practicing only one [perfection], one shall likewise attain the Buddha-way.
Regarding what is called "giving" (*dāna*), in Sanskrit it is *dāna*. There are three kinds: namely, the body, life, and wealth; as well as the Dharma.
As for the giving of body and life—such as the head, eyes, hands, and feet—this is impossible for anyone other than Bodhisattvas who have attained patience (*kṣānti*). Therefore, Śāriputra...
One regresses at the sixth moment of mind. Regarding the gift of material wealth (*āmiṣadāna*), this refers to male and female slaves, elephants, horses, and various precious jewels;
it does not depend on whether these are few or many, but rather consists in giving one’s best according to one’s means. Thus, it is said that a woman, out of greed, gave two coins as a gift.
She was currently serving as a queen. When an old woman gave her foul-smelling rice gruel, she was immediately reborn in the heavens.

Some say that giving up one's body still pertains to the gift of material wealth (*āmiṣadāna*). As for the gift of Dharma (*dharmadāna*), it refers to hearing the teachings on mundane and supramundane wholesome dharmas from the Buddhas or spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), or hearing them from the sūtras and śāstras, and then expounding them for others with a pure mind.
All these are termed "Dharma-giving. If one were to compare material giving with Dharma-giving, the former would not equal even one part in ten million billion of the latter.
Therefore, the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "If a person were to give away bodies as numerous as the sands of the Ganges three times a day for a single day..."

In this manner, one may practice such bodily giving for immeasurable kalpas. Yet, if someone upholds even a single verse of this sutra and expounds it for others, their merit shall surpass that of the former.
Regarding "patience" (an-ri): in Sanskrit it is called *kṣānti*, meaning the ability of the inner mind to remain tranquil and endure external objects of insult.

There are two kinds of patience: namely, patience regarding sentient beings (*jantu-kṣānti*) and patience regarding phenomena (*dharma-kṣānti*). "Patience regarding sentient beings" refers to [the endurance of] external...

When people respond with anger, abuse, beating, or harm, and when phenomena such as cold, heat, wind, rain, hunger, thirst, old age, and illness arise—regarding these two types of objects, one’s mind remains unmoved.
This is like the practice of reflection cultivated by Pūrṇa: if someone comes to abuse him, he rejoices in not responding with a fist;
if he encounters a fist, he rejoices in not responding with a staff; and if he encounters a staff, he rejoices in not responding with a sword.
Add the blade of a sword. If one encounters the harm of a blade, one should reflect: "I desire to leave this poisonous body of the five aggregates as soon as possible;
it is thanks to a virtuous friend that they sever the root of my suffering—how could I not hold them in high esteem?

If one maintains such a mental state, one will not only sever enmity, but one's merit and wisdom will become even more exalted. Thus Yongjia said: "To view malicious words as a source of merit—this then becomes..."
"My spiritual friends" (and so forth).
As for "diligence," in Sanskrit it is called *vīrya*, which means to practice wholesome dharmas with assiduity and not to be self-indulgent.

There are two kinds of diligence: first, physical; second, mental. To mold or paint the forms of the sages, to transcribe the scriptures, to perform prostrations, recite, and preach, and to cultivate various wholesome dharmas without rest—this is called physical diligence.

To diligently practice the path of goodness through meditative concentration and wisdom, with the mind succeeding the mind in continuous succession without interruption—this is called mental diligence.
It is by the power of this single perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) that the other five perfections become complete.
For example, when the World-Honored One Śākyamuni was practicing the causes [of Buddhahood], he surpassed Maitreya in his merit within seven days precisely because of this. Thus, a sutra says:
"There is not a single dharma that arises from indolence" (and so forth).
"Dhyāna" is a term from the Sanskrit language; in its full form, it is called *dhyāna*. This is translated here as "contemplative cultivation.

There are two kinds of dhyāna: namely, the mundane and the supramundane. What is called mundane dhyāna refers to the four fundamental dhyānas, the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*), and the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*);
these are the dhyānas practiced by ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*). Supramundane dhyāna refers to the six subtle [meditations]...

The sixteen special excellences (*ṣoḍaśaviśeṣa*), the universal clarity (*sāmānyapratibhāsa*), up to the three knowledges (*trividyā*) and six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*): these constitute the meditative absorptions shared by the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*).
They include the hundred and eight samādhis such as the *Śūraṅgama* and others, as well as the one hundred and twenty-three samādhis such as the "Immovable" (*acala*) of all Buddhas.
This is the dhyāna cultivated by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; it is not shared with ordinary beings or those of the two vehicles.

As for the functional efficacy of dhyāna, it consists in stilling all miscellaneous discursive thoughts, restraining the mind to a single point, and thereby realizing one's nature to achieve Buddhahood.
Among the Buddhas of the three periods and all Bodhisattvas, there are none who do not enter through this gate. Therefore...

The former masters have said: "Even if one practices various mundane virtues for ten thousand years, it is not equal to settling the mind in tranquil meditation for the duration of a single meal" (and so forth).

Furthermore, were one to discuss the distinction between the heterodox and the orthodox, as well as the expedient means for cultivating contemplation, it would seem that the text becomes overly prolix.
Therefore, I have not recorded it here for your perusal. If you wish to examine the matter in detail, please consult the *Tiantai Mohe Zhiguan* (The Great Calming and Contemplation).

Within it, the characteristics of practice in the Chan gate are explained extensively; distinguishing between the heterodox and the orthodox, and clarifying the partial and the perfect, it is as clear and evident as pointing at one's own palm.
Regarding what is called "wisdom" (*prajñā*): it refers to the illumination that all phenomena are ultimately ungraspable, thereby enabling one to penetrate all things without obstruction.

There are three types of wisdom: first, the wisdom sought by *śrāvakas*, which begins from the four foundations of mindfulness, proceeds through the contemplation of the Four Truths, and culminates in the realization of the wisdom of non-arising; second, the wisdom sought by *pratyekabuddhas*... [text continues]
The wisdom of awakening refers to contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination and realizing non-arising.

Third is the wisdom of seeking the Buddha-way, which means that from the moment a bodhisattva first generates the mind of enlightenment, they diligently practice the six perfections, destroy Māra, sever the fetters, and ultimately achieve perfect awakening, even entering the nirvana without remainder. If a bodhisattva cultivates these three with a pure mind...
Because it sows the seeds of wisdom, it is called *prajñā*. The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"All Buddhas and the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of all Buddhas emerge from this sutra. Therefore, it is said that *prajñā* is the mother of all Buddhas.
Furthermore, this prajñā is shared by both Buddhas and sentient beings; it is only through delusion and awakening that we provisionally distinguish between superior and inferior.
If one understands this principle and investigates the mind accordingly, then the originally existing, equal, and great wisdom will be revealed.

In that case, how could there be any distinction between Buddhas and sentient beings? Thus, the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra says: "In the equal and true dharma-dhātu, the Buddha does not deliver sentient beings. It is also said:

If a bodhisattva does not hear the Prajñāpāramitā, they remain far from the Buddha-way; yet even though one may be among ordinary beings, if they study the Prajñāpāramitā, they are named a "Buddha-to-be.
Now, the myriad practices of a bodhisattva do not exceed the six perfections, and among these six perfections, Prajñā is the synthesis.
If one cultivates Prajñā, one has already fully practiced the six perfections and the myriad deeds.
The Buddha said: "If one were to speak of the causes and conditions of the merit of the six perfections, it would not be exhausted even at the end of an eon," and so forth.
Regarding those who read and recite the sūtras and śāstras: within the teachings of a single lifetime, there are the three collections (tripiṭaka) of Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma;

among these, there are also Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, as well as Exoteric and Esoteric teachings. In the fundamental realm of the Buddha, there is originally no distinction between two, three, great, or small.

It is distinct. It is merely so because it accords with the various capacities of sentient beings. Furthermore, the great intent of the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world was to cause all sentient beings to enter the Mahāyāna;
yet, there were those with inferior capacities who could not participate in the Great Vehicle. For their sake, he himself taught the three vehicles.
This brings about slight benefit and gradually leads one into the Great Vehicle. Therefore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states:

"Entering the Mahāyāna is the foundation; for this reason, I preach this sūtra. May all practitioners understand this meaning: whether it be a sūtra or a treatise, do not discriminate between the Great and Small Vehicles;
according to what one is capable of, all should be received and upheld. Alas! Those who study the Mahāyāna today, seeing only...

Regarding the passages within the Prajñā and Vaipulya sections that promote integration, as well as those texts that praise the Great [Vehicle] and disparage the Small, they have not yet deeply grasped the subtle and esoteric intent of the Tathāgata’s skillful means in establishing teachings according to the capacities of beings;
thus, they raise the banner of great arrogance, which is not a true censure of the Hīnayāna.

This seems somewhat unintelligible. Why? Within the Vaipulya section, those who praise the Great Vehicle and disparage the Small are the followers of the two vehicles who have taken the Small as sufficient and are unable to turn back.
The Tathāgata, wishing to cause them to feel shame for the Small, therefore disparages it.
To cause them to aspire to the Great [Vehicle], it follows next. To cause them to enter the Great [Vehicle], it subsequently teaches Prajñā.

Through such integration and refinement, examining and admonishing at every stage, one is led into the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). It should be understood that these refutations and rebukes are intended only for those whose capacities match the teaching;
they do not concern ordinary beginners of later generations. If this Lesser Dharma were of no benefit to beings, the Buddha—
After the Parinirvāṇa, during the compilation of the sūtras by Kāśyapa and Ānanda, why were these not omitted and instead collected and placed together in a single Piṭaka?
Furthermore, even during the Buddha’s own lifetime, there were those of sharp and dull faculties;

the sharp entered directly into the Great [Vehicle], while the dull entered the Great through the Small. For this reason, the teachings exist in both Great and Small forms; how much more so now in this Final Age?

When individuals are entrusted with the practice of the Dharma on behalf of others, how could there not be differences in their capacities? Therefore, those of superior capacity delight in the Great [Vehicle], while those of inferior capacity follow the Small;
each has what is appropriate for them, and in principle, there is no obstruction. Why, then, do you condemn this?

Furthermore, the reason the Small Vehicle is considered a fault lies only in its attachment to the small and its forgetting of the great. If one simply turns the mind toward the Great, what fault could there be?
There is. It is like an elder instructing his child with "half-words"; there must be a reason for this.
If it were truly as he rebukes, such that one proceeds not by the past but goes directly upon the Great Way, then nothing could be more fortunate.
However, if the people under heaven were all exclusively gentlemen, then indeed it would be so. But if they are mixed with common folk, how could that be the case? Why is this? If one were to...
It is because a country person walking on a great highway is like driving deer and elk to roam through a city market;
thus, the difference between the expedient teachings and the ultimate truth becomes increasingly apparent—how could this be anything other than a matter of security?

Furthermore, some may cite a sutra saying that to recite alone without understanding constitutes slandering the Dharma, being like the labor of an empty mortar that yields no benefit at all. Such a narrow interpretation is hardly worthy of belief.
People are either foolish or wise. The wise grasp the meaning; the foolish cling to the literal text.
