Even though one may be wise, if they do not apply their mind to investigate and seek, they will fail to penetrate the profound principle. Thinking that merely reciting the text is superior, they are lazy in searching for its subtle meaning.
For this reason, the Tathāgata specifically cautioned such individuals, as expressed in the passage "it is said... and so forth; it was not a general admonition.
As for those who are shrouded in the darkness of ignorance—such deluded people cannot even recognize a single character, let alone claim to understand the profound and subtle meaning.
It is difficult to teach such persons to turn their minds toward the Way; yet even if they do turn toward the Way, it is difficult for them to recite and study.
Therefore, merely reciting [the name] is itself a virtuous act; the Great Sage will surely rejoice in this and how could He not praise it? Why [should one hesitate]?
If one dares to reprimand them so as to cause them to lose heart, such people will forever lack the karmic affinity for the Dharma;

they will flow long through the evil realms with no time of escape. If this is so, who could say that the Tathāgata is the Truly All-Knowing One, who gives rise to impartial compassion and universally guides the blind masses through great skillful means? Such deluded people also...

The time when one may be reproved is as follows: although one has not yet fully understood the meaning, if one recites it so that it permeates the mind, and through accumulation over months and years the practice matures and the intellect becomes penetrating, one falsely claims to have realized the truth and gives rise to grasping and attachment, becoming stagnant and unable to progress.
It is precisely at this stage that one should be cautioned and exhorted to advance; it is improper to reproach or admonish them at an untimely moment.
One feels discouraged. Although this person’s merit may not yet have been realized in the present life, the sprouts of goodness have already been sown and will surely grow gradually.
In future lives, they shall become a person of wisdom. Even those who are wise today must have been nothing but fools in their previous lives.

These words are not spoken from mere conjecture; they are found throughout the sutras and treatises. If one considers a lack of understanding to be a fault, [one must acknowledge that it arises from past causes].
As for this, it is like a *dhāraṇī*: its meaning cannot be discerned; how could it be that merely reciting it causes sins to be extinguished and merit to arise?

Furthermore, in the biographies, there are those who attained wisdom by searching through and reciting only a few characters. As for the young pheasant, he became a Dharma Master upon hearing only a rough outline.
The viper, the snake, the clam, and the oyster were liberated from their retribution through the influence of the incense. Such cases as these can indeed [accomplish this].
Do you understand its essential meaning? All who cultivate the Way should know this intent.
It does not matter whether the teaching is great or small, nor the noble or humble status of the person;
whether male or female, lay or ordained, old or young, wise or foolish, understanding or ignorant, refined or unrefined, many or few, long or short—it simply follows...

If one divides [the practice] between recitation and study, then one's efforts will not be in vain. Whether those efforts bear fruit early or late depends solely on whether the person is diligent or indolent.

Furthermore, for one who acts as a teacher, if they do not expound the teachings according to the inclinations and capacities of their students, how would they differ from one who takes a square peg and tries to fit it into a round hole?
This is called a "blind and lame" relationship between teacher and disciple; both fall into ruin. Read [this].
Reciting [the text] benefits oneself; explaining it and transcribing it benefit others. One who cultivates both these benefits is called a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, among the five types of practice, the merit of explaining and transcribing is unsurpassed; let those who study this know it.
Regarding the practice of mindfulness of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas: the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions and the three periods of time are infinite in number and their names are diverse.
If one practices mindfulness of them all collectively, the object of focus is too vast and the mind becomes distracted, making it difficult to achieve samādhi.

One should instead single-mindedly pay homage and maintain mindfulness of a single Buddha or a single Bodhisattva with whom one has a karmic connection; then, the response of the Buddhas will be easily achieved, and one shall behold their true bodies and hear [their teachings].
Through the Dharma, one awakens to the Way and universally beholds the infinite Buddhas of the ten directions, each surrounded by an ocean-like assembly of all Bodhisattvas.

If one does not obtain the opportunity to behold them personally in the present life, one will surely be born in that place according to one's wishes in a future life, where one may personally receive their teachings and make offerings.
Thus, the *Treatise on the Pure Land* states: "The merit of a single Buddha is no different from the merit of all Buddhas."
Because they share the same *dharmatā*, when one recollects a single Buddha, one is thereby recollecting all Buddhas (and so forth).

How is it known that there are those with the necessary conditions? It is said: whether hearing from a virtuous friend or seeing it within the scriptures, whoever follows what they have seen or heard and attaches themselves to faith—such people exist, for although sentient beings generally possess many obstacles, they nonetheless practice.
Among all the various practices of the Path, many are frequently abandoned midway; yet for those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha alone, not one in ten thousand fails.
It is like a person of meager merit in this world who, by borrowing the power of a king, encounters no obstacles wherever they go, lacks nothing they require, and remains fearless in body and mind.
It is the same for those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha: because they are sustained by the Buddha, neither celestial Māras nor non-Buddhist heretics can prevail over them.
They cannot cause disturbance; they obstruct [the arising of afflictions] and increase wisdom. In every lifetime one is born, one shall always remain before the Buddha.
Thus, the *Five Methods for Settling the Mind* (*Pañca-vastuka*) states: "Sentient beings with many obstructions practice the contemplation of the Buddha’s mindfulness. Furthermore, a sutra says:

"If one recollects the Buddha with a tranquil mind and prostrates with the five limbs touching the ground, this constitutes the karma of a deva. If one recites the name with a distracted mind, merely bowing the head and raising the hands, this constitutes the karma of a human."

From that time forth, they will no longer fall into the three evil realms; they will always be born among humans and devas, experiencing supreme and wondrous bliss, and finally encounter a Buddha to realize the sublime fruit.

Regarding the construction of Buddhist temples and monasteries: a place where the relics of the Buddha and sacred images are enshrined is called a "Buddhist temple" (buddhavihāra); a place where the community of monks walks, sits, and lies down is called a... [monastery].
To such a monastic dwelling. If a person reveres the Triple Gem, whether by newly constructing one or by repairing an old one, the merit obtained shall be immeasurable.
The *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "There are five matters concerning a bhikṣu who manages a vihāra."
First, it is to repay the Buddha’s kindness; second, it is to nurture and develop the Buddha-dharma; third, it is to eliminate the self-importance and arrogance of ordinary and inferior beings;
fourth, it is to subdue the pride and haughtiness of future disciples; and fifth, it is to inspire the performance of meritorious deeds by those yet to come.
The *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* states: "The youngest daughter of the elder Sudatta was of such exquisite beauty that there was none like her."
She became the wife of a king and later conceived; she gave birth to a single egg, which soon opened to reveal ten boys.
They were handsome in appearance and possessed extraordinary courage and strength. The elder was amazed by this and took them to the Buddha’s dwelling.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for them, and both the mother and her ten sons realized arhatship. Ānanda asked about their past causes, and the Buddha told him:
Ānanda, after the parinirvāṇa of the past Buddha Vipaśyin, his relics were divided and immeasurable stūpas were erected.
Among them was one stūpa that was on the verge of collapsing. An old woman repaired it, while there were ten young men [who did not].
He encountered him while traveling and immediately set out to cultivate and maintain [the path] together with him. From that time forward, he did not follow the evil realms;
whether among devas or humans, he was always born together with him, receiving blessings and happiness. Now, having encountered me, he has left the household life and attained the Way.
Furthermore, the *Śatavarga-sūtra* states: After the parinirvāṇa of the past Buddha Vipaśyin, during the period of the Final Dharma, there was a man who encountered him while traveling.
There was a slight area of damage on a Buddhist stūpa; he repaired it with mud and purchased gold leaf to gild it.
From that time forward, he did not fall into the evil realms, and whether among devas or humans, his body was always golden in color.
Finally, he was born into the family of an elder in the city of Kāśī; his body was likewise golden, a rarity in the world, and the radiance of his body—
All were illuminated and turned the color of gold. As he gradually grew older, he sought the Buddha to leave the household life and attained the state of an Arhat.

Furthermore, the *Dharmapada-avadāna-sūtra* states: During the time when the Buddha was in the world, there was an Arhat who took the Buddha’s hair and nail-clippings and went to the southern mountains of the country of Kaśmīra to erect a stūpa.
There were always five hundred Arhats who circumambulated and paid homage to it morning and evening. At that time, the mountain...

Among them were five hundred monkeys. Seeing the monks circumambulating the stupa, they immediately began carrying stones together to help the monks build a stupa, circumambulating it and prostrating themselves.
At that time, due to heavy rain, the mountains and rivers suddenly overflowed; the entire troop of monkeys was submerged in the water and died.
They were reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. They soon went to the place where the Buddha was and heard him preach the Dharma;

at once, five hundred devaputras all attained the stage of Srotāpanna (and so forth). Furthermore, these one or two instances cited here are merely those who established a slight connection with the Dharma.
If such a minor cause as this results in such a karmic reward, how much more so for those who have first given rise to a virtuous mind? Entirely...
Even if it were merely a lay practitioner or a monk among that troop of monkeys playfully performing this act, it would still be cause for profound awe;
how much more so when performed with sincere devotion by a human being—how can the merit obtained therein possibly be described?
Regarding the molding and painting of sacred forms: the true Buddha is formless, yet images are provisionally established so that one may take refuge and seek his vows.
This might seem like a form of inversion; however, ordinary people who grasp at signs cannot direct their reverence toward emptiness.

Therefore, it is necessary to borrow images to represent the Truth, just as those who pray for rain fashion a grass dragon to offer their supplications, whereby the true dragon sends down the rain. Thus it is established.
If one venerates it as a provisional image, then the True Buddha will manifest his response. Why, then, make a distinction between the provisional and the real?

As stated in the *Udayana-rāja-sūtra*: when the World-Honored One ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, King Udayana, harboring a heart of longing and veneration, carved a sandalwood image of him and made offerings to it. When the World-Honored One descended, the image rose up and came forth.
At the gate, he welcomed the True Body (the Buddha). The Buddha declined, saying, "I shall soon enter nirvana; it is the image that shall long remain in the world to bring benefit and merit to all.
How could I dare to precede you, O Benevolent One? He then fulfilled these words and entered the gate first.
The Buddha then spoke to him regarding the merit of creating images, saying: "If a person creates an image of the Buddha, their merit shall be immeasurable. In this world...
Born into this world, they do not fall into the evil realms, but are constantly reborn among humans and devas, receiving blessings and happiness.
Their bodies are perpetually golden, their eyes are pure, their countenances are upright, and they are endowed with all the marks of excellence.

If born among humans, they are always born into the families of emperors, great ministers, elders, or virtuous and noble houses of wealth and honor. If they become emperors, they are the most eminent among kings.
They are especially venerable. If they become wheel-turning kings, they rule over the four continents;

if they are born in the heavens, they are the most excellent among the gods, even attaining the status of a king of the six heavens of desire, being the foremost among those six classes of gods; or if they are born in the Brahma heaven.
They will always be revered by the Brahmās and, in their final life, attain rebirth in the Land of Immeasurable Life (*Amitāyus*), where they shall also be foremost among all bodhisattvas.

Furthermore, it is said: "If a person, at the time of death, instructs another to create an image—even one as small as a grain of barley—that person can eliminate the sins of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas. Moreover, a sutra states: "To cultivate..."
Therefore, it is superior to newly acquired [merit] (and so forth). For this reason, in the past there was a poor woman who mended a small crack on her face;
in every successive life her face became golden in color, and she enjoyed wealth, happiness, and sovereignty. In her final birth, she encountered a Buddha and realized the fruit of enlightenment.
Furthermore, there was an elder who treated a broken finger; in every life his finger emitted the light of a lamp, a treasure followed him even in death, and he never lacked for anything.
In the end, he encountered the Buddha, left the household life, and attained the Way. Alas! Such was the deed performed, yet so great was the benefit obtained;
this is because one has sown seeds in the unsurpassed fertile field. Is this not what the ancients meant when they said:
"Sow a single grain of grain in spring, and reap ten thousand ears of grain in autumn"?
Regarding the chanting and singing of praises to the Triple Gem, a sutra states: "Because the beings of this Sahā world possess keen faculties of hearing, they perform the Buddha-work through sound.

Therefore, when one chants and sings, not only does it increase the sense of devotion within one's own mind, but it also causes all those who see or hear—whether in the hidden realms or the manifest world—to give rise to a heart of joy and to further develop the aspiration for the Way. Thus, it brings benefit to both oneself and others; its merit is vast.
Nothing is greater than this.
Regarding the merit of sweeping a stupa, the *Bodhisattvapūrvacaryā-sūtra* states:

After the parinirvāṇa of the past Buddha Dīpaṃkara, during the final age of the True Dharma, there was a poor man who supported himself by selling firewood. While gathering wood in a marsh, he saw from afar... [the marsh].
Among them was a stupa-temple. He went directly to its location and, upon beholding it, prostrated himself;
however, he saw only a place where birds and beasts dwelt, filled with weeds, thorns, and impurities, utterly devoid of human tracks and lacking any who made offerings.
When the poor man saw this, his heart was moved with sorrow, yet not understanding the divine majesty of the Tathāgata, he felt only joy.
He cleared away the grasses and trees and swept away all impurities; having performed his prostrations, he departed.

By virtue of these causes and conditions, after his life ended, he was reborn in the Ābhāsvara Heaven, where he experienced immeasurable bliss. When his celestial lifespan was exhausted, he was reborn one hundred times as a Cakravartin King, ruling over the four continents.
Once his merit as a Cakravartin was exhausted, he constantly became a king, a great clan leader, or a wealthy elder, possessing vast riches.
His wealth was immeasurable; his appearance was upright and handsome, such that all who saw him loved and revered him.
Whenever he wished to travel, the road became purified of its own accord, and amidst the void, a rain of various flowers fell. He experienced such rewards for ninety kalpas.
In his final birth, he encountered Śākyamuni Tathāgata, left the household life, and attained the Way. This present-day Bhadrajyoti is he. Furthermore, Ānanda...
The *Shanhai jing* states: "If a person were to sweep the entire land of Jambudvīpa, it would not equal sweeping an area the size of a cow’s lying-down space at a Buddhist stūpa.
It further says: "Upon the end of life, one will go directly to the Land of Peace and Bliss," and so forth.
Regarding the merit of offering flowers, the *Śatavarga-sūtra* states:

During the period of the bequeathed Dharma of the past Buddha Vipaśyin, there was a person who went to a stūpa and saw withered flowers and the accumulation of dust and grime; he immediately took up [a cloth] to sweep away the dust.
He used it again as an offering. By this cause and condition, for ninety-one kalpas he did not fall into the evil realms, but was constantly reborn among humans and devas.
His body was supple and soft; his complexion was fresh and radiant; his wealth was immeasurable; and he possessed great majesty and virtue.

In the end, he encountered the World-Honored One Śākyamuni, left the household life, and attained the Way. He is none other than the Bhikṣu Mahātejas of today. By sweeping away the ancient dust and flowers, he made an offering.
If the retribution for such [an act] is as great as this, how much more so for one who specifically prepares and offers it?
Its merit is beyond calculation. Regarding the merit of burning incense, the *Śatavarga-vinaya-sūtra* (*Baiyuan jing*) states:

After the parinirvāṇa of the past Buddha Vipaśyin, during the period of his bequeathed Dharma, there was a person who entered a Buddhist stūpa and burned sandalwood incense as an offering to the Buddha’s shrine.
Because of these causes and conditions, for ninety-one kalpas he was born among humans and devas, with upright and handsome features;
from all the pores of his body issued the fragrance of sandalwood, and in the end he encountered a Buddha and attained the fruit of arhatship.
He is none other than the bhikṣu Gandhamādana.
Regarding the merit of offering lamps, the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* states:

In the kingdom of Śrāvastī, there was a woman named Nanda who was poor and solitary, sustaining herself by begging. Seeing the kings and great ministers vying to make offerings to the Buddha, she thought to herself:
"By what sin in my past lives have I been born into such poverty and low station? Though I have encountered this field of merit, I possess nothing [to offer]."
He possessed the seeds [of future merit], and his subsequent retribution was to be known. Moved by deep compassion for himself, he sought to provide an offering.
Having begged all day, he obtained only two coins. Taking them to an oil shop, he intended to buy oil sufficient to make a single lamp.
Carrying it toward the Jetavana, he lit it before the Buddha and made this vow: "May I, in a future life, obtain the lamp of wisdom to extinguish [the darkness of ignorance]."
All grew dark. Having made this vow, he prostrated before the Buddha and departed. Because of his profound resolve, among all the lamps, his light alone was bright and radiant.
When dawn broke, Maudgalyāyana sought to extinguish it, but despite his utmost effort, he could not. Seeing this, the Buddha said to him:
"This is a lamp offered by one who has resolved upon the Great Mind; it is not something you, a śrāvaka, can overturn."
It stirred. Even if you were to pour forth the waters of the four great oceans and unleash the fierce winds of Vairambha, they could not extinguish it.
At dawn, Nanda came to the place where the Buddha was; the Buddha bestowed upon him this prediction:
"In a future age, after two asaṃkhyeya kalpas have passed, you shall attain Buddhahood, and your name shall be King Lamp-Light (Dīpāṅkararāja), fully endowed with the ten titles. Nanda rejoiced.
She left the household life to become a nun and was held in high esteem by the assembly. Furthermore, the *Dṛṣṭānta-paryāya Sūtra* states: "In a past life, the Venerable Aniruddha was a bandit.
While entering a Buddhist stūpa with the intent to steal its contents, he saw that the lamp burning before the image in the stūpa was about to go out;

he straightened it with an arrow so that it shone brightly. Seeing the majesty and beauty of the image, his hair stood on end, and he thought to himself: 'If even others can renounce [worldly things]...'"
The man sought merit; how could I steal from him? He then abandoned the goods and departed. Because of this, for ninety-one *kalpas*, he was constantly reborn in auspicious places.
Gradually abandoning all evils, his merit and blessings increased daily until, in the end, he encountered a Buddha, left the household life, and realized the fruits of enlightenment.

He became foremost in the possession of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), able to see the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system as clearly as looking at an *āmalaka* fruit in the palm of one's hand.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "By merely offering lamps and candles, one is reborn among the six heavens of the desire realm, where the body is constantly radiant.
Regarding those who perform joyful offerings, the *Śatavarga-vinaya-sūtra* (*Baiyuan jing*) says: "In the city of Kapilavastu, there was an elder."
His family was immensely wealthy, possessing immeasurable riches and treasures. His wife became pregnant, and when ten months had passed, she gave birth to a mass of flesh.
Considering this an inauspicious omen, he went to question the Buddha. The Buddha said to the elder, "Simply raise it well.
Having heard this, the elder withdrew with joy. On the seventh day, the mass of flesh opened up, revealing one hundred handsome boys.
He was truly extraordinary. As he gradually grew up, his hundred brothers all joined the Buddha’s order and renounced the household life;
they simultaneously attained the fruit of Arhatship. When the great assembly saw this, they asked the Buddha about their past causes. The Buddha said:

"In the past, after the parinirvāṇa of Vipaśyin Buddha, there was a king who erected a stūpa, enshrined the Buddha’s relics therein, and made offerings to it. At that time, there were [people] from the same city..."
More than one hundred people performed various musical performances as offerings to that stūpa.

By virtue of these causes and conditions, they were reborn among gods and humans for ninety-one kalpas, experiencing happiness and blessings. Now, having encountered me, they have left the household life and realized the fruits of the path.
Regarding the statement on serving and supporting one's teachers and parents: in the mundane world, no deep kindness surpasses that of one's parents;

in the supramundane realm, no great kindness precedes that of one's teachers. Therefore, the Buddha said: "In an age when there is no Buddha, filial piety toward one's parents yields merit equal to making offerings to a Buddha.
Furthermore, the *Lüyào jīng* (Essential Summary of the Sūtra of the Fallen Blue) states: "If a person seeks to cultivate merit, they should constantly practice giving. [With] a golden bowl..."
Silver vessels were filled with silver grain; silver bowls were filled with gold grain. Golden cauldrons contained a hundred flavors; jeweled couches were spread with bedding.
Elephants, horses, and carriages were adorned with various treasures. Of such items as these, there were eighty-four thousand of each.
The merit obtained by giving alms to ordinary people is immeasurable; yet it is not equal to giving a single meal to one person seeking the Way.

Feeding a hundred seekers of the Way is not equal to feeding one who has attained the first fruit (srotāpanna). Feeding a hundred who have attained the first fruit is not equal to feeding one who has attained the second fruit (sakṛdāgāmin).

Feeding a hundred who have attained the second fruit is not equal to feeding one who has attained the third fruit (anāgāmin). Feeding a hundred who have attained the third fruit is not equal to... [feeding one who has attained the fourth fruit].
First, regarding the four fruits [of the śrāvaka path]: feeding one hundred people who have attained these four fruits is not equal to being filial toward one's parents.
Furthermore, the verse by Maitreya Bodhisattva encouraging filial piety says: "In the hall above are two Buddhas; alas, the people of this world do not recognize them.
They are not fashioned with gold and colors, nor are they carved from sandalwood; simply look upon your father and mother in this present life—they are Śākyamuni and Maitreya."
Le: "If one can provide for them [the parents], what need is there to perform other meritorious deeds? It even says: 'While they are alive, let their sweet tastes not be lacking;
after they have died, there is no need to pursue remembrance. If you can apply your mind in this way, Heaven, Earth, the dragons, and the spirits will protect and assist you.
Furthermore, the *Bao'en jing* (Sutra on Repaying Kindness) states: "Parents are the most supreme field of merit within the three realms. Also, the *Vinaya*...
Yaśas said: "The Buddha permitted bhikṣus to provide for their parents with all their heart and throughout their entire lives; otherwise, they would incur a grave offense. He further stated:
"The Buddha permitted that even if one has utterly violated the precepts, one should still provide for one's parents, as well as one's preceptors (upādhyāya), teachers (ācārya), and the sick.
He also stated: "If a renunciant provides for his parents, regarding the three robes (tricīvara)..."
Regarding external items other than these, one may either beg them from a donor or receive them as a benefit from the Saṃgha;

or, from the portion of food regularly provided by the Saṃgha, one should provide half. If one subsists on alms-food, one is also permitted to take half of the meat that fills one's own belly to provide for one's parents.
Furthermore, the Acintyaprabhāsa-sūtra states: "If one uses various kinds of drinks..."
Providing food, various precious jewels, and all manner of offerings does not repay the kindness of one's parents.

If, however, one can lead them and cause them to turn toward the True Dharma, that alone is called repaying their kindness. Furthermore, the *Cibei Chan Jing* (Sutra on Compassionate Repentance) states:
"The kindness of teachers and elders exceeds that of parents. Why? Although parents love their children, they cannot cause them to escape the cage of the triple world. Teachers [can]."
He constantly instructed them in what is good, so that they might leave the three realms of existence and turn toward Bodhi; such was his purpose. The tradition says:
Formerly, there were people from three provinces who had lost their fathers early in life;

they took an elderly man who had no sons as their father and served him with sincere filial piety, whereby they manifested the divine protection of the heavenly deities. Furthermore, there were people from five commanderies who had lost their mothers, and by taking one...
An elderly woman who had no children took [him] as her mother; she served him with total devotion until the end, and in this life she received the reward of an official post from the sovereign.
Alas! If such is the evidence for serving someone who was merely a parent by proxy, how much more so for one’s own biological parents?
What can be said of the merit of filial obedience and support? Furthermore, there was [the case of] one who embraced a bamboo stalk...
Weeping, bamboo shoots sprout amidst the snow; striking the ice, one wails; fish leap from the water. These, too, are the ultimate expressions of filial sincerity.
Viewed from this perspective, neither the teacher nor the parent may be neglected.
Regarding those who speak of worldly benevolence (*ren*) and righteousness (*yi*): benevolence and righteousness are the foundation of all goodness and the way of the Three Kings and Five Emperors;

they do not exceed these two principles. That Confucius and Mencius attained the names of Sage and Worthy was likewise due to this alone. In the worldly way, they are called the Five Constant Virtues (*wuchang*);
in the supramundane Dharma, they are named the Five Precepts (*wu-jie*). Though the names differ, the meaning is the same. Thus, one knows that the laws of human kings are [identical to them].
The Way of kings does not, in any case, transcend benevolence and righteousness (*ren-yi*).

When it is said that they "venerate the elderly and show compassion to the young," this too is nothing other than benevolence and righteousness. This can be understood through the underlying intent: namely, that veneration constitutes righteousness.
Compassion is benevolence. Thus, Confucius said: "Revere those who are old as you revere your own elders; treat those who are young as you treat your own children.
Then the world may be turned over in the palm of one's hand. This principle applies equally to the internal teachings of Buddhism.
One should revere those of superior virtue to receive their instruction, and compassionately nurture those who come after to guide them toward progress.
If this tradition is passed down without ceasing, then the people throughout the realm can be led to the Way. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"In the past, there was a bird named Kapiṃjala who had two close friends: one was a great elephant, and the other was a monkey. They lived together at Pippala..."
They lived in a *nyagrodha* tree. They asked one another, "We do not know who among us is the greatest.
The elephant said, "In the past, I saw this tree beneath my belly; by this inference, I must be the greatest.
The monkey said, "I once crouched on the ground and grasped the top of the tree with my hand; I must be the longest. The bird said, "In the *piṇḍabara* forest..."
In the middle [of the forest], they ate the fruit of this tree; the seeds were expelled with their dung, and from this the tree grew.
"I am the eldest," said the elephant. The bird spoke again, saying, "The elder who was born first should be honored according to propriety.

Immediately, the great elephant carried the monkey on its back, and the bird perched atop the monkey as they traveled about. When all the birds and beasts saw them, they asked, "Why are you acting like this?"

He replied, “It is because they revere the elders. Even the birds and beasts have been transformed by this teaching; they all practice ritual respect, do not encroach upon the people’s fields, and do not harm living beings.

The people of the nation also followed their example and all practiced ritual respect. From antiquity to the present, this transformation has flowed through ten thousand generations, and the land has enjoyed great peace.
(And so forth. Alas! If even birds and beasts show reverence for their elders and comply with ritual propriety, how much more so should humans do the same?
As for the number of residents, could their mental conduct possibly be unrestrained? An external text says: "When one rectifies oneself, the world is rectified.
Is this not what is meant here?
Regarding those who speak of compassion for all sentient beings: among the myriad practices of a bodhisattva, the mind of compassion is the beginning. Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
It is because of sentient beings that great compassion arises; because of great compassion that the bodhicitta is generated;

and because of the bodhicitta that one achieves equal and perfect enlightenment. Furthermore, the *Ullambana Sūtra* states: "If a person were to feed a hundred pratyekabuddhas, it would not be as good as feeding one Buddha.
Feeding a hundred Buddhas is not as good as someone building a stūpa for a Buddha. Moreover, if there is another person who..."

To be able to resolve the mind to take refuge in the Triple Gem is a supreme and excellent merit. Furthermore, the various virtues previously listed, such as giving and so forth, do not equal that of a person who upholds the five precepts.
Upholding the precepts does not equal a compassionate heart that takes pity on all living beings, even down to the crawling insects.
As stated in the *Zhāoyào jīng* (Essentials of Various Sutras): "If a person were to sacrifice incalculable bodies to make offerings to the ten directions..."
The merit of all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Śrāvakas does not equal that of a person who gives a single mouthful of food to an animal, or even gives to the field of compassion such as ants;
the latter’s merit is most supreme. For example, Śāriputra once offered a single meal to the Buddha.
The Buddha turned the gift over to the dog and asked Śāriputra: "You gave me food, and I gave it to the dog; who obtained greater merit? Śāriputra replied:
"The Buddha obtained greater merit by giving to the dog. Furthermore, the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* states:
"In the world-system of Enduring Splendid Adornment, all sentient beings are fully endowed with every form of peace and happiness. If there are sentient beings..."

In that land, practicing the various pure conducts (*brahmacarya*) for hundreds of thousands of millions of years does not equal the merit obtained by giving rise to a mind of loving-kindness and compassion toward sentient beings in this Sahā world for even the duration of a single finger-snap; the latter is many times greater than the former.
Furthermore, the *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra* states: "If there are many rats and sparrows in one's fields or granaries that ravage the grain..."
Rice. Yet, he forms this thought: "Such mice and sparrows have their lives sustained because of me. Having formed this thought, he is filled with joy and harbors no intention to harm them.
You should know that such a person attains immeasurable merit (and so forth). All those who seek the path of the Buddha should train themselves in this manner.

Regarding the expression "rejoicing in the goodness of others": all sentient beings, since beginningless kalpas, have been bound within the wheel of the six realms of existence and have undergone immeasurable suffering without attaining liberation; this is solely due to the power of their jealousy, which obstructs the goodness of others.
Even when they themselves perform virtuous deeds, it is because they desire to surpass others that the fire of their grasping at self and others burns without ceasing.

The period for liberation is far off. If one can rejoice in the goodness of others, then the obstacle of envy will be extinguished, one will achieve the patience of compliance (*anulomikī-kṣānti*), and it will be easy to escape the wheel of suffering.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states: "If a single hair were divided into a hundred parts, and one were to take a drop of water from the great ocean of the trichiliocosm with it, its quantity might be known;
yet the merit of rejoicing in the goodness of others cannot be measured. Furthermore, the *Za jing yao ji* (Essentials of Various Sutras) says:

It is said: "If there is a person who is poor and of meager merit, possessing not even a speck of dust as something to give, yet gives rise to joy in their heart upon seeing others practicing generosity, their merit is equal to that of the giver and no different.
(And so forth. A wise person should therefore urgently reform their past ways and cultivate themselves for the future.
Humility of mind is the sublime medicine for curing the malady of pride. This pride, however, is a great obstacle within the Dharma.
It is like a worldly wheel that cannot reach the summit of a high mountain; likewise, the Wheel of Dharma cannot turn upon the high mountain of self-conceit.
Therefore, those who study the Buddha’s teachings should first subdue their pride and cultivate supreme respect for the Three Jewels.
O Treasure! To revere elders with respect in the middle and to follow the common folk below—this may indeed be called being a virtuous person.
For this reason, the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging constantly prostrated to all, saying, "I do not disparage you. The Great Being Samantabhadra also said:
"Toward all sentient beings, I perform various services and offer various forms of worship, as if honoring my parents, as if serving my teachers."

"Long ago, up until the time of the Tathāgata, there was no difference between them. Furthermore, in recent times, there was the Dharma Master of the Lotus Sūtra, whose conduct was pure and refined, and whom the masses revered.
When he walked, he would look only at the ground as he went. If he saw even a tiny insect in his path, he would think to himself:
'Who knows that this son of the Buddha may have attained the Way before me? He would then move out of the way and proceed."
Students should reflect upon this and strive for emulation.

Speaking with gentle words is a primary task for winning the hearts of the multitude. Now, among the people of the world who commit offenses through the three karmas, those of the mouth are the most serious.
Among the four evils of speech, harsh words are the most extreme. Why is this? It is not merely...
If one gives rise to anger within one's own mind, it causes the other person to harbor resentment as well.
This becomes the root of enmity, which gradually increases so that from kalpa to kalpa they harm one another with no end in sight.

How much better it would be, when speaking with others, to utter gentle words, or to instruct them in what is wholesome so as to bring them joy—even toward all animals, one must not... [give rise to anger].
Furthermore, he utters harsh words. Although that being does not yet understand what the person says, anger manifests before them, causing the animal to see it and become terrified.
Therefore, there is certainly no lack of karmic retribution; once karma is formed, its fruit will surely not be in vain, and one must experience it oneself.
As stated in the *Mukha-saṃvara-sūtra*: "In the past, a Tripiṭaka Bhikṣu, by means of a single evil word..."
Therefore, as retribution, she became a hundred-headed fish; the calamity reached her mother, who likewise became a latrine worm (and so forth). Furthermore, the *Mahā-upāya-kauśalya Sūtra* says:
"When a person is born into this world, disaster issues from the mouth, which is more severe than a fierce fire.
A fierce fire burns only the worldly wealth of the world, but evil speech blazes fiercely to burn the seven noble riches. The tongue within the mouth is a tool that carves the body."
The axe. One must be cautious regarding the fire that consumes the self.
As shown above, everything from generosity and patience to humility and gentle speech is, without exception, a cause for attaining Buddhahood.
If one practices these fully, nothing could be more excellent. Otherwise, according to what is appropriate and pleasing, simply—
It is also possible to attain [enlightenment] by practicing a single matter. Why is this so? A verse in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* says:

"If there are classes of sentient beings who encounter the Buddhas of the past, And whether they hear the Dharma and practice giving, Or uphold the precepts, practice patience, Exert diligence, meditate, or cultivate wisdom— If such people possess a virtuous and gentle mind, All these individuals have already attained the Buddha-way. When the Buddhas pass into extinction...
Having completed their deliverance, those who made offerings to the *śarīra* erected billions of kinds of stupas—made of gold, silver, crystal, ruby, lapis lazuli, and pearls;
pure, vast, and magnificently adorned. Others used sandalwood and other timbers, or bricks, tiles, clay, and earth.
Even those who, in the midst of a wilderness, piled up earth to create a temple for the Buddha, or even children playing who gathered sand to make a stupa for the Buddha.

All such people as these have already attained the path of Buddhahood. If anyone, for the sake of the Buddha, establishes various images—whether made of the seven treasures, brass, red or white copper, iron, wood, or clay;
or made of lacquer and cloth, or painted in colors—whether they do it themselves or cause others to do it, even if it is done as a child’s play, or with grass and wood.
Or with a brush, or even using their fingernails, they drew images of the Buddha. All such people as these have already attained the path of Buddhahood.
If a person, at a stupa or temple, or before a precious image or a painted image, makes offerings with flowers, incense, banners, and canopies out of a reverent heart;
or if they cause others to perform music—beating drums, blowing horns and conchs, or playing flutes, pipes, lutes, and *kōhō* harps.
Lutes, gongs, and bronze cymbals—such various wondrous sounds as these, all were offered in worship.
Or, with a heart of joy, they sang hymns in praise of the Buddha’s virtues; even those who made but a single small sound have all already attained the path to Buddhahood.
If a person, even with a distracted mind, offers but a single flower to a painted image, they will gradually behold immeasurable Buddhas and shall themselves attain realization.

The Unsurpassed Way, widely delivering countless multitudes. Should there be someone who prostrates, or again, merely joins their palms, or even raises a single hand, or again slightly bows their head—if a person with a distracted mind utters "Namo Buddha" but once—[they shall attain liberation].
"Such people as these have all already attained the Way of the Buddha" (and so forth). Alas!
If it were not the case that there is no dharma that is not the work of the Buddha, how could one perform this task with child's play?

How could such minute merit—achieved by a single invocation with a distracted mind—reach such a supreme station? For this reason, our Śākyamuni Buddha appeared in the world, giving rise to compassion for all beings, and through his skillful [means]...

Through wisdom and skillful means, according to their faculties and inclinations, he may demonstrate the practice of seated meditation, the recitation of sutras, or the teaching of mindfulness of the Buddha;
he causes them to cultivate all manner of wholesome deeds, such as giving and ethical discipline, leading them into the path of the Buddha without exception, save for those of the icchantika class.
It is like a physician-king in the world who administers medicine according to the illness, excepting only those whose life span has come to an end.

There is none that is not healed and restored to health. However, some people have not yet understood the Tathāgata’s skillful means and teachings, nor have they reached an understanding of what is appropriate for the inclinations and joys of sentient beings;
each clings to a single aspect, claiming it to be supreme, and even teaches others.

Based on the methods they themselves have observed, some say that seated meditation is foremost, some say that reciting the sutras is first, and others say that mindfulness of the Buddha is [the best].
"Superior. Thus, regarding all dharmas such as giving and precepts, it is said that these alone are [the path], while other virtues are not.

Is this not to know one thing while remaining ignorant of its counterpart? For instance, if one wishes to enter a royal city where the eight gates are unguarded, one should simply be led straight in according to whichever direction one approaches.
Why must those from the eastern road be led through the western gate, or those from the western road [through the eastern]?
When a person is led through the eastern gate, they are needlessly made to undergo toil; though there are eight gates, entry occurs through only one.
The various Dharma-gates are distinct, yet all return to a single point. Why then do you harbor biased attachments and disputes? This is called failing to examine the root of the illness;
it is like the category of "milk medicine" in the Pure Teachings. I exhort all practitioners: you should understand this meaning and, according to what your capacity can bear, follow one [gate].
In practice, advance in merit without ever retreating.

If you vow to be born in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing, you will be reborn among the nine lotuses according to your merit; there you shall behold Amitābha Buddha, hear the Dharma, and awaken to the realization of non-arising.
"An-yang" (Peaceful Nurturing) is also called "Ultimate Bliss" (Sukhāvatī). The adornments of that land and its various joys are beyond the reach of analogy or description.
The *Smaller Amitābha Sūtra* states: "From here, to the west, passing through a hundred thousand myriads of koṭis of Buddha-lands, there is this world."
The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states that the land of Amitābha Buddha is not far from here. These two explanations are merely spoken according to the capacities of sentient beings;
the distance cannot be fixed. It exists solely within the single thought-moment of sentient beings.
Since this mind is without obstruction, how could there be east and west, or near and far? Amitābha is translated here as "Immeasurable Light" (*Amitābha*), and is also called...
Regarding "Immeasurable Life," a sutra states: "The radiance of that Buddha is immeasurable, illuminating one hundred thousand lands.
The lifespan of that Buddha is immeasurable and boundless, lasting for asaṃkhyeya kalpas" (and so forth).

Regarding the "nine lotuses": that Buddha, by means of his forty-eight vows, adorned a pure land and established nine grades of lotuses to receive and guide sentient beings with karmic affinity from the ten directions. Why is this so?
It is because the faculties and natures of sentient beings possess many differences. It is like a worldly king fighting against an enemy; those who achieve merit therein are mostly not equal.
According to their merit, they were rewarded with offices of the first, second, third, fourth, or fifth rank, up to the eighth and ninth ranks;
not a single person was left out. The Buddha is likewise: according to the extent of the karmic achievements of sentient beings, he employs the nine lotuses.

This encompasses all beings without exception. Regarding the matter of how those nine grades of sentient beings are assigned rebirth in the nine lotuses, I shall now briefly cite the scriptural text to demonstrate it.
The *Sūtra on the Visualization of Immeasurable Life* states: "As for those of the highest grade of the highest birth: if there are sentient beings who give rise to three kinds of mind..."
One shall immediately be born in that land. First is the mind of utmost sincerity; second is the profound mind; third is the mind of dedication and aspiration.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of sentient beings who shall attain birth there: first, those with a compassionate heart who refrain from killing and maintain all the precepts;
second, those who read and recite the Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras; and third, those who practice the six recollections (of the Buddha, Dharma, Saṅgha, precepts, giving, and heaven).
[Those who have] bestowed the precepts upon the Sangha and possess these merits will attain rebirth [in the Pure Land] after one day and night, or even up to seven days.

At the time of this person’s death, Amitābha Buddha, together with Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and an immeasurable assembly of Bodhisattvas, will appear before them and extend their hands to welcome them.
Upon seeing this, the practitioner will rejoice and leap for joy, perceiving themselves as riding [upon a lotus].
Upon the Vajra Terrace, following behind the Buddha, they will be reborn in that land in the time it takes to snap one's fingers.

Having arrived, they will immediately behold the physical marks and signs of the Buddha’s body, as well as the Bodhisattvas endowed with perfect features. They will see the groves of radiant jewels as the Buddha expounds the sublime Dharma;
having heard it, they will immediately realize the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Regarding those of the highest grade who are born through middle-level practice: they need not necessarily receive, uphold, read, or recite the Vaipulya sutras. They skillfully understand their meaning and intent;
their minds are not startled or shaken regarding the ultimate truth (paramārtha); they have deep faith in cause and effect and do not slander the Mahāyāna.

When such a person reaches the end of life, a Great Sage comes to welcome them. The circumstances are as described above: the practitioner sees themselves seated upon a purple-golden platform and is immediately reborn.

In the ponds of the seven treasures in that land, the lotuses bloom immediately after one night has passed. Seeing the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas emitting light that illuminates their bodies, their eyes immediately open and become clear.
After the passing of one small kalpa, they attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

As for those of the highest grade who are born in the lower level: they also believe in cause and effect and do not slander the Mahāyāna; they merely give rise to the mind of unsurpassed enlightenment.

When such a person reaches the end of their life, the assembly of sages comes to welcome them. The practitioner sees themselves sitting upon a golden lotus flower and being reborn in the precious pond.
After one day and one night has passed, the lotus flower finally opens. Within seven days, they are able to see the Buddha. Although...
He beheld the Buddha’s body; however, his mind was not yet clearly discerning regarding its various marks. Only after twenty-one days did he see them with perfect clarity.
After three minor kalpas had passed, he attained the Gate of Illumination of the Hundred Dharmas and dwelt in the Stage of Joy (Pramuditā-bhūmi).
Regarding those of middle grade who are born in the superior manner: if there are sentient beings who uphold the five precepts, observe the eightfold fast, and practice various moral disciplines;
who do not commit the five heinous crimes and are free from manifold faults and evils—when such persons reach the end of their lives, the assembly of sages will come to welcome them.
The practitioner will see for themselves that they sit upon a lotus pedestal and are reborn in that land. The lotus flower will then open, and they will hear the multitude...

Through the praise of the Four Noble Truths in sound, they immediately attain the path of Arhatship at that very moment, becoming endowed with the three knowledges, the six supernormal powers, and the eight liberations.
As for those born among the intermediate class: if there are sentient beings who observe the śrāmaṇera precepts for even one day and one night, or...
Having maintained the full precepts with unimpaired dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*), when this person reaches the end of life, the assembly of sages comes to welcome them.
The practitioner sees for themselves that they sit upon a lotus flower; the flower then closes, and they follow behind the Buddha, being born within a jeweled pond.

After seven days have passed, the flower finally unfolds. Opening their eyes and joining their palms in reverence, they praise the Buddha and hear the Dharma. After half an eon has elapsed, they attain perfection.

Regarding the Arhat rebirth in the middle grade, lower level: if there are sentient beings who filially support their parents, serve their teachers and elders, and practice worldly benevolence and righteousness,
when such persons reach the end of their lives, they will encounter virtuous friends who will extensively expound for them the land of Amitābha Buddha.
Having heard this matter, the person from the Land of Joy immediately passed away and was reborn in that land. After seven days had passed, they encountered Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta;
hearing the Dharma with joy, they attained the stage of Srotāpanna and, after the passing of one small kalpa, became Arhats.
Regarding those who attain birth in the highest grade of the lower level: there may be sentient beings who have committed various evil deeds;
although they do not slander the Vaipulya sutras, they have created many unwholesome dharmas and lack a sense of shame or remorse.

When such a person is at the point of death, they encounter a virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) who praises for them the titles of the twelve divisions of the Mahāyāna sutras. Because they hear the names of these various sutras, [they are led to rebirth].
The extremely heavy evil karma of a thousand kalpas is eliminated. Furthermore, the virtuous friend instructs them to recite "Namo Amitābha Buddha.
Because they recite the Buddha’s name, the sins of birth and death from fifty billion kalpas are eradicated.
At that time, that Buddha immediately dispatches transformation Buddhas, a transformation Avalokiteśvara, and a transformation Mahāsthāmaprāpta to the practitioner and says: "Good son,"
"Because you have invoked the name of the Buddha, all your transgressions are extinguished; I come to welcome you.
The practitioner then sees the radiance of the transformation Buddha filling his room. Having seen this, he rejoices and immediately passes away, mounting a precious lotus flower.
Following behind the transformation Buddha, he was born within a jewel pond. After seven times seven days had passed, the lotus flower finally blossomed.
At that time, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva emitted light and preached the Dharma; having heard it, he attained faith and understanding, and gave rise to the mind set on the unsurpassed path.
After ten minor kalpas, he attained entry into the first stage (bhūmi).
Regarding those of the middle grade within the lowest category: there may be sentient beings who violate the five precepts, the eight precepts, or the full set of precepts;
who steal the property of the Saṃgha or the property of the *pratyutpanna-saṃgha*; who preach the Dharma with impurity; and who lack a sense of shame or remorse.

When such a person reaches the end of their life, the various fires of hell arrive all at once. If they encounter a virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), he will immediately praise and explain for them the [Amitābha Sūtra].
Upon hearing of the radiance and majestic virtue of Amitābha Buddha, this person eliminates the sins of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas.
The fierce fires of hell transform into cool breezes that waft celestial flowers; upon each flower are manifested Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who welcome this person.
In the space of a single thought-moment, they are reborn within a lotus flower in the Jewel Pond. Thus it is said in the sutra.

Only after a great kalpa does the lotus finally bloom; then Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta preach the profound Mahāyāna sūtras for them, and having heard this Dharma, they immediately resolve their minds upon the unsurpassed path.

Regarding those born in the lowest grade of the lowest level: there may be sentient beings who have committed the five heinous crimes and the ten evil deeds, possessing all manner of unwholesome acts.
Such persons ought to fall into the evil realms and undergo suffering without end for many kalpas.

At the time of their death, they encounter a virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) who expounds the sublime Dharma and instructs them to practice mindfulness of the Buddha. Yet, being oppressed by suffering, these people find no leisure to practice such mindfulness.
The spiritual friend said: "If you are unable to practice mindfulness of the Buddha, you should instead recite, 'I take refuge in Amitāyus Buddha.
In this manner, with a sincere mind, let the sound not cease until you have completed ten recitations, calling out, 'Namo Amitābha Buddha.'"
By virtue of reciting the Buddha’s name, in every moment of thought, one eliminates the sins of eighty billion kalpas of birth and death.
After the end of life, one sees a golden lotus flower, like a sun-disk, appearing before that person.

In the space of a single thought-moment, one immediately departs for that land and is born within a lotus flower. Only after twelve great kalpas have passed does the lotus flower finally open. [Avalokiteśvara...]
Finally, with a voice of great compassion, he expounds the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*) and the methods for extinguishing sinful karma.

Having heard this, they rejoice and immediately resolve their minds upon the unsurpassed path (and so forth). This constitutes the nine grades of sentient beings who are reborn within the nine lotuses.
Furthermore, regarding those who are reborn in palaces, the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states: "If there are sentient beings who cultivate various meritorious virtues..."

He aspired to be born in that land, but later felt regret and was further filled with doubt. He did not believe in the existence of that Buddha-land, nor did he believe in those who attain rebirth there;
furthermore, he did not believe that by practicing charity and creating merit, one would obtain blessings in future lives.
Although such was his state, he continued to maintain a mindful heart, occasionally believing and occasionally disbelieving, his will wavering and lacking any firm foundation. As death approached...
At the time of death, the Buddha manifests his body so that the person may see it with their own eyes. Although the person is unable to speak, their heart is filled with joy;

they then repent for not having performed various good deeds. Because of this repentance, they are likewise reborn in that land, though they are unable to proceed directly to the presence of the Buddha.
Instead, they enter a border region where they see a city made of the seven treasures, and immediately enter within it.

Born from within a lotus flower, they experience bliss like that of the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven for five hundred years, during which time they do not even hear the names of the Triple Gem (and so forth).

If one relies solely on the various sūtras and śāstras, there is not a single sentient being who hears the name of that land and the title of that Buddha, makes a vow to seek rebirth there, and does not go. As the *Candragarbha-sūtra* states:
"In my age of the Dharma’s decay (*mofa*), among the hundreds of millions of sentient beings who initiate practice and cultivate the Way, not a single one has attained it.
Only the single gate of the Pure Land can serve as a passable path for people (and so forth). Thus, at this time of the Dharma’s decay, if one does not seek the Pure Land, what else is there to do?
Many people harbor doubts and slander regarding this Dharma-gate; yet if they see those seeking rebirth therein..."
[The Master] smiled and stopped him, saying: "To err oneself and lead others astray is to become an enemy of the Buddha. How tragic! How tragic! He continued:
"If it is not so, in a future age you shall surely meet the Honored One Maitreya; at the third assembly under the Dragon Flower tree, you shall all naturally realize the Way."
The *Maitreya-vyākaraṇa-sūtra* states: "In this Jambudvīpa there is a great city named Ketumatī. Within the city there is a great Brahmin named Subrahmanya.
Maitreya takes birth in his family; on the day he leaves the home life, he immediately attains perfect enlightenment beneath a Dragon-flower tree.
The king, the Brahmins, the elders, and all the people [gather together]."
They went to the place where the Buddha was and all together left the household life. At that time, Maitreya Buddha, seeing the great assembly, had this thought:
"These people were sent by Śākyamuni Buddha to be entrusted to me; therefore, they have now all come to my presence.
These people, while within the legacy of Śākyamuni’s Dharma, may have recited and studied the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma."
The Tripitaka [master] may give food and clothing to others; or maintain the precepts and cultivate wisdom; or offer banners, canopies, flowers, and incense to the Buddha;
or bring happiness to suffering sentient beings; or practice patience and meditative concentration.
Or, having built stupas and temples to make offerings to the *śarīra*, they come to my presence by virtue of this merit.

Once they have formed this thought, I preach the Four Noble Truths for them; having heard them, all these people simultaneously attain the path to *nirvāṇa*. Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
At the first assembly under the Dragon Flower tree, he delivered ninety-nine billion śrāvakas; at the second assembly, ninety-six billion śrāvakas;
and at the third assembly, ninety-three billion śrāvakas. Furthermore, the *Baoen jing* (Sutra on Requiting Kindness) states:
"At the third assembly in the Huālín Garden, there were ninety-three billion people. Within the bequeathed Dharma of Śākyamuni, even a single invocation of 'Namo Buddha' [is sufficient]."

Furthermore, the *Maitreya Sūtra* states: "During the Final Dharma Age of Śākyamuni, those who practice seated meditation, recite the sūtras, uphold the precepts, and cultivate merit shall be born in the first assembly;
those who merely uphold the Three Refuges shall be born in the second assembly;
and those who merely hear the Buddha’s name shall be born in the third assembly," and so forth. Judging from this, although we have not yet attained single-minded diligence...

Whether through meditative recitation, upholding the precepts, or cultivating merit—having heard the names of the Buddhas, and having called upon them even once according to one's capacity throughout this lifetime—how could one dare not do so?

Thus, even if one has not yet participated early in the first two assemblies, there is no doubt that one will eventually join the third assembly to hear the Dharma and awaken to the Way. All who possess wisdom should resolve to do so.
Vow: One must encounter this Buddha. If one misses this opportunity, the encounter with a Buddha will be far distant.
Why is this? Within this Bhadrakalpa, there are four kalpas: formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness. Buddhas appear in the world only during the kalpa of abiding.

Furthermore, within the kalpa of abiding, there are twenty periods of increase and decrease. A Buddha must wait for these; during the first eight periods of decrease, time passes in vain without a Buddha appearing.
In the ninth intermediate kalpa of decrease, four Buddhas appeared. That is to say, when the human lifespan was sixty thousand years, Śikhin Buddha appeared;
when it was forty thousand years, Viśvabhū Buddha appeared; when it was twenty thousand years, Kāśyapa Buddha appeared;
and when it was one hundred years, Śākyamuni Buddha appeared. After the Dharma of Śākyamuni had ceased, the human lifespan increased to eighty-four thousand years.
When the lifespan has decreased to one thousand years, Maitreya Buddha will appear.
From the time of Śākyamuni Buddha’s parinirvāṇa until this point, sixty billion years have elapsed; this is the tenth period of decrease.
During the eleventh, twelfth, thirteenth, and fourteenth periods—these four kalpas—no Buddha appears in the world. Therefore, one must advance in merit without fail during these times.
Ler! In the fifteenth *kalpa* of decrease, nine hundred and ninety-five Buddhas will appear in succession to manifest their teachings;
at the end, the Buddha Ruci will appear, after which five *kalpas* will remain.

The various causes of goodness previously explained apply equally to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles. Because the faculties and natures of ordinary beings differ, their dedications (*pariṇāmanā*) are likewise not uniform:
some aspire for the pleasures of humans and devas, while others seek the fruits of the four noble stages.
Although these are indeed wholesome karmic results, they are extremely slow in leading to Buddhahood, involving immeasurable eons in the interim.
In vain one undergoes suffering; if you wish to swiftly leave suffering behind, you should dedicate all the small and great virtues performed toward the Mahāyāna.
You should dedicate them to three places: first, to the four debts of gratitude, the three realms of existence, and all sentient beings within the Dharma-realm;
next, to the fruit of Buddhahood and Bodhi; and finally, to the reality-limit of True Suchness (*tathatā-bhūtakoṭi*).
If one dedicates in this manner, even a hair’s breadth of goodness becomes equal to space.
It is like a single drop of water cast into the great ocean, becoming one with the sea—deep, vast, and without limit or bottom.

This demonstrates the excellence of all wholesome deeds, which applies universally to practitioners of both the Great and Small Vehicles. However, because the faculties and inclinations of sentient beings differ, their cultivation of causes varies accordingly.

These are each distinct. Therefore, the resulting retributions achieved consist of ten thousand varieties. That is to say, there may be sentient beings who seek worldly happiness and cultivate various wholesome karmas;
those of inferior capacity are born among humans, while those of superior capacity are born in the heavens, where they experience happiness according to their respective portions.
Alternatively, there may be sentient beings who loathe the suffering of the three realms and seek the bliss of nirvāṇa, delighting in solitary tranquility and cultivating [the path].

Regarding the wisdom of the various dhyānas: those of dull faculties become śrāvakas, while those of sharp faculties become pratyekabuddhas; this is called "liberation through solitary cultivation," which is censured by all Buddhas.
Alternatively, there may be sentient beings who, though not yet having crossed over themselves, desire first to deliver others;

they diligently cultivate vigor and seek omniscience—this is called the Mahāyāna, and they have already formed the noble embryo. Furthermore, humans and devas are contrasted against the three miserable realms (trāya).
The treatise states that [this world] is a place of pleasure, yet it is not true pleasure. Why is this? Among humans, one is currently scorched by the eight sufferings;

subsequently, one undergoes the unbearable sufferings of the three miserable realms. Even in the heavens, there are the sufferings of the five signs of decline. Once the karmic retribution is exhausted, one falls back into the three evil paths.
Thus, the nature of suffering is evident throughout the cycle of transmigration within the six destinies, from which there is no escape.

How can it be said that this is happiness? Although those of the Two Vehicles have escaped the suffering of birth-and-death through segmented existence (*paricchinna-janma-maraṇa*), they have not yet avoided the suffering of transformation and change (*pariṇāmi-duḥkha*). Exiled to foreign lands, they must seek food and clothing;
their livelihood is difficult, and being content with little, they have not attained mastery. Furthermore, by following such circuitous paths, the days until their return home grow ever more distant.

To practice asceticism for kalpas as numerous as motes of dust—how could that be considered happiness? It is like a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who, from the first moment of generating the mind of enlightenment, feels compassion for all beings;
joining together wisdom and compassion, they ascend the great direct path. Their every action proceeds without obstruction, and before long they arrive home to meet their compassionate father.
There they obtain a treasury of precious jewels, enjoying them with sovereign mastery, lacking nothing whatsoever. Only in this way...

This is what is called true bliss. For this reason, Chan Master Yongming Zhoushan cited a sutra, saying: "If one transforms others through the ten wholesome deeds, it is like administering poison to people;

although they may enjoy satisfaction as humans or devas for a single lifetime, they cannot avoid the outbreak of the poison of birth and death, and ultimately will not escape the cycle of saṃsāra, only to further increase their karmic defilements. If one seeks to enlighten and transform others through the Hīnayāna..."
This is an enemy of the Mahāyāna, a terrifying place like a deep pit from which liberation is difficult to attain. As the Sūtra says:

"It would be better to give rise to the mind of a fox, a wolf, or a jackal than to give rise to the thought of a Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha. If one contemplates this teaching, any person of wisdom [should understand its meaning].
"Why not abandon the small and follow the great?
This refers to the various virtues one performs, namely meditation, recitation, prostration, mindfulness, giving, and precept-keeping.

Although one may perform such virtues, if they are not dedicated toward enlightenment, they are like unbaked clay—merely a laborious effort with no benefit. Whenever one wishes to dedicate [the merit], [one should do so as follows].
One must not dedicate [merit] toward the realms of humans, devas, or the fruits of the two vehicles; rather, one should with a sincere heart dedicate it toward three destinations.
What are these three? First is dedication for the sake of sentient beings, which means vowing that the merit cultivated through these practices be bestowed upon all sentient beings.
Second is dedication toward the fruit of Buddhahood, which means vowing that this merit shall extend universally to all.
May all together attain the Buddha-way. Third is dedication to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).

This means wishing that these cultivated merits be as vast as the *dharmatā* (boundless), and as empty and inexhaustible as space. These constitute the three points of dedication. Furthermore, one point states:
dedicating oneself toward others, dedicating causes toward the fruit, and dedicating phenomena toward principle. This is identical to the former.

This is the meaning. Regarding the four debts of gratitude (*catvāra upakārāḥ*): first is the debt of gratitude to the sovereign. This means that every sip of drink and every morsel of food for the subjects is none other than the sovereign’s grace.
Now that we are the sovereign’s subjects, it is fitting that we serve his affairs, pay the imperial taxes annually, and offer our service to repay his grace.
Yet, we evade labor and avoid military service; we shave our heads and live in peace; we sleep and eat without anxiety. How great is the sovereign’s grace!

Second is the debt of gratitude toward one's teachers: they opened my ignorance, admonished me against evil and exhorted me toward good, enabled me to escape the net of worldly existence, and led me into the Buddha’s household;
thus, the kindness of a teacher is truly profound. Third is the debt of gratitude toward one's parents: beginning from the time of conception, throughout the ten months in the womb...
The mother’s mind does not abandon [the child] even until the time of birth. Though the pain is extreme, once the child is born, she forgets her suffering and immediately feels compassion;
she embraces and nurtures it with milk, washes away its impurities, and when it grows up, she continues to provide for it until her own death.
Relinquishing what one holds dear, one entrusts oneself to a teacher to leave the household life and cultivate supramundane deeds. Among these, the kindness of one's parents is the deepest;

next is the kindness of the four types of benefactors. This refers to us bhikṣus: even though we dwell among mountains and forests, eating without plowing and clothing ourselves without sericulture, all of this is due to the grace of the donors (*dānapati*) from the ten directions.
If one were to compare these four kinds of kindness, the kindness of the benefactors— *Note: The text provided ends abruptly. The translation reflects the content as given.*
This is the most urgent matter. Why? Because a person’s regular diet consists of two meals a day;
if one meal is missed, the edge of the mind is already blunted, and all undertakings will not go as intended. How much more so if both meals are omitted?
And how much more so for two days, three days, or even seven days? Under such circumstances, even one's body and life are difficult to preserve, let alone the cultivation of the Way.
This is the nature of karma. Therefore, one should know that the grace of the donor is the most urgent; the king, the teacher, and one's kin follow in succession.
For this reason, all bhikṣus should understand this intent: even a single prostration, a single thought, a pinch of incense burned, or a single lamp lit [is sufficient].
Offering a single flower, sweeping the stupa, smearing the ground, or any other virtue as small as a single hair— these should first be dedicated to the four debts of gratitude to offer merit,
and thereafter universally bestowed upon all sentient beings.
Though one has not yet perfected the precepts, nor cultivated various virtues, merely forming a connection with the Mahāyāna yields merit twice that of other good deeds.
What is the meaning of the Mahāyāna? It is the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.
Upon hearing this principle of true reality, if one’s mind is not shaken and one gives rise to even a single thought of faith, [that is it].
Their merit is already immeasurable; Because they have resolved upon the Bodhicitta, And are fully endowed with compassion, wisdom, and vows, they shall become the Eye of the World.
They shall act as Teachers of Gods and Humans. Though they remain on the level of ordinary beings, their merit surpasses that of the noble ones of the two fruits.
These are called true sons of the Buddha, Able to repay the kindness of all Buddhas.
"Desiring to enter the Tathāgata’s chamber"—this gate encompasses all words and the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "Only Buddhas and Buddhas can exhaustively fathom the true reality of all phenomena.
It further states: "All worldly activities, livelihoods, and industries are not separate from the true reality."

[The text] contradicts [this]. The Patriarch’s commentary explains: "Each and every arising and ceasing, each and every killing and stealing, the four inversions, the eight heterodoxies, the five heinous crimes, and the ten evils—all are the true mark (*dharmatā*). This matter is manifest; it is the true and eternal right where it is. Who does not possess it?"
What phenomenon is not so? Therefore, a sutra says: "The characteristics of the world are eternally abiding. To awaken to this wondrous principle is called being a Buddha;

to be deluded regarding it is called being a sentient being. Based on this delusion or awakening, one may provisionally distinguish between high and low, yet fundamentally they are no different—just like ice and water, as can be known through analogy.
Thus, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "In the equal and true Dharma-realm, the Buddha does not save sentient beings."

[The passage on] "Birth" (and so forth). If there are sentient beings who, having heard this Dharma, give rise to even a single thought of faith and understanding, their merit surpasses that of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) and cannot be compared to it. Thus, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "This sutra is difficult to uphold;
if one upholds it even for a moment, I shall be joyful, and all Buddhas likewise. This is called the practice of upholding the precepts and practicing *dhūta*. This is...
"The eye of the world for all devas and humans" (and so forth). Furthermore, as stated in various Mahāyāna sūtras, the term "Mahāyāna" has many meanings.
Some say that form is not different from emptiness, and emptiness is not different from form. Others say that Buddhas and sentient beings are equal and without distinction.
Still others say that afflictions are themselves awakening (*bodhi*), and birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) are themselves nirvāṇa. Such are the [teachings].
The words, though different, share the same meaning; both do not transcend the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.
As for the power and efficacy of the Mahāyāna: through faith, one attains Buddhahood in a single instant; through slander, one immediately falls into the hells.
Yet, once the retribution for those sins has been exhausted, one hears this Dharma again and immediately awakens to the Way, as stated in the Mañjuśrī Sūtra.
It is said: There are those who, upon hearing the teaching of Prajñāpāramitā, give rise to slander and lack faith, thereby falling directly into hell.

This is superior to the merit of making offerings to Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Why is this? Making offerings to Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges yields only the merit of birth and death within the human and celestial realms.
However, if one hears the Prajñāpāramitā and falls into hell due to slander, once the retribution for the sin of slandering the Dharma is exhausted, because of having heard the Prajñāpāramitā...

It serves as the seed. Upon merely hearing the teaching of Prajñāpāramitā, one immediately attains the opening of the mind and becomes a Buddha in a single kṣaṇa. Furthermore, the *Acaranga Sūtra* states:

"In the past, there was a Dharma Master named Pure Conduct (*Viśuddha-īryāpatha*), who out of compassion for sentient beings taught and transformed them, causing them to resolve upon Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
There was also a Bhikṣu of Pure Conduct who, although able to protect the precepts, was not yet skilled in [the practice of] Bodhi."
Regarding the path practiced by the Bodhisattva: later, there was a Dharma Master of Pure Conduct who surpassed the Bhikṣu of Proper Conduct.

Knowing that he did not believe in the Mahāyāna precepts, [the latter] slandered him and fell into hell. When his punishment in hell was completed, because he heard this Dharma, it became the cause for his awakening to the Way.
He forcefully spoke a single verse, saying: "Lust is itself the Way; so too are anger and delusion."
Within these three dharmas, all Buddha-dharmas are fully contained. When the bhikṣu Wei-yi heard this, he slandered it;
at the end of his life, he fell into the Avīci Hell, where for ninety hundred thousand *koṭis* of kalpas he underwent various sufferings. Upon emerging from that hell, he...
For six hundred and thirty thousand lifetimes, he was constantly subjected to punishment and slander. His offenses gradually thinned, and later he became a bhikṣu.
