For three hundred and twenty thousand lifetimes after leaving the household life, due to the causal conditions of that karma, he turned away from the Way and returned to secular life;
even for immeasurable thousands of millions of lifetimes thereafter, his faculties remained dull and obtuse. At that time, was the bhikṣu Vīrya someone else? It was none other than [the present one].
"I am that very person. Although I heard this Mahāyāna Dharma and did not believe or accept it, I slandered it and fell into hell.
Once I had finished undergoing that retribution, because of having heard the Mahāyāna, I was finally able to attain Buddhahood (and so forth).

According to the explanations in various sūtras and śāstras, firm adherence to the precepts occurs at the beginning of the Semblance Dharma (*sāṃprata-dharma*). At that time, one is not far removed from the Sage; human nature is [still] slightly..."
"Pure one, it is not difficult to uphold the precepts. Yet even in that era, people upheld them only slightly while transgressing them frequently;
how much more so now in the Age of Dharma’s Decline (*mofa*), when we are ever more distant from the Sages and our human faculties are inferior and lacking in solidity?

Regarding the life-preserving bag of the precepts, how could there not be leaks? If the bag is incomplete, can one possibly cross the ocean of birth and death? Therefore, although one may not protect the precepts,"
However, by merely planting the seeds of the Mahāyāna, one’s merit will surely be doubled. Thus, Master Tiantai said:

"When the Tathāgata appears in the world and preaches the Dharma, those for whom both the Vehicle (the Mahāyāna) and the Precepts are urgent hear the Dharma and awaken to the Way with bodies of humans or devas.

Those for whom the Vehicle is urgent but the Precepts are lax hear the Dharma and attain the Way even with bodies of the three miserable realms. Those for whom the Vehicle is lax but the Precepts are urgent are people attached to pleasure."

"O Celestial One, one who does not participate in the Dharma assembly, whose practice of the Vehicle and the Precepts are both lax, will sink into the evil realms and remain far removed from the Great Way (and so forth).
Observing this, it would be better for the Precepts to be lax than for the Vehicle to be lax."
What is called the bodhicitta is the mind that seeks the Buddha-way above and transforms all sentient beings below.
This mind is praised by all Buddhas of the three periods of time; thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "The initial resolve and the ultimate goal are not two different things.
Of these two minds, the former is more difficult; to seek to save others before one has saved oneself—therefore, I pay homage."
Regarding the initial generation of the mind of enlightenment, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "If one uses clouds of flowers, clouds of garlands, clouds of celestial music,
and even various kinds of celestial incense, lighting various lamps— each lamp-wick as large as Mount Sumeru and each lamp-oil as vast as the waters of the great ocean—
and with such various articles of offering, constantly makes offerings to the [Buddhas] who are beyond measure..."

The merit obtained by all Buddhas, as numerous as the atoms within unspeakably many Buddha-fields, does not equal the merit of a single moment of offering made with the bodhicitta. A hundredth part does not equal it;
a thousandth part does not equal it; indeed, even a fraction of an upaniṣad does not equal it (and so forth).
Regarding "repaying the Buddha's kindness," the *Compassionate Repentance Sutra* (*Cibei chanjing*) states: "The Buddhas' mindfulness of sentient beings exceeds that of parents.
A parent’s love for their child lasts but a single lifetime, whereas the Buddhas’ compassionate mind toward sentient beings is inexhaustible.

Furthermore, when parents see their children turn their backs on kindness and violate righteousness, they give rise to resentment and their compassion diminishes; the Buddhas are not like this. Upon seeing... [text continues]
Seeing that sentient beings do not believe in the scriptural teachings, my compassionate heart grows even more profound;
I would even enter the Avīci Hell to undergo all manner of suffering on their behalf. Such great kindness—how could it ever be repaid?

Even if one were to erect stūpas and temples, vihāras, light lamps and candles, offer banners and canopies, flowers and incense, and various mats and bedding as offerings, these will only bring rewards for oneself in future lives.

Such merit does not constitute repaying the Buddha’s kindness. If one generates the bodhicitta and practices the path of the Pure Land, this is called being a wise person who knows how to repay the Buddha’s kindness (and so forth).

Therefore, although those of the Two Vehicles abide on the stage of fruition, they do not equal even a ten-thousandth part of the merit possessed by an ordinary bodhisattva who has first generated the bodhicitta. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* asks: "Luo..."
The Han pratyekabuddha was one who had already detached from desire (*vītarāga*). There may also be ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) who have merely resolved to attain enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).
How can they be superior? The answer is: there are two kinds of bodhisattvas. The first practices the various *pāramitās*;

the second merely secretly resolves their mind and practices the bodhisattva path. Although their tasks are not yet accomplished, they can surpass those of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*). Why is this?
For example, although a crown prince has not yet ascended the throne, he surpasses all ministers who hold positions of rank, wealth, and nobility.
The *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra* states: "It is not difficult for those who have left the household life to resolve upon bodhicitta;
it is truly difficult for those living in the household to do so. Why? Because they are entangled by many adverse conditions. To resolve upon bodhicitta—
All the devas were greatly rejoiced and spoke these words: "We have now obtained a teacher of gods and humans.
The *Vinaya Sūtra* states: "If one first practices the Mahāyāna and observes the Bodhisattva precepts, should there be an offense in the morning, one ought to acknowledge the transgression;
yet by noon, if the bodhicitta remains uninterrupted, the aggregate of precepts (*śīlaskandha*) is perfected, and thus it is not considered a transgression. Furthermore—
If one commits an offense during the middle watch of the night, but the bodhicitta remains uninterrupted during the final watch, the aggregate of precepts (*śīlaskandha*) is perfected.

The *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* states: "If a person were to strike or mutilate all sentient beings throughout the great trichiliocosm, yet another person with an evil mind were to cause distress to one who has generated the bodhicitta, the latter's transgression would be far greater than the former."
Always delight in dwelling in an araṇya, rather than living among the multitude. When in a group, one must be careful of speech;
when alone, one must guard the mind. Stay far away from evil associates and follow the instructions of virtuous friends.
Let the body never be parted from the kāṣāya robe, let food be taken only in the proper bowl, and let not the hands release the yellow scrolls of scripture.
Do not take pleasure in reading secular books; do not let your eyes gaze upon women—seeing them is like encountering a venomous snake.
Do not sleep during the day unless ill; when you do sleep, you must lie on your right side.
Do not eat leftovers unless out of hunger; when eating, you must practice moderation. When resting, do not spread out fine carpets or bedding; even in sleep, do not indulge in laxity.

When sitting, one must never face west; when walking, one should simply look at the ground. In speech, one should always avoid frivolous laughter; when seeking the essentials, one should not be excessive.
When receiving offerings, divide them into three parts; it is not appropriate to accept them all, nor should one break them.
Do not accumulate many possessions, as this creates conditions that obstruct the Path. Furthermore, do not have a large retinue of followers.
Increasing pride, anger, and conceit—such are the various matters [that arise]. If a śramaṇa does not attend to these urgent primary duties, how can he be called a Buddhist?
Though receiving the fourfold offerings, he is like a fish swallowing a baited hook;
in the future he will surely have to repay his debts, and he shall have neither shame nor fear.
Regarding the term *araṇya*, it is translated here as "a place free from clamor.
Now, one who dwells in an *araṇya* naturally purifies the three karmas and thereby possesses immeasurable merit; thus, attaining the Way is not difficult. Therefore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
One who dwells in an araṇya achieves pure deportment, achieves unagitated sense faculties, and achieves the manifestation of the True Dharma (and so forth).
If one wishes to swiftly attain all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), why not delight in dwelling in an araṇya?
If this were not the case, then one ought to reside beforehand within the monastic community of a monastery; however, this is—

Originally indolent by nature, although he had not yet attained the ability to cultivate the Way independently, seeing others exert themselves with diligence, he felt ashamed and emulated them, never daring to be lax.
In all his movements and actions, even down to the morning gruel and midday meal, he followed the community entirely and never once violated the rules.
Consequently, his practice of the Path proceeded spontaneously as he became free from defilement and entered the ranks of the Śākyaputrīyas, as was customary.
Is this not what is meant by the saying: "When mugwort grows amidst hemp, it straightens itself without being propped up"?
Therefore, those who are indolent would do better to follow the crowd; be most careful not to wander idly among mountains and fields, indulging your passions in evil and wasting your time in vain.
One should regard this as a cause for regret and lamentation in future days. Furthermore, one must not seek comfort or fullness;
therefore, by the edge of mountain streams or on the shores of fishing villages, one builds a thatched hut to dwell and sustain one’s life, remaining distinct from the common laity.
They form alliances with like-minded individuals, addressing them as brothers or even as parents; there is no evil they will not commit.
Not only do they bring ruin upon their own conduct, but they also defile the pure Buddhist monasteries; their transgressions must surely be many.
Regarding the term "virtuous friend" (*kalyāṇamitra*): in the *Vinaya*, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "A virtuous friend is half of the holy life (*brahmacarya*);
it is by the power of a virtuous friend that practitioners are able to accomplish their goal. The Buddha replied, "It is the entirety of the holy life.
If one finds a virtuous companion and dwells together with them until reaching *nirvāṇa*, there is no task that cannot be accomplished.

Because it is accomplished, it is called the "complete holy life" (*brahmacarya*). Furthermore, the *Upatisapasina Sūtra* (Pai jing) says: "There are four kinds of friends: first, the flower-like friend;

this means they are placed on one's head when they are fresh, but discarded on the ground when they wither. They attach themselves when one is wealthy and noble, but abandon one when one is poor and destitute.

Second, the scale-like friend; this means they bow their heads when the object is heavy, but lift them up when the object is light. They show respect when there is something to give, but act with contempt when there is nothing to give. Third...

First, like a mountain friend: this refers to the birds and beasts that gather on a golden mountain; their feathers and fur are bathed in its radiance. It is noble for being able to bring glory to others, and one shares in the joy of its wealth and happiness.
Fourth, like the earth as a friend: this refers to the hundred grains and all material goods, upon which everyone depends.

Through bestowing, providing, and protecting, its kindness is profound, yet it does not seek merit. The *Caiguojing* (Sutra on Cause and Effect) states: "The Brahmin Udāyin was clever and possessed great wisdom."
King Śuddhodana commanded that [the youth] become a friend to the Prince. He addressed the Prince, saying: "A friend possesses three essential qualities:
first, when one sees a fault, they promptly offer counsel and admonition; second, seeing good deeds, they feel deep sympathetic joy; third, when one is in distress or peril, they do not abandon them.
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states: "One who possesses seven qualities becomes a true friend: first, performing what is difficult to do..."

1. To be able to act [for one's sake]; 2. To be able to give when it is difficult to give; 3. To be able to endure when it is difficult to endure; 4. To inform one another of secret matters; 5. To conceal one another’s faults; 6.
Not to abandon one another when encountering suffering; 7. Not to despise one another when they are impoverished. The *Gāthā on Friends* states that there are five qualities of a friend: 1.
Upon seeing them commit evil, to go to a secluded place to instruct, admonish, and stop them; 2. Regarding all urgent matters, one should...
1. Rush to provide rescue and protection. 2. Regarding the three types of private speech, one must not disclose them to others. 3. Always treat one another with respect and praise;

when there is good fortune, one should share it with others to some extent. 4. If one constantly harbors jealousy and arrogance, lacks self-restraint in mind, utters no righteous words, and takes evil people as friends, such a person is called a commoner.
The *Buddha-benxing-jing* (Sutra on the Buddha’s Past Deeds) says: The Buddha and [Nanda]...
[The Buddha] went to a fish market. The Buddha had Nanda take some small mats used for wrapping fish, hold them for a short while, and then discard them.
He then had him smell his hands and asked him about it. Nanda replied, "There is only a stench of raw fish. Again, they went to a perfume shop.

[The Buddha] had him take some paper used for wrapping perfumes, hold it in his cupped hands for a short while, and then discard it. He asked Nanda again. Nanda replied, "I only smell a fragrant scent. The Buddha...
He said to Nanda: "The manner in which good friends and evil friends influence one another through association is likewise so.
If one draws near to a good friend, one will certainly attain great renown (and so forth). As for an evil associate, it is not merely one who reviles, insults, strikes, or scolds me;
rather, it is one who sees me committing evil yet fails to admonish me, but instead rejoices in it and praises it, causing [that evil] to increase."
Even those who perform virtuous deeds for me, or those who respect, honor, and make offerings to me, are all evil friends. Therefore, Master Nanyue said:
"That the monastics and laypeople of the world hold me in high esteem, make offerings to me, and earnestly request that I preach—these are all instigated by evil Māras;
they are not spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), but rather evil associates (pāpamitra). They are like enemies feigning intimacy. How bitter! How bitter! [He said this] to the various kings.
The *kṣatriya* is also like this. "Select, select, select, select.
That which is called *kāṣāya* is named after its color; here it is called "discolored" (*huài-sè*). The *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states:
"Blue, yellow, red, black, and purple—these are all termed discolored. The commentary says: "It destroys the original white color because it contravenes the mind of attachment. It is also threefold.
This is the general designation for robes. As for the three robes: first is the *antarvāsa*, which has five strips; second is the *uttarāsaṅga*, which has seven strips;
third is the *saṃghāṭī*, which has nine strips. Furthermore, there are those with eleven strips up to twenty-five strips.

Regarding the methods for cutting and sewing them according to their respective lengths and widths, these are fully detailed in the *Zhangfu yi* (Ritual for Robes) and the *Liufu yi* (Ritual for the Six Garments).
As explained in the *Wutu* (Illustrations of Objects), the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states that when Śākyamuni Tathāgata made his vows before Ratnagarbha Buddha, he prayed:
"When I attain Buddhahood, my kāṣāya shall possess five kinds of merit. First, those who enter into my Dharma..."

First, those among the fourfold assembly who have committed grave offenses or hold wrong views, if they show reverence and respect for even a single thought-moment, will certainly receive the prediction of enlightenment within the Three Vehicles.
Second, if devas, nāgas, humans, or ghosts can respectfully honor even a small fragment of this *kāṣāya*, they shall immediately attain non-retrogression from the Three Vehicles.
Third, if any spirits, ghosts, or humans obtain even a piece of the *kāṣāya*, or even as little as four [inches]...

First, one will obtain sufficient food and drink. Second, if there are sentient beings who are in mutual conflict, by recollecting the power of the *kāṣāya*, they will immediately give rise to a heart of compassion. Third, if one is amidst an army in battle, by respectfully honoring even a small portion of the *kāṣāya*, [one will be protected].

Fourth, if there are sentient beings who are mutually antagonistic, by recollecting the power of the *kāṣāya*, they will immediately give rise to a heart of compassion. Fifth, if one is in a military array, by reverently honoring even a small fragment of the *kāṣāya*.
One will always prevail over others. If my *kāṣāya* lacked these five powers, I would be deceiving the hundred thousand Buddhas.
It is said that if a dragon obtains even a single thread of the *kāṣāya* and hangs it above its gate, it will be spared from the calamity of the *garuḍa*.
The *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra* states that those who don the *kāṣāya* shall, from the time of Maitreya Buddha until the time of Ruci Buddha, attain [liberation].
They enter *nirvāṇa* without remainder. Chan Master Yongming Shou said: "As for the *kāṣāya*, it is called the Banner of Liberation.
The Buddhas of the ten directions rely upon it to attain the fruits of the Way; the fourfold assembly and non-human beings uphold it to obtain peace and security.
It manifests pure leisure and destroys feverish afflictions. If it were not the supreme garment for transcending the dust of the world, how could [it fulfill these functions]?"
It can rescue those lost on the path; its merit is not in vain. One’s admiration for it is inexhaustible (and so forth).
Regarding the "receptacle" (*yingqi*): in Sanskrit, it is called *pātra*. The Buddha ordained that clay or iron is superior [for its material].
The dimensions of its body and the relative excellence of its merits are as illustrated in the citation from the *Six Requisites Diagram* (*Liubuwutu*). [The eighteen requisites of a bhikṣu...]
Among all things, the *kāṣāya* and the alms bowl are the most urgent necessities. They are like the two wings of a bird or the two wheels of a chariot;

it is impossible to proceed if either one is missing. The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states: "If a bhikṣu receives offerings from others while lacking either his *kāṣāya* or his alms bowl, he incurs the 'ox-head' offense for a thousand kalpas. Therefore, a bhikṣu’s *kāṣāya* and alms bowl must always accompany his person.
One must not be separated from it for even a moment.

As for the term "yellow scrolls," these are the Buddhist scriptures. As previously demonstrated, during the time of Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty, the Buddhist scriptures and the Daoist scriptures were burned together as a test;
the Daoist scriptures turned to ash, while the Buddhist scriptures were not consumed by fire, being merely blackened by smoke and turned yellow.
Thereafter, those who produced the scriptures indicated this by dyeing the paper yellow. Indeed, among the companions one finds in leisure, none can compare to Buddhist books.

What is taught therein consists entirely of the causes and fruits of the practices of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, their immeasurable merits, and their instruction of sentient beings—restraining evil, performing good, abandoning the heterodox, and returning to the orthodox, through various causes and conditions.

These are words of truth. If you can read the text to seek its meaning, admire and look up to the sages and worthies, and feel empathy for yourself and others—maintaining such a state of mind as you pass the days—then the various conditions [of worldly distraction] will gradually subside, body and mind will naturally become pure, and the profound realm may be reached.
Do not be negligent and let the bright days pass in vain. For those who are unable to read the scriptures with self-discipline, they should seek...
One should inquire of those who possess knowledge and study according to one's capacity; even a single day’s lesson of a single phrase is acceptable.

Thus, two days for two phrases, and so on up to ten days for ten phrases, or a hundred days for a hundred phrases—if one does not fail in this daily practice, then one's understanding will not fail to be broad.
However, if one is sluggish such that one does not comprehend what is heard once, then one should hear it a second and a third time.

Even hearing [the Dharma] ten times, what would there be that one could not penetrate? Although one may not yet have fully mastered the profound and subtle meanings, how can this not be different from those days of being entirely ignorant?
By thus gradually practicing and studying, one penetrates the wondrous principles and enters the Gate of Ambrosia;
is this not a source of great joy? Thus, it is still superior to the ignorance of birds or the empty, blind meditation of the blind; is it not surely more excellent than these?
Those who spend their entire days in empty talk and frivolous laughter are merely indolent and lacking in resolve.
If one were truly able to apply effort and study diligently, it has never happened that such a person would fail to achieve understanding.
Regarding what is called "external books" (*bāhya-śāstra*): these refer to the Vedic scriptures, the collected writings of various schools, and so forth—vain discourses that lead people astray.
Thus, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "Furthermore, those who compose secular literary works and praise external books—such persons as these, one must not associate with.
Moreover, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "One who studies external treatises is like one cutting with a knife."
"Mud. Mud accomplishes nothing, yet it daily erodes the blade. It is further said: "One who reads non-Buddhist classics is like one looking at the sun;

it causes the eyes to grow dim. The *Zhi guan fu xing ji* states: "Reading the *Spring and Autumn Annals* and reciting the *Zuo zhuan*, one spends the entire day with the mind wandering among battle arrays and the mouth expounding upon deceitful stratagems.
Such a person is far removed from aiding the Buddha-dharma" (and so forth). As for Zhuangzi, Laozi, and Confucius...
The Way of Mencius, though not a discourse on the ultimate truth, extensively propagates benevolence and righteousness;

therefore, it serves as a gateway for beginners entering the Path and may be consulted from time to time. Why is this? The *Vinaya* states that the Buddha permitted bhikṣus to study external treatises, provided they spent two of the three daily periods—namely, the first and second parts—in reciting the Buddha’s sūtras, and studied external works only during the evening.
It is recorded that within the Jetavana there was a library where the written records of the great trichiliocosm were kept.

The Buddha permitted the bhikṣus to read them all extensively for the purpose of subduing the non-Buddhists; however, he did not allow them to rely upon those views, nor did he permit them to neglect their spiritual practice out of a fondness for such learning.
Regarding the statement that one’s eyes do not gaze upon women: women are the root from which obstacles arise, both in the mundane world and in the supramundane.

As for mundane obstacles: even those in the rank of a prince may, because of them, bring disorder to their state; high ministers and great officers may, because of them, fail to govern their households;
and scholars and commoners may, because of them, lose their integrity. How much more so for those who wish to transcend [the world]?
How could one not be fearful and cautious regarding this world? Furthermore, the afflictions of sentient beings have greed and desire as their root.
If one beholds female beauty, a lustful mind suddenly arises; it blazes so fiercely that it cannot be restrained. By means of various expedients, one eventually commits transgressions.
Once touched, the mind finds no satiety and never withdraws or desists, like a moth rushing into a flame, beyond all control.
It is also like an iron hammer cast into the mud; there will be no time of emergence for it, and all manner of afflictions and hardships arise from it.
For immeasurable kalpas, one transmigrates through birth and death, finding no gateway to enter the Way.

Therefore, within the various scriptural teachings, our Buddha, the Tathāgata, has sternly rebuked it, and the patriarchs of successive generations have likewise discussed and recorded it in their commentaries.
It is likewise so. In the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Prince Mañjuśrīkumārabhūta (Videhamati) spoke most urgently against [attachment to] women.
Therefore, those who wish to cross the river of craving must distance themselves from all women.

If there is a compelling reason and one cannot help but see them, one should regard them as if seeing a venomous snake or avoiding a pit of fire. In the past, the Patriarch Qingliang gazed at her through a curtain.
Mother, how much less could ordinary women look directly upon him?
As for sleeping during the day: among all forms of negligence, this is most improper. The Tathāgata admonished the bhikṣus not even to sleep at night, let alone to sleep during the day;
it is likewise unsuitable according to the ways of the world. Thus, Zhongni rebuked Zai.
I said: "Rotten wood cannot be carved" (and so forth). If one is afflicted by illness and must lie down, one should lie on the right side with the body touching the ground;
one must not lie like a corpse. Regarding leftover food: when the Tathāgata first established the precepts for bhikṣus, they were to eat only once a day.
Later, because Rāhula was young and had left the household life, he cried from hunger. To stop his crying, the Buddha provisionally permitted [the practice].
Regarding the morning gruel: Later generations of bhikṣus, seeing this opening of the door for the morning gruel and the midday meal, took them to be the constant rule.

Consequently, all times outside of these two periods were considered "leftover food" (vighasa). If one misses the morning or midday meals and obtains food at an improper time (vikāla), it is best not to eat;
however, even if one does eat, there is no harm. Why? Because if one is emaciated by hunger and lacks strength, the work of the Path (mārga-karma) will be difficult to accomplish. Thus it ends.
The *Lun* (Treatise) states: "If one does not moderate their diet, it is easy to fall ill. Furthermore, the *Bowuzhi* (Records of the Wide World) says:

"Those who eat a variety of foods are the locus where a hundred ailments and demonic influences converge. The less one eats, the more lucid the mind becomes; the more one eats, the more the body is impaired. Therefore, one must not exceed moderation in eating."
Regarding those who do not use mats or bedding while sleeping: for all practitioners of the Way who fail to achieve success, it is primarily due to the affliction of the "sleep-demon.
Even when using ice beds or snow blankets, one does not perceive their approach until they have arrived; they leave a person devoid of strength.

How much more so when thick mats and bedding are spread out, and one lies down with legs extended—how then can such a state be resisted? Thus, one falls into deep sleep and mental dullness. Just as...
Like a dead person, one does not know the dawn of night or the dusk of day; what leisure is there to restrain the mind and cultivate merit?
Therefore, when a bhikṣu lies down to sleep, he should simply lay his robe across him and rest his head on his clenched fists, never indulging in negligence.

Having rested for a short while, he should immediately rise to rinse his mouth and wash. Then, according to his practice, he should engage in meditation, recitation, prostration, and mindfulness without missing the proper time, throughout his life.
It is not yet finished. Thus, although one has not yet accomplished the Way, such a person is called a "virtuous man" (śiṣṭa). As for sitting without turning one’s back toward the west:

formerly, the ancestral master Uisang of Silla sought exclusively for rebirth in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang); throughout his life, he never sat with his back to the west. Among his disciples...
There was a bhikṣu who had committed an offense. In accordance with the Dharma, he was expelled from the community and departed.
Wandering through other regions, he looked up with longing to his teacher and fashioned an image of him to carry upon his back. When the teacher heard of this, he summoned him and said:
"If you truly remember me, consider that throughout my entire life I have never sat with my back turned to the west; the image should do likewise. Thereupon, he caused the image to face westward.
The seated image then turned its body of its own accord to sit facing west. The Master deemed this auspicious and pardoned their transgressions, restoring them to the community.
Therefore, when seeking the West, one should emulate this example.

Furthermore, when walking, one should look only at the ground and walk while single-mindedly recollecting the Buddha; one must not let the eyes wander left and right to cause the mind to become distracted, as is the manner of those who play.
How much more so during the three seasons of spring, summer, and autumn—how could it be permissible to trample and kill tiny insects and thus commit sins without cause?
Moreover, when speaking with others, one must not laugh mockingly or utter false words in a loud voice.
One should grasp only the essentials and avoid unnecessary complexity. Thus, even the non-Buddhist classics state: "The gentleman uses few words;
if he has something to say, he reflects three times before speaking, so that his speech is free from superfluous branches."
Regarding the threefold division of the offerings received: the *Vinaya* states that if a bhikṣu accepts a gift from a donor, he must divide it into three parts:
one part for the Three Jewels, one part for his fellow practitioners and for the poor and sick, and one part for his own use.
Thus, one has already perfected both compassion and reverence, being able to repay the kindness of the donor and becoming a true son of the Śākya.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu must not accumulate excessive personal possessions; if he possesses much wealth, he will spend his days and nights calculating its value.
Some are preoccupied with schemes for gain; some fear being robbed by others; some fear being seized by the king; and some fear loss due to water or fire.
Holding such thoughts in their minds, they do not forget them even for a short time. How could they have the leisure to mindfulness of the Buddha or recite the sutras?

Even if they do recite or contemplate, their minds are intermingled with various distracting conditions and lack single-minded concentration; it is evident that their spiritual achievements will not be accomplished. For this reason, the Tathāgata admonished the bhikṣus:
Apart from the three robes, one must not keep any extra clothing. Furthermore, one should not have many attendants.
Before attaining the Way, all such attendants cause much harm to oneself and provide no benefit whatsoever. Why is this? Arrogance, anger, and pride grow because of them.
These three mental states are great obstacles within the Dharma; therefore, the Sūtra says that for a practitioner who cultivates the mind—
One should always delight in seclusion and dwell alone in quietude. To possess many things in abundance constitutes the work of Māra.
As for the "four requisites," they are food and drink, clothing, bedding, and medicine.
When there is a donor who, for the sake of seeking merit, reduces their own portion for supporting wife and children to give as an offering to the Saṃgha, yet the Saṃgha lacks moral discipline—
Furthermore, if one lacks proper dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*) and neglects meditation, recitation, and devotional mindfulness, then even the offerings of the faithful cannot be properly digested;
how much less can it be said that they will bring merit? In such a case, one will inevitably have to repay this debt in the future—how could one not stand in awe of this?

Moreover, there are many ways to repay debts and requite kindness, making them difficult to describe definitively. Now, following the teachings of the sutras, I shall briefly indicate three grades, namely: light, medium, and heavy.

[The category of] the middling. What is meant by "light"? If a monk, though knowing cause and effect, lacks dignified deportment and is unable to cultivate his mind and practice according to the Dharma, thereby acting in opposition to the intentions of the donor and failing to accord with principle in his affairs, he shall later become a slave or servant to that patron’s household to manage their domestic affairs, doing so without weariness or indolence in heart. What is meant by the "middling"? If a monk merely [speaks] with his mouth...

To speak of cause and effect while one’s mind is discordant—with the giver, the recipient, and the object given—arbitrarily discriminating between self and other, debating right and wrong, and failing to give rise to even a single thought of gratitude for kindness received:
such a person will later become a camel, a donkey, an ox, or a horse, pulling carts, plowing fields, carrying loads, and transporting goods;
enduring hunger, thirst, and the lash of the whip without shrinking from toil and suffering. What does this mean?

This is grave. If the Sangha is ignorant of cause and effect and constantly gives rise to greed, then even when a donor provides a thousand pieces of wealth and offers various provisions of a hundred flavors, they will not consider it sufficient.

Like the ocean that receives all flowing waters, they will later be reborn as pigs, sheep, geese, or ducks, offering their own bodies for consumption; this is the third way of repaying the donor's kindness. Thus it is said.

Repaying debts does not end with a single lifetime; it follows the frequency and proximity of the favors received, spanning two, three, or even ten, a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, or a million lifetimes—it cannot be definitively determined.
Such cause and effect follow one another like a form and its shadow, without the slightest deviation.
For instance, Master Yun Guang could not escape the retribution of being reborn as an ox, and so too was the case for the Silla bhikṣu.

It transformed into tree shoots. Such manifest proofs are too numerous to record in full; they are detailed in the *Zhulin zhuan* (Biographies of Pearl Forest) and the *Li Guizu zhuan* (Biographies of Li Guizu).
Therefore, in such scriptures as the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, the Buddha admonished the bodhisattvas, saying:
"It would be better to have one's body cut and pierced by hundreds of thousands of swords and spears than ever to break the precepts while receiving the offerings of faithful donors."

Regarding the robes one is given: it would be better to swallow hot iron balls for hundreds of thousands of kalpas than ever to receive food or drink offered by a faithful donor with a mouth that has broken the precepts.

Alas! If one considers this admonition, then how could we—who are shaven-headed men devoid of the precepts—allow ourselves to be heedless and indulge our passions, accepting the offerings of the faithful at will? Therefore, one must indeed...

At the time of eating, one should measure the source from which the food comes and assess whether one’s own virtues are complete or deficient to determine if one is worthy of the offering. One should guard the mind against faults, making the abandonment of greed and other such defilements the primary principle.
One should regard the food as wholesome medicine for treating the withered body, accepting this meal solely for the sake of accomplishing the work of the Path.
Again, he reflects: "My mouth is like a furnace; whether it be sandalwood or filth, I burn whatever comes my way.

Therefore, I must neither rejoice in nor loathe what is refined or coarse. Thus, Master Changlu said: "If one does not eliminate extravagance in food and drink, when will the time of liberation arrive?
Furthermore, regarding clothing, he reflects: "It is intended only to conceal the ugliness of the physical form; it is not for the sake of adornment."
To have a beautiful body, why must one insist on taking what is fine and light while discarding what is coarse and heavy?

For this reason, those of superior faculties who are resolved upon the Way forget the necessities of their bodies and mouths; they simply boil *lí* (brackish grass) to satisfy hunger and wear fine grass to cover their forms.
Those of middling capacity constantly practice begging for food, wearing only the three robes made of a hundred patches. As for those of inferior capacity, they may not [attain such purity].
It is so. One must certainly rely on the conditions of almsgiving to survive; yet the debt of that donor’s kindness is no small matter. Therefore, one ought to receive it with moderation and measure.
Coarse vegetables and simple food are difficult to digest, so one cannot be provided entirely with fine rice. A garment of coarse cloth is also quite acceptable.
What need is there for silk, brocade, or fine gauze? Why is this so? Exquisite flavors and rare delicacies shorten one’s lifespan;
expensive and ornate garments diminish one’s merit. If lifespan and merit are not yet complete, how can the work of the Path be accomplished?

Therefore, our Greatly Awakened One, the Benevolent One, abandoned the golden wheel-turning kingdom to enter the mountains; his food consisted of nothing more than a single grain of wheat and a single grain of hemp, and his clothing was but coarse deerskin.
By performing such difficult practices and ascetic austerities, one achieves unsurpassed Bodhi. I announce this universally to all students who have newly begun their training:
look up to the lofty character of our Original Teacher; do not be attached to the nourishment of body and mouth, but diligently cultivate the merits of meditative concentration and wisdom.
Ascend quickly to the gate of liberation and first rescue those who have received your kindness. This is called knowing gratitude and repaying it. Why should you worry?
The toil of repaying debts.
These many matters as described above are scattered throughout various sutras and treatises; now they are gathered here into concise verses, wherein the meaning of an entire lifetime is condensed.
It is like a single drop of water from the ocean, yet it contains the flavor of all its hundred rivers.
Having once tasted and known the various flavors, let no one among the students treat this lightly;
now there is nowhere to rest. Although one may have received the rank of a monk, if one examines their conduct, it is clear that the category of precepts (*śīla-skandha*) is lacking;

meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is lacking; recitation and mindfulness (*svādhyāya-smṛti*) are lacking; ritual repentance (*pūjā-vidhi*) is lacking; and the practice of giving (*dāna*) is lacking.
Down to even the smallest good, there is not a single thing practiced; as for all manner of evils, there is not one that is not committed.

How can you feel no shame before the Buddhas and devas? The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "One who cannot save oneself from illness, yet seeks to save those who are ill—should one who conceals their own faults while wishing to reform the faults of others not also be a person to be ashamed of? Indeed.
Now, I have merely taken up the principle of saving others before one has saved oneself.

I have wandered through the mountains and fields and reached the capital cities, where I have observed those who have shaved their heads and donned the black robes; they are as numerous as bamboo and reeds, with the exception of those of middle or superior capacity.
As for the remaining base and ignorant folk, the deeds they perform are truly shameful.

There may be some bhikṣus who cannot even understand secular documents, let alone claim to comprehend the meaning of the Buddha’s sutras. Because they lack the merit of past lives, they are now destitute;
finding it difficult to sustain their livelihood, they worry about the expenses of maintaining their own bodies and mouths, and thus falsely rely on Buddhist services to [support themselves]. Both...

In groups of twos and fives, they wander from house to house throughout the village, begging in a pitiful manner; they harbor only the desire to take much for themselves, never considering the merit it brings to others.
Once they have gathered their wealth, they squander it without restraint, claiming they are performing superior deeds—this is the karma that creates hungry ghosts.

Furthermore, there may be bhikṣus who merely memorize texts; having mastered only one or two sūtras, they recite them according to the words while remaining ignorant of their underlying meaning and intent. Moreover—
Having heard and witnessed the events from the beginning to the end of Śākyamuni Buddha’s entire life, some individuals claim to be Dharma masters;

yet they preach the Dharma with impurity, deceiving and deluding the masses, and unworthily accepting the offerings of the faithful without any sense of shame or remorse—thereby creating the karma for rebirth as an animal.

Or there are those who merely assume the name of "Chan monks," wearing the *kāṣāya* robe and *saṃghāṭī*, carrying a staff and gourd-bowl; outwardly they appear to have forgotten all worldly concerns, yet inwardly they possess no true virtue.

They have not yet perfected their meditative practice; they merely cling to the *gong'an* (public cases) of the ancients and do not refrain from disparaging the Mahāyāna sūtras (thereby creating the karma for the Avīci Hell).
Or there are those who leave the household life to study the Way based on Chan and the Teachings;

as soon as they enter the gate, they fail to exhaustively fathom the profound and subtle principles of Chan and the Teachings, each giving rise to deluded attachments and further destroying one another (thereby creating the karma for the Hell of Contentious Discourse). Or there are bhikṣus who violate...
The Buddha’s prohibitions on the Dharma: engaging in business and usury, possessing vast wealth, or relying on the power of kings, dukes, and high ministers;
being arrogant due to one's own riches and strength to look down upon others who are poor and weak; being greedy and lustful, addicted to alcohol; praising and reciting secular texts;
befriending worldly people and harmonizing with them in song; or delighting in various entertainments, chess, gambling, lutes, harps, flutes, and pipes.
Unwholesome dharmas—thus, indulging their passions, there is no evil they do not commit (thereby forming karma for the three miserable realms).

Alas! How can it be said that these people do not know of the retribution of good and evil karma? Because the desire for gain and profit is strong, they act upon it regardless. Even the external scriptures say:

"If one punishes according to the crime, there will be none who are spared. Why then do they not fear this? For this reason, even when dwelling in the mountains and wilds, they cannot avoid the reproach of being like farmers or woodcutters.
To frequent the City God’s temple is to frequently incur the censure of high officials. For this reason, it endangers the Dharma;
one must not even cast a sidelong glance at such a thing. Indeed, the Dharma does not propagate itself; its propagation depends on people. If people are incapable, how can the Dharma endure for long?
In the past, the Wei Emperor destroyed the Great Dharma because, at that time, the śramaṇas violated the Buddha’s teachings.
Regarding the precepts: it is because of much indulgence in negligence that one invites calamity upon oneself, after which the king merely imposes it.
One must take this as a warning. Observing the current situation, it is almost like that world; how perilous, how perilous!
Although this humble monk lacks intelligence, out of great apprehension and fear, I have uttered these reckless words. I entreat you, virtuous sirs, not to say—
The words of a madman are not worthy of belief. Behold that clear mirror; let each uphold their own resolve.

By using the dharma as a plug to dam the sea of birth and death, one delivers both oneself and others. Transmitting it from one to another in succession so that the dharma does not fall, its benefit is vast indeed.
Furthermore, those of antiquity valued the dharma and did not take [the status of] the person into account, just as the Heavenly Emperor bowed to a beast.
The Master said: "When I requested verses from the ghost on Mount Himavat, if even a single word or phrase was beneficial to me, how could the faults and evils of the Master affect me?
It is like gold within a foul-smelling bag; one does not discard the gold because of the stench of the bag."

Moreover, what is recorded here is not based on mere conjecture; it consists entirely of the words of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. Those who come here should examine this in detail. An external tradition says:
"To know a single feather of a phoenix is sufficient; to know a single thread of brocade is complete. It further says: "As for a tree of girth enough to embrace with both arms..."
A journey of a thousand li begins with a single hair-tip; the long road starts beneath one's feet. It is the same for those who study the Buddha:
if one peruses this verse, one has already dipped a finger into the teachings of this era and has taken the first step toward the practice of the five stages.
The wise should contemplate this and keep it in mind; do not treat it lightly, and do not be negligent.
*Verses on the Life and Deeds of Śākyamuni Tathāgata*, Scroll Lower (End).
The Great Master Nāgārjuna, the Founder of Tiantai, said: "Those who have heard [the teachings] but lack wisdom do not understand the true nature of reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*)."
For example, as one with eyes sees nothing in great darkness, so too one who possesses wisdom but lacks extensive learning does not know the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
For example, as a lamp sheds no light in the midst of great brightness, so too that which is spoken should be accepted by one who possesses both learning and wisdom;
one who lacks both learning and wisdom is called a "human-bodied ox. Now there is the Elder Pūrṇa...

He entrusted himself early on to the fourth-generation successor of the White Lotus Society, the State Preceptor Zhenjing, the Chan Master Juehai Yuanming Foyin Jingzhao, the Grand Overseer of the Buddhist Teachings, and settled beneath his hall. He shaved his head and donned the monastic robes, receiving the Dharma name Yunmo.
His mastery of the textual meanings of his school was thorough; he participated in the selection for the monastic examinations and ranked among the upper tier.
Having attained the reputation of being a master of mountain caves and grottoes as described above, he walked with high distinction upon the paths of fame;

yet all at once, he cast it aside like worn-out sandals. He then traveled to sacred mountains and sublime sites such as Mount Kimgang and Mount Wutai, eventually reaching Mount Shixing where he established a single hermitage and remained there for a long time.
There, he spent his days reciting the Lotus Sutra, chanting the name of Amitābha, painting Buddhist images, and copying scriptures.

I have been engaged in this for nearly twenty years. With my remaining strength, I have searched through Buddhist scriptures and ancestral texts to compose a verse account of the deeds of our Original Teacher, along with annotations, totaling two fascicles. This is intended to enlighten the ignorant; its benefit is indeed vast. Alas!

The kalpas of formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness of this Sahā world are of such immense duration, and the lifespans and fortunes across the three realms and five destinies vary so greatly in quality.
The distinctions between suffering and happiness; the Tathāgata’s skillful means in manifesting the four lands and three bodies according to the capacities of beings;

the chronological sequence of the teachings given during the five periods; the various sections of the sūtras regarding the partial and complete, the biased and perfect, the original and the trace, and the provisional and the real;
furthermore, the flourishing or decline of the remaining Dharma after his parinirvāṇa, its geographical spread, and the methods for later students to practice and enter the Way.
The principles of these skillful means are like a bright mirror set upon its stand; there is not even a hair’s breadth of deviation.
It can truly be said that what our Patriarch spoke of—namely, "that which is spoken should be received with clarity"—is manifest here. How excellent! How unprecedented!
As for the style of its prose, I revere it without the slightest reservation. Written on the eighth day of the second month in the third year of the Tianli era, the Gengwu year.
Śramaṇa Qiba of the White Lotus Society at Mount Wande.
